segments.label: §72, de source block1
segments.text: Ein Wort ist ein Laut, der einen Begriff bezeichnet.

segments.label: §72, de source block2
segments.text: Es liegt also in dem Wort allemal Einheit des Lauts, die bei verbundenen durch den Accent bewirkt wird, und Einheit des Begriffs.

segments.label: §72, de source block3
segments.text: Das einfache Wort ist das wahre Individuum in der Sprache.

segments.label: §72, de source block4
segments.text: Denn es enthält vollständig die ganze Verstandeshandlung der Sprache, es ist sogar selbst die Form, in welcher der Geist das in seine Subjectivitaet verwandelte Object wieder, als solches, aus sich hinausstellt (39.); dasjenige aber, was herauskommt, wenn man es selbst wieder zergliedert, die Sylbe und der Buchstabe, ist nicht mehr Sprache, sondern nur Element derselben.

segments.label: §72, de source block5
segments.text: Alle, auch die zusammengesetzten Wörter sind die Bestandtheile, der Stoff der Rede, und in dem Wörtervorrath einer Sprache liegt also der gesammte Gedankenstoff einer Nation.

segments.label: §72, de source block6
segments.text: Das Wort theilt die ganze, im Vorigen entwickelte Natur der Sprache, es hat dieselbe Objectivitaet und Subjectivitaet (40.), übt die gleiche Macht auf den Menschen aus (42.), und ist ebenso seiner Freiheit unterworfen (51.), es bildet die Gegenstände zu der eignen ideellen Welt, die in der Sprache überhaupt an die Stelle der wirklichen tritt (39.).

segments.label: §72, de source block7
segments.text: Die eigenthümliche Auffassung der Dinge durch die Sprache liegt vorzüglich darin, dass die individuelle Subjectivitaet, sich immer gleich bleibend, alle Bestandtheile der Sprache auf dieselbe Weise nimmt und behandelt, an jeden sich anschliesst, und sie stammt mehr aus dem ideellen, als dem materiellen Theil der Sprachen, mehr aus der durch sie gegebenen Vorstellungsart, als aus den in ihr gebrauchten Lauten.

segments.label: §72, de source block8
segments.text: Die Wörter, die in wenig veränderten Tönen, und bestimmte Gegenstände bezeichnend, von Geschlechten zu Geschlechten und Nationen zu Nationen übergehen, können daher nur wenig sichtlich diese Eigenthümlichkeit an sich tragen, die sich erst in ihrem Gebrauche, und in der Art, wie sie sich gegenseitig ergänzen, beschränken und bestimmen, offenbart.

segments.label: §72, de source block9
segments.text: Wo also, wie bei den Sprachen ungebildeter Nationen, dieser Gebrauch nur aus dürftigen Sprachproben bekannt ist, da reicht die blosse, eben darum auch unvollständige Wörterkenntniss nicht hin die Eigenthümlichkeit der Sprache gerade von ihrer wichtigsten Seite zu ergründen.

segments.label: §72, sol source block1
segments.text: A word is a sound that designates a concept.

segments.label: §72, sol source block2
segments.text: A word therefore always has unity of sound, which is produced by accent where sounds are combined, and unity of concept.

segments.label: §72, sol source block3
segments.text: The simple word is the true individual in language.

segments.label: §72, sol source block4
segments.text: For it contains in full the entire operation of the understanding in language. It is even itself the form in which the mind sets outside itself again, as an object, what it has transformed into its own subjectivity (§39). What one obtains by analysing the word itself, however, the syllable and the letter, consists merely of elements of language and is no longer language.

segments.label: §72, sol source block5
segments.text: All words, including compound words, are the constituents and material of speech, and the vocabulary of a language therefore contains the entire material of a nation's thought.

segments.label: §72, sol source block6
segments.text: The word shares in the whole nature of language as developed above. It has the same objectivity and subjectivity (§40), exercises the same power over the human being (§42), and is likewise subject to human freedom (§51). It shapes objects into an ideal world of its own, which in language as a whole takes the place of the actual world (§39).

segments.label: §72, sol source block7
segments.text: The distinctive way in which language apprehends things consists chiefly in this, that individual subjectivity, remaining constant, takes and treats all the constituents of language in the same way and attaches itself to each of them. This way of apprehending things arises more from the ideal than from the material part of languages, more from the mode of presentation they provide than from the sounds used in them.

segments.label: §72, sol source block8
segments.text: Words that pass from generation to generation and from nation to nation, with little change in sound and designating definite objects, can therefore bear this distinctive character only faintly on their face. It emerges only in their use and in the way they supplement, limit, and determine one another.

segments.label: §72, sol source block9
segments.text: Where this use is known only from scanty samples, as with the languages of uncultivated nations, mere knowledge of the words, which for that very reason is also incomplete, is insufficient to get to the bottom of what is distinctive about the language in its most important respect.

segments.label: §72, muse source block1
segments.text: A word is a sound which designates a concept.

segments.label: §72, muse source block2
segments.text: There always lies in the word, therefore, unity of sound — which, where sounds are combined, is effected by the accent — and unity of concept.

segments.label: §72, muse source block3
segments.text: The simple word is the true individual in language.

segments.label: §72, muse source block4
segments.text: For it contains completely the whole act of the understanding performed by language; it is indeed itself the form in which the mind places outside itself again, as such, the Object transformed into its subjectivity (39.); but that which results when it is itself in turn analysed — the syllable and the letter — is no longer language, but only an element of it.

segments.label: §72, muse source block5
segments.text: All words, even compound words, are the constituents, the material of discourse, and in the stock of words of a language there therefore lies the entire thought-material of a nation.

segments.label: §72, muse source block6
segments.text: The word shares the whole nature of language developed in what precedes; it has the same objectivity and subjectivity (40.), exercises the same power over man (42.), and is equally subject to his freedom (51.); it forms objects into its own ideal world, which in language in general takes the place of the real one (39.).

segments.label: §72, muse source block7
segments.text: The distinctive apprehension of things through language lies principally in this, that individual subjectivity, always remaining the same as itself, takes and treats all the constituents of language in the same way, attaching itself to each one; and it derives more from the ideal than from the material part of languages, more from the mode of presentation given through language than from the sounds used in it.

segments.label: §72, muse source block8
segments.text: Words which pass, in little-changed tones and designating determinate objects, from generation to generation and from nation to nation can therefore bear this distinctiveness visibly upon them only to a slight extent; it is revealed only in their use and in the way in which they mutually supplement, limit, and determine one another.

segments.label: §72, muse source block9
segments.text: Where, therefore, as with the languages of uncultivated nations, this use is known only from scanty specimens of language, mere knowledge of words, incomplete for that very reason, does not suffice to fathom the distinctiveness of the language precisely in its most important aspect.

segments.label: §72, claude source block1
segments.text: A word is a sound that designates a concept.

segments.label: §72, claude source block2
segments.text: In the word, therefore, there is always unity of sound, which where sounds are combined is brought about by the accent, and unity of concept.

segments.label: §72, claude source block3
segments.text: The simple word is the true individual in language.

segments.label: §72, claude source block4
segments.text: For it contains completely the whole act of the understanding that belongs to language; indeed it is itself the form in which the mind sets the object that it has transformed into its subjectivity outside itself again, as object (39.); but what results when the word itself is analysed in turn, the syllable and the letter, is no longer language, but only an element of it.

segments.label: §72, claude source block5

segments.label: §72, claude source block6

segments.label: §72, claude source block7

segments.label: §72, claude source block8
segments.text: The words which, in little-altered tones and designating definite objects, pass from generation to generation and from nation to nation can therefore bear this peculiarity only in a scarcely visible way; it reveals itself only in their use, and in the way in which they mutually complete, limit and determine one another.

segments.label: §72, claude source block9
segments.text: Where, therefore, as with the languages of uncultivated nations, this use is known only from meagre specimens of the language, the mere knowledge of words, which is for that very reason also incomplete, does not suffice to fathom the peculiarity of the language precisely on its most important side.

segments.label: §73, de source block1
segments.text: Die Anzahl der in einer Sprache möglichen Wörter beruht auf der Anzahl der in ihr möglichen Sylben (62.a.) und den besondren in ihr für die Wortbildung herrschenden Regeln und Gewohnheiten (62.b.).

segments.label: §73, de source block2
segments.text: Bestimmen lässt sich dieselbe füglich nur da, wo sie verhältnissmässig gering ist, und durch die Sprache ganz oder grösstentheils wirklich erschöpft wird.

segments.label: §73, de source block3
segments.text: Dies kann beinahe nur bei den Sprachen mit einsylbigen Wörtern der Fall seyn.

segments.label: §73, sol source block1
segments.text: The number of possible words in a language depends on the number of possible syllables in it (§62.a) and on its particular rules and habits of word formation (§62.b).

segments.label: §73, sol source block2
segments.text: This number can readily be determined only where it is relatively small and the language actually makes use of all or most of the possibilities.

segments.label: §73, sol source block3
segments.text: This can occur almost exclusively in languages with monosyllabic words.

segments.label: §73, muse source block1
segments.text: The number of words possible in a language depends on the number of syllables possible in it (62.a.) and on the special rules and customs governing word-formation in it (62.b.).

segments.label: §73, muse source block2
segments.text: It can properly be determined only where it is relatively small and is wholly or for the most part actually exhausted by the language.

segments.label: §73, muse source block3
segments.text: This can be the case almost only with languages with monosyllabic words.

segments.text: The number of words possible in a language depends on the number of syllables possible in it (62.a.) and on the particular rules and habits that prevail in it for word-formation (62.b.).

segments.label: §73, claude source block3
segments.text: This can be the case almost only in the languages with monosyllabic words.

segments.label: §74, de source block1
segments.text: Wenn man aber diese Sprachen als eine eigne Gattung zusammenfasst, so muss man wohl verstehen, in welcher Art dies geschieht.

segments.label: §74, de source block2
segments.text: Rein factisch kann diese Abtheilung nicht genannt werden.

segments.label: §74, de source block3
segments.text: Denn ein grosser Theil aller, auch noch so vielsylbiger Sprachen lässt sich auf einsylbige Wurzeln durch Zergliederung zurückführen, und geht man in Gedanken auf den Ursprung der Sprachen zurück, so ist das Natürlichste, dem einfachen Begriff auch nur einen einfachen Laut zu widmen.

segments.label: §74, de source block4
segments.text: Doch darf man dies nicht so verstehen, als müsste nothwendig jedes Stammwort einsylbig seyn.

segments.label: §74, de source block5
segments.text: Denn in unsrer Sprachuntersuchung, in der wir nie bis auf den Anfang zurückzugehen vermögen, ist der Begriff des Stammworts selbst nur ein Verhältnissbegriff, und jede unsrer Sprachen kann mit vielen mehrsylbigen Wörtern, neben einsylbigen, begonnen haben.

segments.label: §74, de source block6
segments.text: Dagegen besitzen auch die einsylbigen Sprachen diese Eigenschaft nicht rein, und wenn in ihnen zwei Wörter zu einem zusammengesetzten Begriff zusammenkommen, so hängt es nur von dem Accent ab, der dieselben verbindet, oder doch noch, jedes einzeln hervorstossend, trennt.

segments.label: §74, de source block7
segments.text: Nun zu entscheiden, ob diese Trennung auch im Verstände die Begriffe weiter auseinander hält, oder ob die Verknüpfung der Begriffe die Eigenthümlichkeit der Aussprache nur als solche, nicht als Wortscheidung ansehen lässt, dürfte wohl an Unmöglichkeit gränzen.

segments.label: §74, de source block8
segments.text: Dagegen lässt sich wohl mit Grunde behaupten, dass die Spaltung der Töne da, wo die nahe Verbindung die Begriffe zu Eins macht, den Einfluss stört, welchen die Abtheilung der Rede in richtige und angemessene Wortganze auf den Geist hervorbringt.

segments.label: §74, de source block9
segments.text: In jedem einzelnen Fall mag es gleichgültig seyn, ob die Lautabtheilung mit der Gedankenabtheilung gleichen Schritt hält oder nicht.

segments.label: §74, de source block10
segments.text: Aber in der Masse ist die Wichtigkeit unverkennbar, und die durchgängige Zerschneidung der Laute in einzelne Sylben muss auf den Fluss der Gedanken unvortheilhaft einwirken.

segments.label: §74, de source block11
segments.text: Indess hat man wohl nie in China selbst die Untersuchung auf diese feineren geistigen Einflüsse der Sprache gerichtet, und in der Natur stellt sich ein Misverhältniss gewöhnlich immer wieder durch andre daneben eintretende Umstände her, so dass im Ganzen wieder dieselbe Erscheinung, als wo es nicht vorhanden ist, hervorkommt.

segments.label: §74, sol source block1
segments.text: When these languages are grouped together as a class of their own, however, one must be clear about the basis on which this is done.

segments.label: §74, sol source block2
segments.text: This classification can hardly be called purely factual.

segments.label: §74, sol source block3
segments.text: For a large proportion of languages, however polysyllabic they may be, can be traced back by analysis to monosyllabic roots, and if one goes back in thought to the origin of languages, the most natural thing is to assign just one simple sound to a simple concept.

segments.label: §74, sol source block4
segments.text: This should not, however, be taken to mean that every stem word must necessarily be monosyllabic.

segments.label: §74, sol source block5
segments.text: For in our investigation of language, in which we can never go back to the very beginning, the concept of a stem word is itself only a relative concept, and any of our languages may have begun with many polysyllabic words alongside its monosyllabic ones.

segments.label: §74, sol source block6
segments.text: Conversely, even monosyllabic languages do not exhibit this property in its pure form. When two words in them come together to form a compound concept, it is solely the accent that either binds them together or still keeps them apart by bringing each out separately.

segments.label: §74, sol source block7
segments.text: It would probably be all but impossible to decide whether this separation also keeps the concepts further apart in the understanding, or whether their connection leads one to regard the peculiarity of pronunciation as merely that, without taking it to mark a division between words.

segments.label: §74, sol source block8
segments.text: There is good reason, however, to maintain that keeping the sounds separate where the close connection makes the concepts one interferes with the effect on the mind of dividing speech into proper and appropriate units, each forming a whole word.

segments.label: §74, sol source block9
segments.text: In any individual case it may make no difference whether the division of sounds keeps pace with the division of thought.

segments.label: §74, sol source block10
segments.text: Taken together, however, the cases are unmistakably important, and the systematic breaking up of sounds into separate syllables must adversely affect the flow of thought.

segments.label: §74, sol source block11
segments.text: Yet these subtler effects of language on the mind have probably never been investigated in China itself, and in nature an imbalance generally rights itself through other circumstances that come into play alongside it, so that the overall result is the same as where no imbalance exists.

segments.label: §74, muse source block1
segments.text: But if these languages are grouped together as a distinct genus, one must properly understand in what way this is done.

segments.label: §74, muse source block2
segments.text: This division cannot be called purely factual.

segments.label: §74, muse source block3
segments.text: For a large part of all languages, however polysyllabic they may be, can be traced back by analysis to monosyllabic roots; and if one goes back in thought to the origin of languages, the most natural thing is to assign to the simple concept likewise only a simple sound.

segments.label: §74, muse source block4
segments.text: Yet this must not be understood as if every stem-word must necessarily be monosyllabic.

segments.label: §74, muse source block5
segments.text: For in our investigation of language, in which we are never able to go back to the beginning, the concept of the stem-word is itself only a relative concept, and any of our languages may have begun with many polysyllabic words alongside monosyllabic ones.

segments.label: §74, muse source block6
segments.text: On the other hand, the monosyllabic languages, too, do not possess this property in purity; and when in them two words come together to form a composite concept, it depends only on the accent whether it connects them or, thrusting each forth singly, still separates them.

segments.label: §74, muse source block7
segments.text: To decide now whether this separation also holds the concepts further apart in the understanding, or whether the linking of the concepts makes the peculiarity of pronunciation appear only as such, not as a division between words, would probably border on impossibility.

segments.label: §74, muse source block8
segments.text: On the other hand, it may well be asserted with good reason that the splitting of the tones, where close combination makes the concepts into one, disturbs the influence which the division of discourse into correct and appropriate word-wholes produces on the mind.

segments.label: §74, muse source block9
segments.text: In each individual case it may be indifferent whether the division of sound keeps pace with the division of thought or not.

segments.label: §74, muse source block10
segments.text: But in the aggregate the importance is unmistakable, and the thoroughgoing cutting up of the sounds into individual syllables must act disadvantageously on the flow of thoughts.

segments.label: §74, muse source block11
segments.text: Meanwhile, investigation has probably never in China itself been directed to these finer mental influences of language; and in nature a disproportion is ordinarily always redressed by other circumstances that intervene alongside it, so that on the whole the same phenomenon emerges again as where it is not present.

segments.text: This should not, however, be taken to mean that every stem word must necessarily be monosyllabic.

segments.label: §74, synthesis source block5
segments.text: For in our investigation of language, in which we can never go back to the very beginning, the concept of a stem word is itself only a relative concept, and any of our languages may have begun with many polysyllabic words alongside its monosyllabic ones.

segments.label: §74, synthesis source block6
segments.text: Conversely, even monosyllabic languages do not exhibit this property in its pure form. When two words in them come together to form a compound concept, it is solely the accent that either binds them together or still keeps them apart by bringing each out separately.

segments.label: §74, synthesis source block7
segments.text: It would probably be all but impossible to decide whether this separation also keeps the concepts further apart in the understanding, or whether their connection leads one to regard the peculiarity of pronunciation as merely that, without taking it to mark a division between words.

segments.label: §74, synthesis source block8
segments.text: There is good reason, however, to maintain that keeping the sounds separate where the close connection makes the concepts one interferes with the effect on the mind of dividing speech into proper and appropriate units, each forming a whole word.

segments.label: §74, synthesis source block9
segments.text: In any individual case it may make no difference whether the division of sounds keeps pace with the division of thought.

segments.label: §74, synthesis source block10
segments.text: Taken together, however, the cases are unmistakably important, and the systematic breaking up of sounds into separate syllables must adversely affect the flow of thought.

segments.label: §74, synthesis source block11
segments.text: Yet these subtler effects of language on the mind have probably never been investigated in China itself, and in nature an imbalance generally rights itself through other circumstances that come into play alongside it, so that the overall result is the same as where no imbalance exists.

segments.label: §74, revised source block1
segments.text: When these languages are grouped together as a class of their own, however, one must be clear about the basis on which this is done.

segments.label: §74, revised source block2
segments.text: This classification cannot be called purely factual.

segments.label: §74, revised source block3
segments.text: For a large proportion of languages, however polysyllabic they may be, can be traced back by analysis to monosyllabic roots, and if one goes back in thought to the origin of languages, the most natural thing is to assign just one simple sound to a simple concept.

segments.label: §74, revised source block4
segments.text: This should not, however, be taken to mean that every stem word must necessarily be monosyllabic.

segments.label: §75, de source block1
segments.text: Schon der Begriff einsylbiger Sprachen muss daher mit gewisser Einschränkung verstanden werden, und die mehrsylbigen können ursprünglich einsylbig gewesen seyn.

segments.label: §75, de source block2
segments.text: Die Wortabtheilung, die dieser Classification zum Grunde liegt, beruht sogar in Absicht der Laute auf Umständen, die, wie eben gezeigt worden, um so schwieriger zu beurtheilen sind, als sie keine genaue Kenntniss des lebendigen Vortrags der Rede voraussetzen.

segments.label: §75, de source block3
segments.text: Dennoch bleibt der einsylbige Bau einer kleinen Anzahl von Sprachen eine höchst merkwürdige Erscheinung, die, gerade ihrer Seltenheit wegen, die aufmerksamste Betrachtung verdient.

segments.label: §75, de source block4
segments.text: Durchaus falsch ist die Vorstellungsweise, diese Sprachen, gleichsam wie Kindersprachen, als auf einer Stufe ursprünglicher Unvollkommenheit stehen geblieben anzusehen.

segments.label: §75, de source block5
segments.text: Die Ursachen der Einsylbigkeit müssen gewiss ganz anders und viel tiefer aufgesucht werden.

segments.label: §75, de source block6
segments.text: Da aber diese Eigenschaft den Amerikanischen Sprachen fremd ist, so habe ich ihr nur hier im Gebäude der Sprache überhaupt ihre passende Stelle anweisen wollen.

segments.label: §75, sol source block1
segments.text: The very concept of monosyllabic languages must therefore be understood with some qualification, and polysyllabic languages may originally have been monosyllabic.

segments.label: §75, sol source block2
segments.text: Even as regards the sounds, the division into words underlying this classification depends on circumstances that, as we have just seen, are all the harder to judge because no precise knowledge of how speech is delivered in actual use can be taken for granted.

segments.label: §75, sol source block3
segments.text: Nevertheless, the monosyllabic structure of a small number of languages remains a highly remarkable phenomenon, deserving the closest attention precisely because of its rarity.

segments.label: §75, sol source block4
segments.text: It is altogether mistaken to regard these languages as children’s languages, as it were, that have remained at a stage of original imperfection.

segments.label: §75, sol source block5
segments.text: The causes of monosyllabism must surely be sought in quite a different way and at a much deeper level.

segments.label: §75, sol source block6
segments.text: Since this property is foreign to the American languages, however, my aim here has simply been to assign it its proper place in the structure of language in general.

segments.label: §75, muse source block1
segments.text: Even the concept of monosyllabic languages must therefore be understood with a certain restriction, and the polysyllabic ones may originally have been monosyllabic.

segments.label: §75, muse source block2
segments.text: The division into words on which this classification is based rests, even with respect to the sounds, on circumstances which, as has just been shown, are all the more difficult to judge inasmuch as they do not presuppose exact knowledge of the living delivery of discourse.

segments.label: §75, muse source block3
segments.text: Nevertheless, the monosyllabic structure of a small number of languages remains a highly remarkable phenomenon which, precisely because of its rarity, deserves the most attentive consideration.

segments.label: §75, muse source block4
segments.text: It is entirely false to regard these languages, as though they were child languages, as having stopped at a stage of original imperfection.

segments.label: §75, muse source block5
segments.text: The causes of monosyllabicity must certainly be sought in a quite different way and much more deeply.

segments.label: §75, muse source block6
segments.text: Since, however, this property is foreign to the American languages, I have wished to assign it its fitting place only here, in the edifice of language in general.

segments.label: §76, de source block1
segments.text: Dasselbe gilt in den mehrsylbigen Sprachen von der Gleichförmigkeit des Baues der Stammwörter, die z. B. in den Semitischen Sprachen angetroffen wird.

segments.label: §76, sol source block1
segments.text: The same applies, in polysyllabic languages, to the uniformity in the structure of stem words found, for example, in the Semitic languages.

segments.label: §77, de source block1
segments.text: Wo die Wortbildung an keine so feste Form gebunden ist, da bleibt die Anzahl der möglichen Wörter unbestimmt, und eine Menge von zusammentretenden Umständen, von denen sich nur selten Rechenschaft geben lässt, bestimmt, welche davon wirklich ins Daseyn gerufen werden.

segments.label: §77, de source block2
segments.text: Aber immer muss man annehmen, dass jedes durch ein andres, vor ihm vorhandenes entstanden ist.

segments.label: §77, de source block3
segments.text: Denn alle Veränderungen in der Sprache geschehen (43.) allmählich, und immer wird nur das schon ganz oder zum Theil Gehörte nachgesprochen.

segments.label: §77, de source block4
segments.text: Die Untersuchung der Wortlaute befindet sich daher überall an der Mitte einer Kette, deren Anfang ihr unzugänglich bleibt.

segments.label: §77, de source block5
segments.text: Es bedarf aber kaum der verwahrenden Bemerkung, dass darum nicht alle noch vorhandene Sprachen Theile der nemlichen Kette zu seyn brauchen, da es (46.) verschiedene, lange oder niemals mit einander in Verbindung getretene Wörterentwicklungen geben könnte.

segments.label: §77, de source block6
segments.text: Da jedoch die Gleichheit der Sprachwerkzeuge und ihrer Gesetze überall dieselben und nur eine gewisse Anzahl von Wortlauten möglich macht, so kann (47.) die blosse Einerleiheit oder Verwandtschaft des Tons für sich nicht über ihren historischen oder physiologischen Unterschied entscheiden.

segments.label: §77, de source block7
segments.text: Die Verwandtschaft lässt sich auf zwiefache Weise denken, durch Ableitung, indem der einfachere durch Anhängung, Vorschlag oder Einschiebung zum mehr oder minder Zusammengesetzten wird, und durch Anklang, indem der einfache Ton, auch einfach, aber verändert, wiederklingt, oder eine verwandte Idee durch einen verwandten bezeichnet wird.

segments.label: §77, de source block8
segments.text: Von dieser Entstehung jedes Worts aus einem andren Wort dürften höchstens die Naturlauten nachgeahmten auszunehmen seyn, die zwar gewöhnlich gleichfalls von Geschlecht zu Geschlecht und Nation zu Nation übergehen, aber auch plötzlich entstehen können, obgleich sie auch in diesem Fall sich immer der Lautanalogie der übrigen Sprache anschliessen werden.

segments.label: §77, sol source block1
segments.text: Where word formation is not bound to so fixed a form, the number of possible words remains indeterminate, and which of them are actually called into being is determined by a host of converging circumstances that can rarely be accounted for.

segments.label: §77, sol source block2
segments.text: One must always assume, however, that each word arose through another that existed before it.

segments.label: §77, sol source block3
segments.text: For all changes in language occur gradually (§43), and what is repeated in speech has invariably been heard before, in whole or in part.

segments.label: §77, sol source block4
segments.text: The investigation of word sounds therefore always finds itself in the middle of a chain whose beginning remains inaccessible to it.

segments.label: §77, sol source block5
segments.text: It scarcely needs pointing out, however, that the languages still in existence need not therefore all be parts of the same chain, since there could have been separate lines of development of words that came into contact only after a long time, or never did so at all (§46).

segments.label: §77, sol source block6
segments.text: Since, however, the sameness of the organs of speech and of the laws governing them makes the same limited set of word sounds possible everywhere, mere identity or affinity of sound cannot in itself decide the distinction between the historical and physiological grounds of that resemblance (§47).

segments.label: §77, sol source block7
segments.text: The affinity can be conceived in two ways, through derivation, when the simpler sound becomes more or less composite by the addition of something at the end, at the beginning, or within it, and through echo, when the simple sound recurs, still simple but altered, or when a kindred idea is designated by a kindred sound.

segments.label: §77, sol source block8
segments.text: The only possible exceptions to this emergence of each word from another are words that imitate natural sounds. These too usually pass from generation to generation and from nation to nation, but they can also arise suddenly, in which case they will still conform to the sound analogies of the rest of the language.

segments.label: §77, muse source block1
segments.text: Where word-formation is bound to no such fixed form, the number of possible words remains indeterminate, and a multitude of concurring circumstances, of which an account can only rarely be given, determines which of them are actually called into existence.

segments.label: §77, muse source block2
segments.text: But it must always be assumed that each one has arisen through another that existed before it.

segments.label: §77, muse source block3
segments.text: For all changes in language take place gradually (43.), and what is repeated in speaking is always only what has already been heard, wholly or in part.

segments.label: §77, muse source block4
segments.text: The investigation of word-sounds therefore finds itself everywhere in the middle of a chain whose beginning remains inaccessible to it.

segments.label: §77, muse source block5
segments.text: There is, however, hardly any need for the cautionary remark that not all languages still in existence need on that account be parts of the same chain, since (46.) there could be different developments of words that have never, or for a long time have not, entered into connection with one another.

segments.label: §77, muse source block6
segments.text: Since, however, the sameness of the organs of speech and of their laws makes the same word-sounds, and only a certain number of them, possible everywhere, mere identity or affinity of tone cannot by itself decide (47.) concerning their historical or physiological difference.

segments.label: §77, muse source block7
segments.text: Affinity can be conceived in two ways: by derivation, in that the simpler sound becomes, by addition at the end, addition at the beginning, or insertion, the more or less composite one; and by similarity of sound, in that the simple tone sounds again, still simple but changed, or a related idea is designated by a related tone.

segments.label: §77, muse source block8
segments.text: From this origin of every word from another word, at most those imitated from sounds of nature might be excepted; they ordinarily pass likewise from generation to generation and from nation to nation, but can also arise suddenly, although even in this case they will always conform to the sound-analogy of the rest of the language.

segments.label: §77, claude source block3

segments.label: §77, claude source block4

segments.label: §77, claude source block5
segments.text: It hardly needs the cautionary remark, however, that not all languages still extant need on that account be parts of the same chain, since (46.) there could be different developments of words which did not come into connection with one another for a long time, or never did.

segments.label: §77, claude source block6
segments.text: Since, however, the sameness of the organs of speech and of their laws everywhere makes possible the same word-sounds, and only a certain number of them, the mere identity or kinship of tone cannot by itself (47.) decide the question of its historical or physiological difference.

segments.label: §77, claude source block7
segments.text: Kinship can be conceived in two ways: through derivation, in that the simpler tone becomes something more or less compound by suffixing, prefixing or insertion; and through assonance, in that the simple tone sounds again, likewise simple but altered, or a kindred idea is designated by a kindred tone.

segments.label: §78, de source block1
segments.text: Hier, wo nur dem Gange der Wortbildung in einer gegebenen Sprache nachgeforscht werden soll, kommt es bloss darauf an, die zusammengesetzten Wortlaute in immer einfachere, soweit dies möglich ist, zu zergliedern, die Analogie dieser Zusammensetzung zu entwickeln, und die gefundenen einfachsten Wörter wiederum unter sich in ihren Lautverhältnissen zu vergleichen.

segments.label: §78, de source block2
segments.text: Daraus ergeben sich nun auf der einen Seite die Gesetze und Gewohnheiten der Wortbildung der Nationen, auf der andren der Umfang, die Vollständigkeit und die Alterthümlichkeit ihres Wortbaus.

segments.label: §78, de source block3
segments.text: Zu den ersteren gehören die Veränderungen der Wörter durch die Vocalreihe, die Einschiebungen und Veränderungen der Consonanten, die Erweiterungen der Wörter durch Vor- und Nachklänge, die Sylbenwiederholungen und Versetzungen.

segments.label: §78, de source block4
segments.text: An diesem Allem lässt sich sehr oft der rohere oder feinere Sprachsinn der Nationen erkennen.

segments.label: §78, sol source block1
segments.text: Here, where the question is simply how word formation proceeds in a given language, all that is required is to analyse compound word sounds into progressively simpler ones as far as possible, to work out the analogy governing their composition, and then to compare the simplest words thus found with one another in respect of their sound relationships.

segments.label: §78, sol source block2
segments.text: This reveals both the laws and habits of word formation among nations and the extent, completeness, and antiquity of their word structure.

segments.label: §78, sol source block3
segments.text: The laws and habits include changes to words by variation along the vowel series, the insertion and alteration of consonants, the extension of words by sounds added at the beginning or end, and the repetition and transposition of syllables.

segments.label: §78, sol source block4
segments.text: All this very often reveals how coarse or refined a nation's sense of language is.

segments.label: §78, muse source block1
segments.text: Here, where only the course of word-formation in a given language is to be investigated, the sole concern is to analyse composite word-sounds into ever simpler ones, as far as this is possible, to develop the analogy of this composition, and in turn to compare the simplest words thus found with one another in their sound-relations.

segments.label: §78, muse source block2
segments.text: From this there result, on the one side, the laws and customs of the word-formation of nations and, on the other, the extent, completeness, and archaic character of their word-structure.

segments.label: §78, muse source block3
segments.text: To the former belong the alterations of words through the vowel-series, the insertions and alterations of consonants, the extensions of words by sounds placed before and after, repetitions of syllables, and transpositions.

segments.label: §78, muse source block4
segments.text: In all this the cruder or finer sense for language of nations can very often be recognized.

segments.label: §78, claude source block1
segments.text: Here, where only the course of word-formation in a given language is to be investigated, the sole concern is to analyse the compound word-sounds into ever simpler ones, so far as this is possible, to develop the analogy of this composition, and to compare the simplest words thus found with one another in turn in their sound-relations.

segments.label: §78, claude source block2
segments.text: From this there result, on the one hand, the laws and habits of the nations' word-formation, and on the other the extent, the completeness and the antique character of their word-structure.

segments.label: §78, claude source block3
segments.text: To the former belong the alterations of words through the series of vowels, the insertions and alterations of consonants, the expansions of words by fore- and after-sounds, the syllable repetitions and transpositions.

segments.label: §78, claude source block4
segments.text: In all this the cruder or finer sense of language of the nations can very often be recognized.

segments.label: §78, synthesis source block1
segments.text: Here, where the question is simply how word formation proceeds in a given language, all that is required is to analyse compound word sounds into progressively simpler ones as far as possible, to work out the analogy governing their composition, and then to compare the simplest words thus found with one another in respect of their sound relationships.

segments.label: §78, synthesis source block2
segments.text: This reveals both the laws and habits of word formation among nations and the extent, completeness, and antiquity of their word structure.

segments.label: §78, synthesis source block3
segments.text: The laws and habits include changes to words by variation along the vowel series, the insertion and alteration of consonants, the extension of words by sounds added at the beginning or end, and the repetition and transposition of syllables.

segments.label: §78, synthesis source block4
segments.text: All this very often reveals how coarse or refined a nation’s sense of language is.

segments.label: §79, de source block1
segments.text: Je näher eine Sprache aus einer schon vollständig geformten entnommen ist, desto weniger steigt sie zu einfachen Lauten auf, die in dem Wörtervorrath mehrerer von diesen kaum überhaupt angetroffen werden.

segments.label: §79, de source block2
segments.text: Nur da wo bedeutende Stämme Jahrhunderte hindurch, in grosser Freiheit von fremder Vermischung, ihre Sprache von Geschlecht zu Geschlecht fortgetragen haben, und der Ursprung sich in Dunkel verliert, erscheint der weite und alterthümliche Bau, in dem sich lange Geschlechtsreihen von Wörtern auf ihre Grundlaute zurückführen lassen, diese noch in ihrer Einfachheit Bedeutung haben, jede Analogie sich an zahlreichen Beispielen erweist, jede mit andren in derselben Sphäre oder Gattung befindliche Lautbeschaffenheit mehrere dieser oder alle neben sich findet, und in welchem mithin strenge Analogie den Geist durch ein vielumfassendes System von Wortklängen führt.

segments.label: §79, de source block3
segments.text: Dies wirkt nun, ausser dem Einfluss einer solchen Fülle und Regelmässigkeit auf den Gebrauch, auch in sich, im klaren Bewusstseyn, wie in dunklem Gefühl auf die Nation zurück, und die Spracherzeugung in ihr wird fruchtbarer für Alles, womit sie in Berührung steht, wenn sich der Welt von Ideen auch eine sich selbst leicht und wundervoll ordnende Welt von Tönen zur Seite stellt.

segments.label: §79, de source block4
segments.text: Der Bau einer solchen Sprache knüpft jeden Einzelnen an viel entferntere Zeiten, an einen viel ursprünglicheren Zustand des Menschengeschlechts, an eine unendlich erscheinende Masse einmal da gewesener, und sich doch immer auf irgend eine Weise berührender und wieder hervorrufender Gedanken und Empfindungen an.

segments.label: §79, sol source block1
segments.text: The more directly a language is drawn from one already fully formed, the less far it goes back to simple sounds, which are hardly to be found at all in the vocabularies of several such languages.

segments.label: §79, sol source block2
segments.text: It is only where major tribes have handed down their language from generation to generation for centuries, largely free from admixture from outside, and where its origin is lost in obscurity, that this extensive and ancient structure appears. In it long genealogies of words can be traced back to their basic sounds, and these still have meaning in their simplicity. Each analogy can be demonstrated by numerous examples, and each sound feature that shares a sphere or class with others is found alongside several or all of them. Strict analogy thus guides the mind through a comprehensive system of word sounds.

segments.label: §79, sol source block3
segments.text: Beyond the influence of such abundance and regularity on usage, this structure also acts in its own right upon the nation, both in clear consciousness and in obscure feeling. The production of language among its people becomes more fruitful for everything it comes into contact with when alongside the world of ideas there stands a world of sounds that orders itself with ease and in a wondrous way.

segments.label: §79, sol source block4
segments.text: The structure of such a language connects each individual with far more distant times, with a far more original state of humankind, and with a seemingly infinite mass of thoughts and sensations that once existed and yet continually, in one way or another, touch and call forth one another again.

segments.label: §79, muse source block1
segments.text: The more directly a language has been taken from one already completely formed, the less does it go back up to simple sounds, such as are hardly encountered at all in the stock of words of several of these languages.

segments.label: §79, muse source block2
segments.text: Only where considerable tribes have for centuries, in great freedom from foreign mixture, carried their language onward from generation to generation, and its origin is lost in darkness, does that broad and archaic structure appear in which long genealogical series of words can be traced back to their fundamental sounds, these still have meaning in their simplicity, every analogy proves itself in numerous examples, every sound-quality finds beside it several or all of the others situated in the same sphere or genus, and in which consequently strict analogy guides the mind through a comprehensive system of word-sounds.

segments.label: §79, muse source block3
segments.text: This now reacts upon the nation, in addition to the influence of such fullness and regularity on use, also in itself, in clear consciousness as in obscure feeling; and the production of language in it becomes more fruitful for everything with which it stands in contact, when a world of tones that orders itself easily and wonderfully takes its place beside the world of ideas.

segments.label: §79, muse source block4
segments.text: The structure of such a language links every individual to far more distant times, to a far more original state of the human race, to a mass, appearing infinite, of thoughts and sensations that have once existed and yet always in some way touch and recall one another.

segments.label: §79, claude source block1
segments.text: The more closely a language is taken from one already fully formed, the less it ascends to simple sounds, which in the vocabulary of several of these are scarcely met with at all.

segments.label: §79, claude source block2

segments.label: §79, claude source block3

segments.label: §80, de source block1
segments.text: Hierin liegt (55.) das Regelsystem der Wortbildung, das man, auch bei der bloss lexikalischen Vergleichung der Sprachen, von den Tönen selbst zu unterscheiden hat.

segments.label: §80, de source block2
segments.text: Die Grundlage desselben ist das Lautsystem.

segments.label: §80, de source block3
segments.text: Denn je feiner und geistiger sich das Gehör und der Sprachsinn in diesem erweist, desto sorgfältiger wird jede, vielleicht anfangs nur zufällig, durch Einschiebung eines Hauchs, eines Vocals, eines Nasenlauts, entstehende Abänderung des Tones beachtet, und durch die ähnlichen Fälle durchgeführt, und desto analogischer werden ihr andre gleichartige Veränderungen angebildet.

segments.label: §80, de source block4
segments.text: Von verwandten Nationen gehen die Grundzüge dieses Systems in verwandte Sprachen über, und die Gleichartigkeit der Sprachen lässt sich in vieler Hinsicht richtiger an der lexikalischen Analogie, als an der grammatischen erkennen.

segments.label: §80, de source block5
segments.text: Denn sie beruht nicht, wie diese auf allgemeinen Denkgesetzen, sondern heftet sich unmittelbar an den Ton.

segments.label: §80, de source block6
segments.text: Je individueller aber eine Gleichartigkeit ist, desto sichrer weist sie auf einen geschichtlichen Zusammenhang hin.

segments.label: §80, de source block7
segments.text: Doch müssen die Fälle wohl beachtet werden, wo Wörter, in deren Bau Analogien dieser Art angedeutet sind, in andre Sprachen ohne diese Analogien selbst, d. h. ohne das Gefühl derselben bei der andren Nation, und daher ohne Fortbildung durch sie, übergegangen sind, und nun Theile einer Sprache werden, in welcher gar kein solcher Bau in solcher Vollkommenheit, oder ein andres System desselben vorhanden ist.

segments.label: §80, sol source block1
segments.text: Herein lies the system of rules of word formation (§55), which must be distinguished from the sounds themselves even in a purely lexical comparison of languages.

segments.label: §80, sol source block2
segments.text: Its foundation is the sound system.

segments.label: §80, sol source block3
segments.text: For the more refined and discerning the ear and the sense of language prove to be in the sound system, the more carefully each modification of sound, arising perhaps at first by mere chance through the insertion of an aspiration, a vowel, or a nasal sound, is attended to and carried through similar cases, and the more closely other changes of the same kind are modelled on it by analogy.

segments.label: §80, sol source block4
segments.text: From kindred nations the main features of this system pass into kindred languages, and in many respects the similarity in kind between languages can be discerned more accurately from lexical analogy than from grammatical analogy.

segments.label: §80, sol source block5
segments.text: For lexical analogy attaches directly to sound, whereas grammatical analogy rests on general laws of thought.

segments.label: §80, sol source block6
segments.text: The more individual the similarity in kind, however, the more surely it points to a historical connection.

segments.label: §80, sol source block7
segments.text: Careful attention must be paid, however, to cases where words whose structure shows traces of analogies of this kind have passed into other languages without the analogies themselves. The other nation has no sense of those analogies, and consequently no further development takes place by their means. The words thus become parts of a language where such a structure is nowhere developed to the same degree of perfection, or where that structure follows a different system.

segments.label: §80, muse source block1
segments.text: Herein lies (55.) the system of rules of word-formation, which, even in the merely lexical comparison of languages, must be distinguished from the tones themselves.

segments.label: §80, muse source block2
segments.text: Its basis is the sound-system.

segments.label: §80, muse source block3
segments.text: For the finer and more intellectual the hearing and the sense for language prove themselves to be in this system, the more carefully is every modification of the tone — arising perhaps at first only by chance, through insertion of a breath, a vowel, a nasal sound — attended to and carried through in similar cases, and the more analogically are other changes of the same kind formed after it.

segments.label: §80, muse source block4
segments.text: From related nations the fundamental features of this system pass over into related languages, and the sameness of kind of languages can in many respects be recognized more correctly from lexical analogy than from grammatical analogy.

segments.label: §80, muse source block5
segments.text: For it does not rest, as the latter does, on general laws of thought, but attaches itself immediately to the tone.

segments.label: §80, muse source block6
segments.text: The more individual a sameness of kind is, however, the more surely it points to a historical connection.

segments.label: §80, muse source block7
segments.text: Care must, however, be taken to note the cases where words in whose structure analogies of this kind are indicated have passed into other languages without these analogies themselves — that is, without the feeling for them in the other nation, and therefore without further development by it — and now become parts of a language in which no such structure exists in such perfection, or in which a different system of it exists.

segments.label: §80, claude source block1
segments.text: Herein lies (55.) the system of rules of word-formation, which, even in the merely lexical comparison of languages, one has to distinguish from the tones themselves.

segments.label: §80, claude source block2
segments.text: Its foundation is the sound-system.

segments.label: §80, claude source block3

segments.label: §80, claude source block4

segments.label: §80, claude source block6
segments.text: But the more individual a likeness in kind is, the more surely it points to a historical connection.

segments.label: §80, claude source block7

segments.label: §81, de source block1
segments.text: Aus diesem inneren Zusammenhange der Wörter, auch in ihren Lauten, folgt nunmehr von selbst, dass die Wörter mehrerer Sprachen zum Behuf der Auffindung ihrer Gleichartigkeit nicht dürfen unmittelbar mit einander verglichen werden, sondern erst eine Vergleichung derselben in jeder einzeln vorausgehen muss.

segments.label: §81, de source block2
segments.text: Die alphabetische Nebeneinanderstellung der Wörter verschiedener Sprachen reisst jede von diesen aus ihrem natürlichen Zusammenhang.

segments.label: §81, de source block3
segments.text: Wenn aber die Vergleichung der Wörter einer Sprache unter einander geschehen ist, so ergeben sich für die mit einer andren zwei Gegenstände: die Regeln der lexikalischen Analogie und die Grundlaute, und mit den ersteren die von einer Sprache in die andre übergegangenen wirklich nach diesen Regeln geformten zusammengesetzten Wörter.

segments.label: §81, de source block4
segments.text: Eine Vergleichung, die ihre Gewähr in sich selbst trägt, kann nur auf diese Weise geschehen.

segments.label: §81, de source block5
segments.text: Wenn man aber, wie es sehr oft der Fall ist, aus Mangel an Hülfsmitteln, oder weil eine Sprache gar keinen so einsichtlich ausgeführten inneren Bau hat, und weil man auch den vorhandenen doch nie ganz vollständig erkennt, auf die unmittelbare Wörtervergleichung zurückgewiesen wird, so muss man doch die beiden zu vergleichenden Wörter erst möglichst genau jedes in seiner Sprache, ihrer Entstehung nach, erforschen, um nicht wirklich verschiedene wegen bloss scheinbarer Lautähnlichkeit, als gleichartig, anzusehen.

segments.label: §81, sol source block1
segments.text: It now follows from this internal connectedness of words, extending even to their sounds, that to discover similarities in kind between languages one must first compare the words within each language before comparing them across languages.

segments.label: §81, sol source block2
segments.text: Setting the words of different languages side by side in alphabetical order tears each of those languages out of its natural context.

segments.label: §81, sol source block3
segments.text: Once the words of one language have been compared with one another, two objects of comparison with another language emerge, the rules of lexical analogy and the basic sounds. With the rules come the compound words that actually were formed according to them and passed from one language into the other.

segments.label: §81, sol source block4
segments.text: Only in this way is a comparison possible that carries its own warrant.

segments.label: §81, sol source block5
segments.text: Very often, however, one is thrown back on direct comparison of words, either for want of resources or because a language has no internal structure worked out with such clarity, and also because one never fully grasps even the structure that is there. One must still investigate the origin of each word to be compared as precisely as possible in its own language, lest one take genuinely different words to be of the same kind on the strength of a merely apparent resemblance in sound.

segments.label: §81, muse source block1
segments.text: From this inner connection of words, in their sounds also, it now follows of itself that the words of several languages must not be compared immediately with one another for the purpose of discovering their sameness of kind, but that a comparison of them in each language separately must first precede.

segments.label: §81, muse source block2
segments.text: The alphabetical placing side by side of the words of different languages tears each of these languages out of its natural context.

segments.label: §81, muse source block3
segments.text: But when the comparison of the words of one language with one another has been made, two objects result for comparison with another language: the rules of lexical analogy and the fundamental sounds, and, together with the former, the composite words that have passed from one language into the other and are actually formed according to these rules.

segments.label: §81, muse source block4
segments.text: A comparison that carries its guarantee in itself can be made only in this way.

segments.label: §81, muse source block5
segments.text: But if, as very often happens, from lack of aids, or because a language has no inner structure executed in so intelligible a manner, and because even that which exists is never known quite completely, one is thrown back on immediate comparison of words, the two words to be compared must nevertheless first be investigated as exactly as possible, each in its own language, as to their origin, so as not to regard words that are really different as of the same kind on account of merely apparent similarity of sound.

segments.label: §81, claude source block1
segments.text: From this inner connection of words, in their sounds as well, it now follows of itself that the words of several languages may not, for the purpose of discovering their likeness in kind, be compared directly with one another, but that a comparison of them within each language singly must first precede.

segments.label: §81, claude source block2
segments.text: The alphabetical juxtaposition of the words of different languages tears each of these languages out of its natural connection.

segments.label: §81, claude source block3
segments.text: But once the comparison of the words of one language among themselves has been carried out, two objects present themselves for the comparison with another: the rules of lexical analogy and the fundamental sounds, and, together with the former, the compound words actually formed according to these rules that have passed from one language into the other.

segments.label: §81, claude source block4
segments.text: A comparison that carries its warrant within itself can take place only in this way.

segments.label: §81, claude source block5
segments.text: If, however, as is very often the case, from want of aids, or because a language has no inner structure so perspicuously carried out, and because even the structure that exists is never quite completely recognized, one is thrown back upon the direct comparison of words, one must nevertheless first investigate the two words to be compared as exactly as possible, each in its own language, with respect to their origin, so as not to regard words that are really different as alike in kind on account of a merely apparent similarity of sound.

segments.label: §81, synthesis source block1
segments.text: This internal connection among words, which extends to their sounds, has a clear consequence. To find out in what respects the words of different languages are of the same kind, we must first compare the words within each language and only then compare them across languages.

segments.label: §82, de source block1
segments.text: In allen hier betrachteten Beziehungen ist nur auf die Abhängigkeit der Wortbildung von der Tonbehandlung der Nation gesehen worden, auf die Art, wie sie dem Vorrath ihrer Wortlaute Umfang und Mannigfaltigkeit giebt.

segments.label: §82, de source block2
segments.text: Es gesellt sich aber der Wortbildung auch hauptsächlich Rücksicht auf die Bedeutung zu, und wenn z. B. die Entstehung von λαμβάνω aus λάβω blosse Tonveränderung ist, so führt die von legen aus liegen eine Nuance des Sinnes mit sich.

segments.label: §82, de source block3
segments.text: Ganz auf der Bedeutung beruht die Wortbildung durch Zusammensetzung, in welcher immer mehrere Begriffe verbunden werden, entweder zu einem neuen dritten, oder, wie bei der Bildung durch Vor- und Nachsilben, bloss zu verschiedner Bestimmung des Hauptbegriffs.

segments.label: §82, de source block4
segments.text: Die Lautverhältnisse wirken dabei nur gelegentlich auf untergeordnete Weise mit.

segments.label: §82, sol source block1
segments.text: In all the respects considered here, attention has been confined to the dependence of word formation on a nation's treatment of sound, to the way it gives scope and variety to its stock of word sounds.

segments.label: §82, sol source block2
segments.text: Consideration of meaning, however, also plays a principal role in word formation. For example, while the formation of *λαμβάνω* from *λάβω* is a mere change of sound, the formation of *legen* from *liegen* brings with it a shade of difference in sense.

segments.label: §82, sol source block3
segments.text: Word formation by compounding rests entirely on meaning. Several concepts are always combined, either to form a new, third concept or, as in formation by prefixes and suffixes, simply to give the principal concept a different determination.

segments.label: §82, sol source block4
segments.text: Sound relationships enter into this only occasionally and in a subordinate way.

segments.label: §82, muse source block1
segments.text: In all the relations considered here, attention has been paid only to the dependence of word-formation on the nation's treatment of tone, to the way in which it gives extent and manifoldness to the stock of its word-sounds.

segments.label: §82, muse source block2
segments.text: But regard for meaning is also principally associated with word-formation; and if, for example, the origin of *λαμβάνω* from *λάβω* is mere alteration of tone, that of *legen* from *liegen* carries with it a nuance of sense.

segments.label: §82, muse source block3

segments.label: §82, muse source block4
segments.text: The sound-relations cooperate in this only occasionally and in a subordinate way.

segments.label: §82, claude source block2

segments.label: §83, de source block1
segments.text: In der Wahl der Laute für die Begriffe lässt sich die Sprache natürlich durch die klareren und dunkleren Beziehungen leiten, welche das Gefühl und die Einbildungskraft, der Individualität der Nationen gemäss, unter ihnen findet.

segments.label: §83, de source block2
segments.text: Geschichtlich verliert sich dies aber in die Zeiten der Spracherfindung, an welche keine Untersuchung mehr reicht, und durch die allmähliche Sprachumänderung, wo bald der Ton von dem Grundton, bald der Begriff von dem Grundbegriff nach und nach weiter abgebeugt wird, erleidet dies Verhältniss zwischen Ton und Bedeutung sehr oft eine gänzliche Abänderung.

segments.label: §83, de source block3
segments.text: Auch ist das, seiner Natur nach, unbestimmtere Gefühl, auf dem es beruht, in verschiedenen Völkern verschieden, und gerade die Nationen, die ursprünglichere, d. h. weniger Spuren grosser Umwälzungen an sich tragende Sprachen besitzen, dulden in ihren Silben weniger zusammenstossende Consonanten, und entbehren mithin ein Mittel mehr, den Charakter des Wortlauts zu bestimmen.

segments.label: §83, de source block4
segments.text: Es ist also eine gar nicht ungewöhnliche Erscheinung, starke und selbst widrige Begriffe mit sanften und weichen Lauten und umgekehrt gepaart zu sehen, und in geschichtlichen Sprachuntersuchungen ist auf diese Analogie durchaus kein Gewicht zu legen.

segments.label: §83, de source block5
segments.text: Phantasie und Scharfsinn finden darin einen weiten, aber höchst unsichren Boden, und für zehn, solche Uebereinstimmung des Tons mit der Bedeutung beweisende Beispiele geräth man auf eine viel grössere Anzahl, in welchen sie fehlt.

segments.label: §83, de source block6
segments.text: Dagegen wäre es gleich unrichtig, die Aufmerksamkeit ganz davon abzuwenden.

segments.label: §83, de source block7
segments.text: Denn es ist nicht zu läugnen, dass in Sprachen von hohem Alter und weitem und mannigfaltigem Wortbau sich das Gefühl einer solchen unverkennbaren Uebereinstimmung häufiger aufdringt, als in andren.

segments.label: §83, de source block8
segments.text: Wo sie aber in einer unvermischt gebliebenen Muttersprache Jahrhunderte hindurch auf dieselbe Nation fortwirkt, da erhöht und verstärkt sie den Einfluss der Sprache, bei der Alles darauf ankommt, durch die engste Verschmelzung des Tons mit dem Begriff aus dem Wort ein eignes, zwischen dem Menschen und der Welt, zugleich abhängig und unabhängig von beiden, schwebendes Wesen zu machen.

segments.label: §83, de source block9
segments.text: Vorzüglich sichtbar ist dies im Deutschen, und den von ihm abhängenden Sprachen.

segments.label: §83, sol source block1
segments.text: In choosing sounds for concepts, language is naturally guided by the clearer and more obscure relations that feeling and imagination, in keeping with the individuality of nations, find between them.

segments.label: §83, sol source block2
segments.text: Historically, however, this goes back into the lost ages in which language was invented, beyond the reach of any inquiry. As language gradually changes, now the sound diverges progressively from the basic sound, now the concept from the basic concept, and this relation between sound and meaning very often changes altogether.

segments.label: §83, sol source block3
segments.text: The feeling on which this relation rests, being by nature less determinate, also varies from one people to another. And precisely those nations with more original languages, that is, languages bearing fewer traces of great upheavals, tolerate fewer consonants coming together in their syllables and thus lack a further means of shaping the character of the word sound.

segments.label: §83, sol source block4
segments.text: It is therefore by no means unusual to see strong and even disagreeable concepts paired with gentle and soft sounds, and vice versa, and no weight whatever should be placed on this analogy in historical investigations of language.

segments.label: §83, sol source block5
segments.text: Fancy and acumen find ample but highly uncertain ground here, and for every ten examples that demonstrate such agreement between sound and meaning, one comes upon a far greater number in which it is absent.

segments.label: §83, sol source block6
segments.text: It would, however, be equally mistaken to disregard it altogether.

segments.label: §83, sol source block7
segments.text: For there is no denying that in languages of great antiquity and of extensive and varied word structure, the feeling of such unmistakable agreement forces itself upon us more often than in others.

segments.label: §83, sol source block8
segments.text: Where this agreement continues to act for centuries on the same nation in a mother tongue that has remained unmixed, it heightens and strengthens the influence of language. For language, everything depends on making the word, through the closest fusion of sound with concept, into a being in its own right, suspended between the human being and the world, at once dependent on and independent of both.

segments.label: §83, sol source block9
segments.text: This is especially apparent in German and in the languages that depend on it.

segments.label: §83, muse source block1
segments.text: In the choice of sounds for concepts, language naturally allows itself to be guided by the clearer and obscurer relations which feeling and imagination, in accordance with the individuality of nations, find among them.

segments.label: §83, muse source block2
segments.text: Historically, however, this is lost in the times of the invention of language, which no investigation can any longer reach; and through gradual alteration of language, in which now the tone is gradually deflected further from the fundamental tone, now the concept from the fundamental concept, this relation between tone and meaning very often undergoes a complete alteration.

segments.label: §83, muse source block3
segments.text: Moreover, the feeling, by its nature more indeterminate, on which it rests, is different in different peoples; and precisely those nations which possess more original languages — that is, languages bearing fewer traces of great upheavals — tolerate fewer colliding consonants in their syllables, and consequently are without one more means of determining the character of the word-sound.

segments.label: §83, muse source block4
segments.text: It is therefore a by no means unusual phenomenon to see strong and even repugnant concepts paired with gentle and soft sounds, and vice versa; and in historical investigations of language no weight at all is to be placed on this analogy.

segments.label: §83, muse source block5
segments.text: Fantasy and acumen find in this a wide but highly uncertain field; and for ten examples proving such agreement of tone with meaning, one comes upon a far greater number in which it is absent.

segments.label: §83, muse source block6
segments.text: On the other hand, it would be equally incorrect to turn attention wholly away from it.

segments.label: §83, muse source block7
segments.text: For it cannot be denied that in languages of great age and of broad and manifold word-structure the feeling of such an unmistakable agreement presents itself more frequently than in others.

segments.label: §83, muse source block8
segments.text: But where it continues to act for centuries in a mother tongue that has remained unmixed, upon the same nation, it heightens and strengthens the influence of language, in which everything depends on making the word, through the closest fusion of tone with concept, into a distinctive being hovering between man and the world, at once dependent on and independent of both.

segments.label: §83, muse source block9
segments.text: This is especially visible in German and in the languages dependent on it.

segments.label: §84, de source block1
segments.text: Die Wortlaute gehen zwar zugleich mit ihren Bedeutungen von Geschlecht zu Geschlecht und von Stamm zu Stamm über; da aber der Begriff beweglicher ist, als der sinnlich wahrnehmbare Laut, und nach Verhältnissen, die bald in ihm, bald im Individuum, bald auch in den äussern Umständen liegen, leichtere Uebergänge bildet, so entstehen häufigere Abbeugungen der Bedeutungen, als des Tons.

segments.label: §84, de source block2
segments.text: Man kann daher die Wortlaute als Formen ansehen, die aus grauem Alterthume her sich bis auf uns erhalten, und in sich einen mehr oder minder wechselnden Gehalt aufbewahrt haben, durch den sich jedoch immer ein, wenn gleich oft nur lose verknüpfender Faden hindurchschlingt.

segments.label: §84, de source block3
segments.text: Schon insofern wird in der Untersuchung des Sprachbaus eine, in der Natur allerdings nicht vorhandene, Trennung des Wortes als Laut und als Begriff nothwendig.

segments.label: §84, de source block4
segments.text: Denn die stätige Reihe der Vorstellungen erfordert, ebenso als die stätige Reihe der Töne, Eintheilung in den Wortlauten entsprechende Gedankeneinheiten, durch welche ideale Objecte aufgefasst und verknüpft werden können.

segments.label: §84, sol source block1
segments.text: Word sounds pass down with their meanings from generation to generation and from tribe to tribe. But the concept is more mobile than the sound perceptible to the senses and makes transitions more readily, depending on circumstances that lie sometimes in the concept itself, sometimes in the individual, and sometimes in external conditions. Meanings therefore shift more frequently than sound does.

segments.label: §84, sol source block2
segments.text: Word sounds may therefore be regarded as forms that have survived from hoary antiquity down to our own time, preserving within themselves a more or less variable content through which a thread always winds, though it often binds the parts together only loosely.

segments.label: §84, sol source block3
segments.text: On this ground alone, the study of the structure of language requires a separation of the word as sound from the word as concept, even though this separation does not exist in nature.

segments.label: §84, sol source block4
segments.text: For the continuous sequence of presentations, just like the continuous sequence of sounds, requires division into units of thought corresponding to the word sounds, by means of which ideal objects can be apprehended and connected.

segments.label: §84, muse source block1
segments.text: Word-sounds do indeed pass, together with their meanings, from generation to generation and from tribe to tribe; but since the concept is more mobile than the sensibly perceptible sound, and forms easier transitions according to relations that lie now in it, now in the individual, now also in external circumstances, deflections of meanings arise more frequently than deflections of tone.

segments.label: §84, muse source block2
segments.text: One may therefore regard word-sounds as forms that have preserved themselves down to us from hoary antiquity, and have preserved within themselves a more or less changing content, through which, however, there always winds a thread, albeit often only a loosely connecting one.

segments.label: §84, muse source block3
segments.text: Already in this respect there becomes necessary, in the investigation of linguistic structure, a separation of the word as sound and as concept, a separation that admittedly does not exist in nature.

segments.label: §84, muse source block4
segments.text: For the continuous series of presentations requires, just as does the continuous series of tones, division into units of thought corresponding to the word-sounds, through which ideal Objects can be apprehended and connected.

segments.label: §84, claude source block1
segments.text: The word-sounds do indeed pass, together with their meanings, from generation to generation and from tribe to tribe; but since the concept is more mobile than the sound perceptible to the senses, and, according to relations that lie now in the concept itself, now in the individual, now also in external circumstances, forms easier transitions, deflections of the meanings arise more frequently than deflections of the tone.

segments.label: §84, claude source block2
segments.text: The word-sounds may therefore be regarded as forms which have been preserved down to us from hoary antiquity and have stored up within themselves a more or less changing import, through which, however, there always winds a thread, even if often one that connects only loosely.

segments.label: §84, claude source block3
