segments.label: §85, de source block1
segments.text: Jeder solcher Gedankeneinheiten, mithin jedem Worte entspricht ein Gegenstand, entweder ein in der Natur körperlich aufzuzeigender, oder ein durch den Geist, mehr oder minder unabhängig von sinnlicher Wahrnehmung, gebildeter.

segments.label: §85, de source block2
segments.text: Denn obgleich das Wort selbst in diesem letzteren Fall dieser Gegenstand ist, so muss man das Wort im Allgemeinen und an sich von dem in einem bestimmten Augenblick von einem bestimmten Individuum gedachten, ebenso wie auf gleiche Weise die ganze Sprache unterscheiden.

segments.label: §85, de source block3
segments.text: Das Wort macht, dass sich die Seele den in demselben gegebenen Gegenstand vorstellt.

segments.label: §85, de source block4
segments.text: Diese Vorstellung muss von dem Gegenstande unterschieden werden ; sie kann individuell verschieden seyn, und muss es, da sie von allen Seiten bestimmt ist, der Gegenstand aber, als Object, immer nur allgemeiner gefasst werden kann; sie hat neben dem objectiven Theil, der sich auf den Gegenstand bezieht, einen subjectiven, in der Art der Auffassung liegenden, sowohl in der intellectuellen Ansicht, als in der diese begleitenden Empfindung.

segments.label: §85, de source block5
segments.text: Wiederum aber bedarf es kaum der Bemerkung, dass diese Trennung nur auf der Abstraction beruht, dass das Wort keine Stätte ausser dem Denken haben kann, und ebensowenig der Gegenstand desselben, wenn dieser ein unkörperlicher ist, dass es selbst jedesmal ganz von dem Geiste hervorgebracht wird, dass es wahrhaft seine Vollständigkeit und Individualität nur in dem jedesmaligen Denken hat, und als Bestandtheil der Sprache, als Object der Sprachuntersuchung, nur eine allgemeine, auf verschiedene, jedoch durch seine Natur beschränkte Weise individualisirbare Form ist.

segments.label: §85, de source block6
segments.text: Auch bei sinnlichen Gegenständen bleibt dies der Fall, da niemals sie geradezu, sondern immer nur diejenige Vorstellung von ihnen der Seele gegenwärtig werden, welche das Wort von ihnen giebt.

segments.label: §85, sol source block1
segments.text: To each such unit of thought, and hence to every word, there corresponds an object, either one that can be pointed out in corporeal form in nature or one formed by the mind more or less independently of sense perception.

segments.label: §85, sol source block2
segments.text: For although in the latter case the word itself is this object, we must distinguish the word in general and in itself from the word thought by a particular individual at a particular moment, and make the same distinction for language as a whole.

segments.label: §85, sol source block3
segments.text: The word causes the soul to form a presentation of the object given in it.

segments.label: §85, sol source block4
segments.text: This presentation must be distinguished from the object. It can and must vary from one individual to another, since it is determinate in every respect, whereas the object, considered as object, can only ever be grasped in more general terms. Alongside the objective part, which relates to the object, the presentation has a subjective part that lies in the mode of apprehension, both in the intellectual view and in the feeling that accompanies it.

segments.label: §85, sol source block5
segments.text: Again, it hardly needs saying that this separation rests solely on abstraction. The word can have no place outside thinking, and neither can its object if that object is incorporeal. The mind produces the word in its entirety on every occasion. The word truly has its completeness and individuality only in each act of thinking, and as a constituent of language and an object of linguistic inquiry it is merely a general form that can be individualised in various ways within the limits set by its nature.

segments.label: §85, sol source block6
segments.text: The same holds for objects of sense, since what becomes present to the soul is always the presentation that the word gives of them, never the objects themselves directly.

segments.label: §85, muse source block1
segments.text: To each such unit of thought, and consequently to every word, there corresponds an object, either one that can be pointed out corporeally in nature, or one formed by the mind, more or less independently of sensible perception.

segments.label: §85, muse source block2
segments.text: For although in this latter case the word itself is this object, one must distinguish the word in general and in itself from the word thought at a determinate moment by a determinate individual, just as one must in the same way distinguish the language as a whole.

segments.label: §85, muse source block3
segments.text: The word causes the soul to present to itself the object given in the word.

segments.label: §85, muse source block4
segments.text: This presentation must be distinguished from the object; it can be individually different, and must be so, since it is determined on all sides, whereas the object, as Object, can only ever be grasped more generally; besides the objective part, which refers to the object, it has a subjective part, lying in the mode of apprehension, both in the intellectual view and in the sensation accompanying it.

segments.label: §85, muse source block5
segments.text: But again, it hardly needs remarking that this separation rests only on abstraction, that the word can have no place outside thinking, and just as little can its object, if the latter is an incorporeal one, that the word itself is each time produced wholly by the mind, that it truly has its completeness and individuality only in the thinking of the moment, and as a constituent of language, as an Object of linguistic investigation, is only a general form, individualizable in different ways, though in ways limited by its nature.

segments.label: §85, muse source block6
segments.text: This remains the case also with sensible objects, since it is never they directly, but always only that presentation of them which the word gives of them, that becomes present to the soul.

segments.label: §86, de source block1
segments.text: Darauf dass jedes Wort einer Sprache eine gewisse Weite für die Möglichkeit verschiedenartiger Vorstellungen besitzt, beruht die Möglichkeit, dass sich in derselben Sprache die Vorstellungsweisen ganz verschiedener Individualitäten der Menschen und Zeiten vereinigen, und bei der Einerleiheit der allgemeinen Sprache dennoch jedes (50.) seine eigene haben kann.

segments.label: §86, de source block2
segments.text: Denn das Verstehen ist kein Zusammentreffen der Vorstellungsweisen in einem untheilbaren Punkt, sondern ein Zusammentreffen von Gedankensphären, von welchen der allgemeinere Theil sich deckt, der individuellere überragt.

segments.label: §86, de source block3
segments.text: Dadurch wird das geistige Fortschreiten des Menschengeschlechts möglich, indem jede gewonnene Erweiterung des Denkens in den Besitz Anderer übergehen kann, ohne in ihnen der Freiheit Fesseln anzulegen, welche zur Aneignung, und zu neuer Erweiterung nothwendig ist, und indem zugleich die Formen des Denkens, die Sprachen, die Veränderungen erfahren, welche ihnen, wie Allem, was an irdische Erscheinung gebunden ist, in ihrem Entwicklungsgange vorgeschrieben sind.

segments.label: §86, de source block4
segments.text: In jeder Bedeutung eines Worts ist also die Aufmerksamkeit darauf zu richten, wie es die individuelle Vorstellungsweise frei lässt und bestimmt, und es kann eine Geschichte der Wörter und ihrer einzelnen Bedeutungen durch alle die verschiedenen Arten durchgeführt werden, wie sie genommen und gebraucht worden sind.

segments.label: §86, sol source block1
segments.text: Each word in a language allows a certain latitude for different presentations. This makes it possible for the modes of presentation of very different individuals and ages to come together in the same language, and for each to have a language of its own even while the common language remains the same (50).

segments.label: §86, sol source block2
segments.text: For understanding is no coincidence of modes of presentation at an indivisible point. It is a meeting of spheres of thought whose more general parts coincide and whose more individual parts extend beyond the overlap.

segments.label: §86, sol source block3
segments.text: This makes possible the intellectual progress of humankind. Every advance in the scope of thinking can pass into the possession of others without fettering the freedom they need to make it their own and extend it further. At the same time, the forms of thinking, the languages, undergo the changes prescribed in the course of their development for them, as for everything bound to appear on earth.

segments.label: §86, sol source block4
segments.text: In every meaning of a word, then, we must attend to how it leaves the individual mode of presentation free and how it determines it. A history of words and their particular meanings can trace all the different ways in which they have been understood and used.

segments.label: §86, muse source block1
segments.text: On the fact that every word of a language possesses a certain latitude for the possibility of different kinds of presentations rests the possibility that, in one and the same language, the modes of presentation of quite different human individualities and ages can unite, and that, despite the sameness of the general language, each person (50.) can nevertheless have his own.

segments.label: §86, muse source block2
segments.text: For understanding is not a meeting of modes of presentation in an indivisible point, but a meeting of spheres of thought, of which the more general part coincides, the more individual projects beyond it.

segments.label: §86, muse source block3
segments.text: Through this the mental progress of the human race becomes possible, in that every enlargement of thinking that has been won can pass into the possession of others without laying fetters in them on the freedom that is necessary for appropriation and for new enlargement, and in that at the same time the forms of thinking, the languages, undergo the changes prescribed for them, as for everything bound to earthly appearance, in their course of development.

segments.label: §86, muse source block4
segments.text: In every meaning of a word, therefore, attention is to be directed to how it leaves the individual mode of presentation free and how it determines it, and a history of words and of their individual meanings can be carried through all the different ways in which they have been taken and used.

segments.label: §87, de source block1
segments.text: Der zu der Klarheit und Bestimmtheit des Worts gesteigerte Begriff ist allemal der Erfolg des Zusammenwirkens der ganzen Seelenkraft, und da es nun die Eigenthümlichkeit des Wortes ist, diesen Begriff durch den Ton, wie durch einen elektrischen Schlag, hervorzurufen, so strahlt die Wirkung desselben durch die ganze Seele nach allen Richtungen hin.

segments.label: §87, de source block2
segments.text: Die Einheit einer Kraft lässt sich nicht in Theile zerspalten, indess leuchten in der Bildung und dem Einfluss des Worts doch drei grosse und hauptsächliche Beziehungen hervor, unter denen jedes betrachtet und geprüft werden kann: seine logische Construction, seine sinnliche Geltung und sein Eindruck auf das Gefühl.

segments.label: §87, de source block3
segments.text: Jedes dieser drei Stücke erscheint aber wieder in dem Wort auf eine zwiefache Weise, da man die Vorstellung des Gegenstandes selbst (85.) von derjenigen unterscheiden muss, welche das Wort, seiner Bildung und Entstehung nach, von ihm giebt, und von diesen beiden Vorstellungen keine die andere aufhebt, sondern beide in ein gewisses Verhältniss zu einander treten.

segments.label: §87, sol source block1
segments.text: A concept raised to the clarity and determinacy of a word is always the result of the whole power of the soul working together. Since it is characteristic of the word to evoke this concept through sound, as if by an electric shock, its effect radiates in every direction through the whole soul.

segments.label: §87, sol source block2
segments.text: The unity of a power cannot be split into parts. Yet three principal aspects stand out in the formation and influence of the word, and each word can be considered and examined under them. They are its logical construction, its sensory import and its impression on feeling.

segments.label: §87, sol source block3
segments.text: Each of these three aspects in turn appears in the word in two ways, since we must distinguish the presentation of the object itself (85) from the presentation the word gives of it by virtue of its formation and origin. Neither presentation cancels the other, and the two enter into a definite relation with each other.

segments.label: §87, muse source block1
segments.text: The concept raised to the clarity and determinateness of the word is in every case the result of the co-operation of the whole power of the soul, and since it is now the peculiarity of the word to call forth this concept through the tone, as through an electric shock, its effect radiates through the whole soul in all directions.

segments.label: §87, muse source block2
segments.text: The unity of a power cannot be split into parts, yet in the formation and influence of the word three great and principal relations do stand out, under which every word can be considered and tested: its logical construction, its sensible validity, and its impression on feeling.

segments.label: §87, muse source block3
segments.text: Each of these three items, however, appears again in the word in a twofold way, since one must distinguish the presentation of the object itself (85.) from that which the word, according to its formation and origin, gives of it, and of these two presentations neither cancels the other, but both enter into a certain relation to one another.

segments.label: §88, de source block1
segments.text: Das Wort giebt dem Begriffe Gestaltung, und durch den Ton, unmittelbar vor dem Ohr, und mittelbar vor allen sinnlichen Kräften der Seele, sinnliche Geltung.

segments.label: §88, de source block2
segments.text: Das Wort fasst jeden Begriff, als einen allgemeinen auf, bezeichnet, streng genommen, immer Classen der Wirklichkeit, selbst wenn es ein Eigenname ist, da es alsdann alle, der Zeit und dem Räume nach, verschiedenen Zustände des Bezeichneten (ihn als eine Classe vorstellend, in welcher er in allen diesen Zuständen eben so, wie verschiedene Individuen in einem Gattungsbegriffe, enthalten ist) zusammenfasst.

segments.label: §88, de source block3
segments.text: Es macht aber sich selbst, und mithin auch den in ihm enthaltenen Begriff zu einem Individuum der Sprache.

segments.label: §88, de source block4
segments.text: Es kann daher Jenen nur von einem einzelnen Standpunkte aus nehmen, darf jedoch nichts aufgeben von seinem Gehalt, und dies wird erreicht, indem das Wort der Seele nach jenen drei Hauptbeziehungen hin eine bestimmte Anregung ertheilt, durch welche die Begriffserzeugung zwar vollständig, aber von einer scharf bestimmten Seite aus geschieht.

segments.label: §88, de source block5
segments.text: Dadurch entstehen in den gleichbedeutenden Wörtern mehrerer Sprachen verschiedene Vorstellungen desselben Gegenstandes, und diese Beschaffenheit des Worts trägt hauptsächlich dazu bei, dass jede Sprache eine eigne Weltansicht gewährt.

segments.label: §88, sol source block1
segments.text: The word gives shape to the concept and, through sound, gives it sensory import directly for the ear and indirectly for all the sensory powers of the soul.

segments.label: §88, sol source block2
segments.text: The word apprehends every concept as a general one and, strictly speaking, always designates classes of reality. This holds even for a proper name, since it gathers together all the states of what it designates that differ in time and space, presenting it as a class in which it is contained in all these states just as different individuals are contained in a generic concept.

segments.label: §88, sol source block3
segments.text: Yet the word makes itself, and hence also the concept it contains, an individual within language.

segments.label: §88, sol source block4
segments.text: It can therefore take up the concept only from a single standpoint, yet it must give up none of the concept's content. The word achieves this by giving the soul a definite stimulus along those three principal lines, so that the concept is produced in full, but from a sharply defined side.

segments.label: §88, sol source block5
segments.text: This is how words with the same meaning in several languages give rise to different presentations of the same object. This property of the word is a principal reason why each language affords a view of the world of its own.

segments.label: §88, muse source block1
segments.text: The word gives the concept shape, and through the tone, immediately before the ear, and mediately before all the sensible powers of the soul, sensible validity.

segments.label: §88, muse source block2
segments.text: The word grasps every concept as a general one, designates, strictly taken, always classes of reality, even when it is a proper name, since it then comprehends together all the states of what is designated, different in time and space (presenting it as a class in which it is contained in all these states just as different individuals are contained in a generic concept).

segments.label: §88, muse source block3
segments.text: But it makes itself, and consequently also the concept contained in it, into an individual of language.

segments.label: §88, muse source block4
segments.text: It can therefore take that concept only from a single standpoint, yet it must give up nothing of its content, and this is achieved in that the word imparts to the soul, in the directions of those three principal relations, a determinate excitation, through which the generation of the concept does indeed take place completely, but from a sharply determinate side.

segments.label: §88, muse source block5
segments.text: Through this there arise, in the words of several languages that have the same meaning, different presentations of the same object, and this constitution of the word contributes principally to each language affording a world-view of its own.

segments.text: Thereby there arise, in the words of like meaning in several languages, different presentations of the same object, and this constitution of the word chiefly contributes to each language's affording a world-view of its own.

segments.text: It can therefore take up the concept only from a single standpoint, yet it must give up none of the concept’s content. The word achieves this by giving the soul a definite stimulus along those three principal lines, so that the concept is produced in full, but from a sharply defined side.

segments.label: §88, revised source block5
segments.text: This is how words with the same meaning in several languages give rise to different presentations of the same object. This property of the word is a principal reason why each language affords a view of the world of its own.

segments.label: §89, de source block1
segments.text: So wie die Sprache und in ihr das Wort die individuelle Natur der Welt verallgemeinert, so vergeistigt sie die in äusserer und innerer Wahrnehmung stoffartige.

segments.label: §89, de source block2
segments.text: So wie aber das Wort selbst wieder in der Sprache Individuum wird, so wird es auch in ihr körperlich durch Annahme des Tons, und dient dem Geiste zum Stoff neuer Wirksamkeit.

segments.label: §89, de source block3
segments.text: Das eine und das andre geschieht aber zugleich und in untheilbarer Einheit, synthetisch, und Allgemeinheit und Individualitaet, Geistigkeit und Stoffartigkeit durchdringen einander im Wort, was, da jene Begriffe sich sonst aufheben würden, nur dadurch möglich ist, dass das Wort, als Sprachbestandtheil ausser der Seele gedacht, nichts als eine Anregung zum Denken, als vollendeter Begriff in der Seele gedacht, das Denken selbst ist, und der menschlich geistigen Kraft dies unaufhörliche Entwickeln und Rückkehren des Allgemeinen und Unsinnlichen aus Individuellem und Sinnlichem und in dasselbe eigenthümlich angehört.

segments.label: §89, de source block4
segments.text: Blicken wir nun auf die oben (87.) erwähnten drei Hauptrichtungen zurück, nach welchen hin das Wort die Seele anregt, so kann dasselbe nur insofern sinnliche und Empfindungsgeltung besitzen, als es sich dieselbe auf dem Gebiete der Intellectualität zu erhalten vermag.

segments.label: §89, de source block5
segments.text: Dies geschieht aber nur, indem dieser Sinnen- und Gefühlsgehalt zugleich, und wieder synthetisch, als Stoff vernichtet und als Form erhalten wird, was das Werk der Einbildungskraft ist, der Vermittlerin der entgegengesetzten Naturen in der Menschheit.

segments.label: §89, de source block6
segments.text: Da nun auch der Verstandesgehalt des Wortes sich nur auf ihrem Gebiete mit dem sinnlichen vereinigen kann, so ist dieses Gebiet eigentlich die Sphäre, in welcher das Wort schwebt, indem die Einbildungskraft die Gesammtkräfte der Seele zum Hervorbringen oder Verstehen desselben zusammenfasst.

segments.label: §89, sol source block1
segments.text: Just as language, and the word within it, generalises the individual nature of the world, so it spiritualises that nature which has the character of material in outward and inward perception.

segments.label: §89, sol source block2
segments.text: Yet just as the word itself in turn becomes an individual in language, it also takes on corporeal form in language by assuming sound, and serves the mind as material for further activity.

segments.label: §89, sol source block3
segments.text: Both take place at once and in indivisible unity, synthetically, and generality and individuality, spirituality and materiality interpenetrate in the word. Since these concepts would otherwise cancel one another, this is possible only because the word, conceived as a constituent of language outside the soul, is merely a stimulus to thinking, whereas conceived as a completed concept in the soul it is thinking itself. It is characteristic of the power of the human mind that the general and the non-sensory should ceaselessly develop out of the individual and the sensory and return into them.

segments.label: §89, sol source block4
segments.text: Returning now to the three principal directions mentioned above (87) in which the word stimulates the soul, we see that the word can have import for sense and feeling only insofar as it can retain that import in the intellectual domain.

segments.label: §89, sol source block5
segments.text: This happens only when the content of sense and feeling is at once, and again synthetically, destroyed as material and preserved as form. This is the work of the imagination, which mediates between the opposed natures in humankind.

segments.label: §89, sol source block6
segments.text: Since the intellectual content of the word can unite with the sensory content only in the domain of the imagination, this domain is properly the sphere in which the word hovers, as the imagination gathers all the powers of the soul to produce or understand it.

segments.label: §89, muse source block1

segments.label: §89, muse source block2

segments.label: §89, muse source block4
segments.text: If we now look back at the three principal directions mentioned above (87.), in which the word excites the soul, the word can possess sensible validity and validity for sensation only in so far as it can preserve the same for itself in the domain of intellectuality.

segments.text: This happens, however, only in that this content of sense and feeling is at the same time, and again synthetically, destroyed as material and preserved as form, which is the work of the imagination, the mediatress of the opposed natures in mankind.

segments.text: Since now the intellectual content of the word, too, can unite with the sensible content only in its domain, this domain is properly the sphere in which the word hovers, in that the imagination gathers together the total powers of the soul for producing or understanding it.

segments.label: §89, synthesis source block2

The capacity for this unceasing development of the general and non-sensory out of the individual and sensory, and their return into them, is characteriztic of human mental power.

segments.label: §90, de source block1
segments.text: Die Art, wie das Wort, immer nach jenen drei Richtungen hin, die Gegenstände äusserer und innerer Wahrnehmung vor die Seele bringt, kann man das Objective in demselben, seine Materie, die Art aber, wie die Vermögen der Seele, nach jenen Richtungen, zu einander in Verhältniss treten, und sich zur Einheit des Zusammenwirkens verschmelzen, das Subjective in demselben, seine Form nennen.

segments.label: §90, sol source block1
segments.text: We may call the way the word brings objects of outward and inward perception before the soul, always along those three lines, what is objective in the word, its matter. We may call the way the faculties of the soul enter into relation with one another along those lines and fuse into a unity of action what is subjective in the word, its form.

segments.label: §90, muse source block1
segments.text: The way in which the word, always in those three directions, brings the objects of outer and inner perception before the soul may be called the Objective in it, its matter, but the way in which the faculties of the soul, in those directions, enter into relation to one another and fuse into the unity of co-operation may be called the Subjective in it, its form.

segments.label: §90, claude source block1

segments.label: §91, de source block1
segments.text: Beides liegt unläugbar in der Sprache und in jedem einzelnen ihrer Wörter; indem es die Individualitaet der Sprechenden war, hat es sich an die Laute geheftet, und kehrt durch sie in die lebendige Individualitaet zurück.

segments.label: §91, de source block2
segments.text: Denn die wundervolle Art der Verkörperung einer geistigen Zeugung, welche eine gleiche im Andren hervorbringt, ist ja die wahrhaft eigenthümliche Natur der Sprache, und ruht vorzüglich auf ihrem Hauptbestandtheil, dem Wort.

segments.label: §91, de source block3
segments.text: Die Form ist aber noch wichtiger, als die Materie.

segments.label: §91, de source block4
segments.text: Denn sie hängt an der ganzen Sprache, und wenn daher diese auch als todte oder fremde von einer sehr verschiedenen Individualitaet aufgefasst wird, nöthtigt sie dieselbe dennoch, ihre Anschauungsweise anzunehmen, indem sie sie von allen Seiten mit derselben umstrickt.

segments.label: §91, de source block5
segments.text: Die Materie vermag nicht nur dies nicht, sondern die besondere Vorstellungsweise des Gegenstandes bleibt auch nicht einmal immer im Worte erkennbar, oder wird wenigstens nicht mehr so, als bei dessen Entstehung gefühlt; die Individualitaet des Worts geht in der Allgemeinheit des Begriffes verloren.

segments.label: §91, de source block6
segments.text: Ich habe hierauf schon im Vorigen (87.) in dem Unterschiede zwischen der Vorstellung von dem Gegenstande und der des Wortes von ihm hingedeutet.

segments.label: §91, de source block7
segments.text: Dieser Unterschied wird freilich nur dadurch möglich, dass das Wort, als verkörperter Begriff, nach und nach von sehr verschiedenen Individualitäten verschiedenen Anschauungsweisen angepasst wird, in welchen der jedesmalige Gebrauch den Gegenstand gar nicht so darstellt, als der erste Erfinder; aber so verstanden lassen sich ganze Reihen von Beispielen davon aufzeigen.

segments.label: §91, de source block8
segments.text: Die Ausdrücke für körperliche Gegenstände sind gewiss zum grössten Theile aus Eigenschaften entstanden, die an denselben vorzüglich auffielen, und sind nichts anders, als zu Adjectiven gewordene Substantiva, unsinnliche Begriffe werden metaphorisch nach körperlichen bezeichnet, grammatische, bloss die Verbindung der Rede bestimmende, nach Wörtern für Sachbegriffe.

segments.label: §91, de source block9
segments.text: In allen diesen Fällen geht sehr häufig, ja mehrentheils, der Charakter der ursprünglichen Bezeichnung unter, und der Begriff des Gegenstandes tritt allgemein, oder anders genommen, an die Stelle.

segments.label: §91, de source block10
segments.text: Schwerlich ist bei dem Indischen dwipa für Elephant immer an die Eigenschaft des doppelten Trinkens durch den Rüssel und den Mund gedacht worden, wenigen, die das deutsche Vernunft und zurück gebrauchen, fällt es ein, dass jenes von vernehmen, dieses von Rücken kommt.

segments.label: §91, de source block11
segments.text: Viele Wörter, die ehemals gar keine solche Nebenbedeutung hatten, werden späterhin nur scherzhafter, ironischer oder verächtlicher Weise gebraucht.

segments.label: §91, de source block12
segments.text: So wechselt die Materie des Worts ; selbst zwischen demselben Ton und demselben durch ihn bezeichneten Gegenstand findet der Geist einen Spielraum bequemer Weite, verschieden nuancirte Vorstellungsarten einzuschieben; eigentlich aber wird unter demselben Schall jedesmal ein andres Wort ausgesprochen.

segments.label: §91, de source block13
segments.text: Denn nur das wirklich gedachte oder gesprochene ist das eigentliche Wort, das sich gleichsam todt in der Sprache forterbende nur die immer wieder, und immer etwas anders belebte Hülle.

segments.label: §91, de source block14
segments.text: In dem gedachten oder gesprochenen ist allemal Materie und Form zugleich durch den Charakter des Worts und der Sprache und durch den des Sprechenden bestimmt.

segments.label: §91, sol source block1
segments.text: Both are undeniably present in language and in every one of its words. As the individuality of the speakers, they have attached themselves to the sounds and through them return to living individuality.

segments.label: §91, sol source block2
segments.text: For this marvellous way of embodying a begetting of the mind that brings forth a like begetting in another person is precisely what is truly distinctive about language, and it depends chiefly on its principal constituent, the word.

segments.label: §91, sol source block3
segments.text: Form, however, is even more important than matter.

segments.label: §91, sol source block4
segments.text: For form inheres in the whole language. Thus even when a person of very different individuality apprehends it as a dead or foreign language, it still compels that person to adopt its mode of intuition by surrounding them with it on every side.

segments.label: §91, sol source block5
segments.text: Matter has no such power. The particular mode of presenting the object does not even always remain discernible in the word, or at least is no longer felt as it was when the word arose. The individuality of the word is lost in the generality of the concept.

segments.label: §91, sol source block6
segments.text: I already pointed to this above (87) in distinguishing the presentation of the object from the presentation the word gives of it.

segments.label: §91, sol source block7
segments.text: This distinction is admittedly possible only because the word, as an embodied concept, is gradually adapted by people of very different individualities to different modes of intuition, in which each new use presents the object quite differently from the way its first inventor did. Understood in this way, whole series of examples can be adduced.

segments.label: §91, sol source block8
segments.text: Expressions for corporeal objects have certainly arisen for the most part from properties that were especially striking in those objects and are simply nouns that have become adjectives. Non-sensory concepts are designated metaphorically in terms of corporeal ones, and grammatical concepts, which merely determine the way discourse is connected, are designated after words for concepts of things.

segments.label: §91, sol source block9
segments.text: In all these cases the character of the original designation is very often, indeed usually, lost, and the concept of the object takes its place, understood in general terms or in some other way.

segments.label: §91, sol source block10
segments.text: The Indian word *dwîpa* for ‘elephant’ can hardly have always prompted people to think of the animal's twofold manner of drinking through trunk and mouth. Few who use the German *Vernunft* and *zurück* think of the former as coming from *vernehmen* or the latter from *Rücken*.

segments.label: §91, sol source block11
segments.text: Many words that formerly had no such secondary meaning are later used only jocularly, ironically or contemptuously.

segments.label: §91, sol source block12
segments.text: This is how the matter of the word changes. Even between the same sound and the same object designated by it, the mind finds ample room to introduce differently nuanced modes of presentation. Strictly speaking, however, a different word is uttered each time under cover of the same audible sound.

segments.label: §91, sol source block13
segments.text: For the word proper is only the word actually thought or spoken. What is handed down in language as if dead is merely the shell, brought to life again and again, and always a little differently.

segments.label: §91, sol source block14
segments.text: In the word as thought or spoken, matter and form are always determined together by the character of the word and the language, and by that of the speaker.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block3
segments.text: Form, however, is even more important than matter.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block4
segments.text: For form inheres in the whole language. Thus even when a person of very different individuality apprehends it as a dead or foreign language, it still compels that person to adopt its mode of intuition by surrounding them with it on every side.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block5
segments.text: Matter has no such power. The particular mode of presenting the object does not even always remain discernible in the word, or at least is no longer felt as it was when the word arose. The individuality of the word is lost in the generality of the concept.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block6
segments.text: I already pointed to this above (§87) in distinguishing the presentation of the object from the presentation the word gives of it.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block7
segments.text: This distinction is admittedly possible only because the word, as an embodied concept, is gradually adapted by people of very different individualities to different modes of intuition, in which each new use presents the object quite differently from the way its first inventor did. Understood in this way, whole series of examples can be adduced.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block8
segments.text: Expressions for corporeal objects have certainly arisen for the most part from properties that were especially striking in those objects. They are simply nouns that have become adjectives. Non-sensory concepts are designated metaphorically in terms of corporeal ones. Grammatical concepts, which merely govern the linking of discourse, are designated after words for concepts of things.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block9
segments.text: In all these cases the character of the original designation is very often, indeed usually, lost, and the concept of the object takes its place, understood in general terms or in some other way.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block10
segments.text: It is unlikely that the Indian word *dwipa* ‘elephant’ has always called to mind the quality of drinking twice, through the trunk and through the mouth. Few people who use the German words *Vernunft* ‘reason’ and *zurück* ‘back’ think that the former comes from *vernehmen* ‘perceive’ and the latter from *Rücken* ‘back’.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block11
segments.text: Many words that formerly had no such secondary meaning are later used only jocularly, ironically or contemptuously.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block12
segments.text: This is how the matter of the word changes. Even between the same sound and the same object designated by it, the mind finds ample room to introduce differently nuanced modes of presentation. Strictly speaking, however, a different word is uttered each time under cover of the same audible sound.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block13
segments.text: For the word proper is only the word actually thought or spoken. What is handed down in language as if dead is merely the shell, brought to life again and again, and always a little differently.

segments.label: §91, synthesis source block14
segments.text: In the word as thought or spoken, matter and form are always determined together by the character of the word and the language, and by that of the speaker.

segments.label: §92, de source block1
segments.text: Dies trifft mit dem oben (86.) Bemerkten zusammen, dass die Natur des Wortes, auch in der gleichen Sprache, dem Einzelnen bis auf einen gewissen Grad seine eigne Sprache zu haben erlaubt.

segments.label: §92, de source block2
segments.text: Es ist aber darin verschieden, dass jenes auch da statt findet, wo die Materie und Form des Wortlauts vollkommen empfunden werden, hier von dem entgegengesetzten Falle geredet wird.

segments.label: §92, de source block3
segments.text: Es offenbart sich also hier eine zwiefache Weite der Lautform, als Hülle des Begriffs.

segments.label: §92, sol source block1
segments.text: This accords with the observation above (86) that the nature of the word allows individuals, even within the same language, to have a language of their own up to a point.

segments.label: §92, sol source block2
segments.text: The difference is that the earlier observation also applies where the matter and form of the word sound are fully felt, whereas here we are speaking of the opposite case.

segments.label: §92, sol source block3
segments.text: The sound form, as the shell of the concept, thus proves to allow latitude in two ways.

segments.label: §92, muse source block1
segments.text: This coincides with what was remarked above (86.), that the nature of the word, even in the same language, allows the individual to have, up to a certain degree, a language of his own.

segments.label: §92, muse source block2
segments.text: It is, however, different therein, that that takes place even where the matter and form of the word-sound are completely felt, whereas here the opposite case is being spoken of.

segments.label: §92, muse source block3
segments.text: Here, therefore, a twofold latitude of the sound-form, as husk of the concept, reveals itself.

segments.label: §92, claude source block1
segments.text: This coincides with what was remarked above (86.), that the nature of the word, even within the same language, permits each individual to have, up to a certain degree, a language of their own.

segments.label: §92, claude source block2
segments.text: It differs, however, in that the former occurs even where the matter and form of the word-sound are perfectly felt, whereas here the opposite case is being spoken of.

segments.label: §92, claude source block3
segments.text: Thus a twofold breadth of the sound-form, as envelope of the concept, reveals itself here.

segments.label: §93, de source block1
segments.text: Wenn sich in den Wörtern einer Sprache die ursprüngliche Anschauungsweise der Gegenstände nach und nach verwischt, so ist nicht zu läugnen, dass eine gewisse Individualitaet und sinnliche Lebendigkeit in ihr untergeht.

segments.label: §93, de source block2
segments.text: Aber es ist darum nicht zu sagen, dass sie nicht vielleicht dadurch auf der andren Seite gewinnt.

segments.label: §93, de source block3
segments.text: Denn die Vorzüge der Sprachen werden nicht durch den partiellen Reichthum von Bildern und Begriffen bestimmt, den sie der Seele zuführen, sondern durch ihre Einwirkung auf das Denken und Empfinden überhaupt.

segments.label: §93, de source block4
segments.text: So gewährt z. B. die (90.) angeführte Bezeichnung der Gegenstände durch ihre Eigenschaften, solange sie in einer Sprache lebendig ist, grössere Fülle der Anschauung, aber sie hat auch, ohne anderer geringerer zu erwähnen, den Nachtheil, dass sie die Freiheit beim Vorstellen des Gegenstandes zu einseitig beschränkt, und, Substantiva zu sichtlich aus Adjectiven bildend, die Uebereinstimmung stört, in welcher die Sprache, der Natur auch in ihrer Form folgend, zum Ausdruck selbständiger Wesen in dieser auch mit Selbständigkeit begabte Wörter gebrauchen muss.

segments.label: §93, de source block5
segments.text: Viel angemessener wirkt das Uebereinkommen des Begriffs mit dem Laut nach dunklem Verwandtschaftsgefühl (83.), da die Seele dadurch gestimmt und geleitet, aber nicht in der Weise der Vorstellung beschränkt wird.

segments.label: §93, de source block6
segments.text: Wenn die Sprachuntersuchung sich auf diese Beziehungen richtet, sie in den Wörtern aufsucht, ohne sie hineinzulegen, und auf diese Weise den immer der Muttersprache, auch unbewusst, verwandten Sprachsinn der Nation weckt, und dadurch klarere Einsicht und ein feineres Gefühl der Sprache bewirkt; so kann die ursprüngliche Individualitaet der Wörter wieder heller ans Licht treten, und ordnet sich nun, ohne weiter zu schaden, der durch die Zeit freier und intellectueller gewordenen Auffassung der Gegenstände unter.

segments.label: §93, sol source block1
segments.text: When the original mode of intuition of objects gradually becomes blurred in the words of a language, a certain individuality and sensory vividness undeniably perish in it.

segments.label: §93, sol source block2
segments.text: The language may nevertheless gain in another respect by this very process.

segments.label: §93, sol source block3
segments.text: For what determines the merits of languages is their effect on thinking and feeling in general, beyond the particular riches of images and concepts they bring to the soul.

segments.label: §93, sol source block4
segments.text: For example, the designation of objects by their properties, mentioned in §90, affords a greater fullness of intuition as long as it remains alive in a language. But among its disadvantages is that it restricts freedom in forming a presentation of the object by favouring one side too much. By forming nouns too visibly from adjectives, it also disrupts the correspondence with nature that requires language, if it is to follow nature in its very form, to use words endowed with independence in that form to express independent beings.

segments.label: §93, sol source block5
segments.text: The accord of concept and sound through an obscure feeling of kinship (83) has a much more fitting effect, since it attunes and guides the soul while leaving its mode of presentation unrestricted.

segments.label: §93, sol source block6
segments.text: If linguistic inquiry attends to these relations, looks for them in words without reading them into the words, and in this way awakens the nation's sense of language, which always has an affinity with its mother tongue even without conscious awareness, it brings about clearer insight and a finer feeling for language. The original individuality of words can then come to light again more distinctly and, without doing further harm, take its place under a mode of apprehending objects that has grown freer and more intellectual with time.

segments.label: §93, muse source block1
segments.text: If in the words of a language the original mode of intuiting objects gradually becomes effaced, it is not to be denied that a certain individuality and sensible liveliness perishes in it.

segments.label: §93, muse source block2
segments.text: But it is not on that account to be said that it does not perhaps gain thereby on the other side.

segments.label: §93, muse source block3
segments.text: For the merits of languages are not determined by the partial wealth of images and concepts that they supply to the soul, but by their effect on thinking and feeling in general.

segments.label: §93, muse source block4
segments.text: Thus, for example, the designation of objects by their properties, cited at (90.), affords, so long as it is alive in a language, greater fullness of intuition, but it also has, not to mention other lesser ones, the disadvantage that it restricts too one-sidedly the freedom in presenting the object, and, forming substantives too visibly from adjectives, disturbs the agreement in which language, following nature also in its form, must, for the expression of independent beings, use in that form words also endowed with independence.

segments.label: §93, muse source block5
segments.text: Much more appropriately acts the agreement of the concept with the sound according to an obscure feeling of kinship (83.), since the soul is thereby attuned and guided, but not restricted in the manner of presentation.

segments.label: §93, muse source block6
segments.text: If linguistic investigation directs itself to these relations, seeks them out in the words without putting them into them, and in this way awakens the linguistic sense of the nation, which is always akin, even unconsciously, to the mother tongue, and thereby effects clearer insight and a finer feeling for the language, then the original individuality of the words can step forth again more brightly into the light, and now subordinates itself, without doing further harm, to the apprehension of objects that has in the course of time become freer and more intellectual.

segments.label: §93, claude source block1
segments.text: When in the words of a language the original mode of intuition of objects is gradually effaced, it cannot be denied that a certain individuality and sensuous liveliness perishes in it.

segments.label: §93, claude source block2
segments.text: But it cannot on that account be said that the language does not perhaps gain thereby on the other side.

segments.label: §93, claude source block3
segments.text: For the excellences of languages are not determined by the partial wealth of images and concepts which they bring to the soul, but by their effect on thinking and sentiment in general.

segments.label: §93, claude source block4
segments.text: Thus, for example, the designation of objects by their properties cited above (90.), so long as it is alive in a language, affords a greater fullness of intuition; but it also has, not to mention other, lesser ones, the disadvantage that it restricts too one-sidedly the freedom in presenting the object to oneself, and that, forming substantives too visibly out of adjectives, it disturbs the agreement in which language, following nature in its own form too, must use, for the expression of beings that are self-subsistent in nature, words likewise endowed with self-subsistence.

segments.label: §93, claude source block5
segments.text: Far more fitting in its effect is the accord of the concept with the sound according to an obscure feeling of affinity (83.), since the soul is thereby attuned and guided, but not restricted in the manner of presentation.

segments.label: §93, claude source block6
segments.text: When linguistic investigation turns to these relations, seeks them out in words without reading them into them, and in this way awakens the nation's linguistic sense, which is always akin, even unconsciously, to the mother tongue, and thereby brings about clearer insight and a finer feeling for the language, the original individuality of words can again come more brightly to light, and now subordinates itself, without doing further harm, to the apprehension of objects that has through time become freer and more intellectual.

segments.label: §94, de source block1
segments.text: Nicht leicht werden zwei Sprachen in der Form ihrer Wörter ein vollkommenes Gleichgewicht zwischen den verschiedenen Anregungen halten, welche die Seele dadurch erfährt.

segments.label: §94, de source block2
segments.text: Eine dieser Anregungen wird vorwalten vor der anderen, und auch die Kraft verschieden seyn, mit der, worauf vorzüglich die Klarheit und Bestimmtheit des Denkens beruht, diese Anregungen in dem Begriffe zur Vorstellung des Gegenstandes zusammenschlagen.

segments.label: §94, de source block3
segments.text: Forschungen dieser Art lassen sich nur an hochgebildeten Sprachen machen, allein auch das blosse Gefühl nimmt die Unterschiede wahr.

segments.label: §94, de source block4
segments.text: In einer herrscht eine grössere sinnliche Klarheit, eine andre stimmt mehr das Gefühl, eine dritte begnügt sich trockner mit logischer Bestimmung.

segments.label: §94, de source block5
segments.text: Diesen Charakter kann die sich ändernde Richtung der Nation abändern, aber, unaufhörlich seinen Einflüssen unterliegend, niemals verlassen.

segments.label: §94, de source block6
segments.text: Er bestimmt auch zum Theil den Gebrauch, den man von der Sprache macht, den mehr poetischen, philosophischen, wissenschaftlichen Charakter ihrer Literatur, und wird wieder durch diesen bestimmt.

segments.label: §94, sol source block1
segments.text: Two languages will scarcely maintain a perfect balance in the form of their words among the different stimuli that the soul receives through them.

segments.label: §94, sol source block2
segments.text: One stimulus will predominate over another. The force with which these stimuli converge in the concept to form the presentation of the object will also vary, and on it the clarity and determinacy of thinking chiefly depend.

segments.label: §94, sol source block3
segments.text: Only highly cultivated languages permit inquiries of this kind, yet feeling alone can also perceive the differences.

segments.label: §94, sol source block4
segments.text: In one language a greater sensory clarity prevails, another does more to attune feeling, and a third rests more drily content with logical determination.

segments.label: §94, sol source block5
segments.text: As the nation's direction changes, it can modify this character, but it can never leave it behind, since it is continually subject to its influences.

segments.label: §94, sol source block6
segments.text: This character also partly determines the use made of the language and the more poetic, philosophical or scientific character of its literature, which in turn helps determine it.

segments.label: §94, muse source block1
segments.text: Two languages will not easily keep, in the form of their words, a perfect equilibrium among the different excitations that the soul experiences through them.

segments.label: §94, muse source block2
segments.text: One of these excitations will predominate over another, and the force will also be different with which — and on this the clarity and determinateness of thinking pre-eminently rest — these excitations strike together in the concept into the presentation of the object.

segments.label: §94, muse source block3
segments.text: Investigations of this kind can be made only on highly cultivated languages, but mere feeling, too, perceives the differences.

segments.label: §94, muse source block4
segments.text: In one there reigns a greater sensible clarity, another attunes feeling more, a third contents itself more drily with logical determination.

segments.label: §94, muse source block5
segments.text: The changing direction of the nation can alter this character, but, incessantly subject to its influences, can never abandon it.

segments.label: §94, muse source block6
segments.text: It also partly determines the use that is made of the language, the more poetic, philosophical, scientific character of its literature, and is in turn determined by the latter.

segments.label: §94, claude source block1
segments.text: Not easily will two languages maintain, in the form of their words, a perfect equilibrium between the different stimuli which the soul thereby receives.

segments.label: §94, claude source block2
segments.text: One of these stimuli will predominate over the other, and the force too will differ with which these stimuli strike together in the concept into the presentation of the object, on which the clarity and determinacy of thinking chiefly rests.

segments.label: §94, claude source block3

segments.label: §94, claude source block4

segments.label: §94, claude source block5
segments.text: The changing orientation of the nation can modify this character, but, being unceasingly subject to its influences, can never abandon it.

segments.label: §94, claude source block6
segments.text: It also in part determines the use that is made of the language, the more poetic, philosophical or scientific character of its literature, and is in turn determined by this.

segments.label: §95, de source block1
segments.text: Bei der Materie der Wörter tritt nun die Natur der Gegenstände hinzu, und es entstehen mithin bei jedem Worte die Fragen : was fasst das Wort, als seinen Gegenstand, zusammen? wie bezeichnet es dies Zusammengefasste ? und welchen Nebenbegriff verbindet es, nach begleitendem Gefühle, mit dieser Bezeichnung?

segments.label: §95, de source block2
segments.text: Werden diese Fragen nach einander aus einem zwiefachen Standpunkte angestellt, einmal aus dem Einer Sprache in Rücksicht auf die Mannigfaltigkeit der Gegenstände, dann aus dem Standpunkte dieser in Rücksicht auf die Wörter mehrerer Sprachen, so wird, wenigstens der Richtung nach, das Verhältniss der Bezeichnung zum Bezeichneten erschöpft.

segments.label: §95, de source block3
segments.text: Die Sprache verfährt nemlich bei der Wortbildung auf eine gleichmässige Weise, und diese ist es, welche durch Prüfung einer bedeutenderen Anzahl von Wörtern erforscht werden muss.

segments.label: §95, sol source block1
segments.text: When we consider the matter of words, the nature of the objects also comes into play, and three questions arise for every word. What does the word bring together as its object? How does it designate what it has brought together? What subsidiary concept does it associate with this designation in accordance with the accompanying feeling?

segments.label: §95, sol source block2
segments.text: If these questions are put in turn from two standpoints, first from that of a single language with respect to the variety of objects, then from that of the objects with respect to the words of several languages, the relation of the designation to what is designated will have been covered exhaustively, at least as far as the directions of inquiry are concerned.

segments.label: §95, sol source block3
segments.text: For a language proceeds uniformly in forming words, and it is this uniform procedure that must be investigated by examining a substantial number of words.

segments.label: §95, muse source block1
segments.text: With the matter of words there now comes in addition the nature of the objects, and there thus arise, with every word, the questions: what does the word comprehend together as its object? how does it designate what is thus comprehended together? and what subsidiary concept, according to accompanying feeling, does it connect with this designation?

segments.label: §95, muse source block2
segments.text: If these questions are put in succession from a twofold standpoint, first from that of one language with respect to the manifoldness of objects, then from the standpoint of the latter with respect to the words of several languages, the relation of the designation to what is designated will be exhausted, at least as to direction.

segments.label: §95, muse source block3
segments.text: Language, namely, proceeds in word-formation in a uniform way, and it is this way that must be investigated through the examination of a considerable number of words.

segments.label: §95, claude source block1
segments.text: With the matter of words the nature of the objects now comes in as well, and with every word there accordingly arise the questions: what does the word gather together as its object? how does it designate what is thus gathered together? and what accessory concept does it, in accordance with accompanying feeling, connect with this designation?

segments.label: §95, claude source block2
segments.text: If these questions are put one after another from a twofold standpoint, first from that of one language with regard to the manifoldness of objects, then from the standpoint of the objects with regard to the words of several languages, the relation of the designation to what is designated is exhausted, at least as regards direction.

segments.label: §95, claude source block3
segments.text: For language proceeds in word-formation in a uniform manner, and it is this manner that must be explored by examining a considerable number of words.

segments.label: §96, de source block1
segments.text: Der materielle Gehalt der Wörter scheint durch die Gegenstände des Denkens von selbst bestimmt.

segments.label: §96, de source block2
segments.text: Die vergleichende Untersuchung mehrerer Sprachen zeigt aber das Gegentheil, und da das Wort nicht unmittelbar von dem Gegenstande, sondern von dessen Auffassung abhängt, ja viele Gegenstände erst von der Seele gebildet werden, so muss es nothwendig so seyn.

segments.label: §96, de source block3
segments.text: Das erste hier vorwaltende Gesetz ist nun das einer richtigen Eintheilung des Gedankenstoffs durch die Sprache, oder anders ausgedrückt, dass der Gegenstand des Worts von festen Gränzen umschrieben sey, alles enthalte, was zur Vollendung seines Begriffs gehört, und nichts, was ihm nicht wesentlich ist, sondern nur zufällig anhängt.

segments.label: §96, de source block4
segments.text: Selbst bei Ausdrücken für körperliche Gegenstände sind ihre Bedeutungen nicht immer den festen Naturgränzen angemessen, sondern schwanken zwischen ihnen herum; noch häufiger findet sich diese Unbestimmtheit bei intellectuellen Bezeichnungen; und ganz gewöhnlich ist es bei den Sprachen, mit welchen wir hier zunächst zu thun haben, dem Begriff Bestimmungen beigemischt zu finden, die seine Allgemeinheit stören, und die er nur zum Nachtheil der Deutlichkeit mit sich herumtragen muss.

segments.label: §96, de source block5
segments.text: Dagegen giebt es aber auch in mehreren Sprachen neue und vortreflich gebildete Begriffe, die als wahrhafte Erweiterungen des Denkens gelten müssen.

segments.label: §96, de source block6
segments.text: Denn der Besitz eines Worts für einen bisher nicht in diesen Gränzen gedachten Begriff ist, wenn es eine Masse Gedankenstoffes betrifft, die zu Gewinnung erweiterter Ansichten befördernd in das Denken eingreifen kann, von unermesslichem Gewinn.

segments.label: §96, de source block7
segments.text: In dieser Vertheilung der Begriffe auf die Wörter offenbart sich nun zunächst der Sinn der Nation für richtige und scharfe Naturauffassung und logische Genauigkeit; aber in höheren Beziehungen geht daraus das glückliche Schöpfungsvermögen des Geistes hervor.

segments.label: §96, de source block8
segments.text: Gewiss aber darf man sich dies nur sehr selten so vorstellen, als würde einem rein gedachten Begriff ein neues Wort gegeben; gewöhnlich wird nur ein bisher in niedrigerer oder unbestimmterer Bedeutung genommenes umgestempelt.

segments.label: §96, sol source block1
segments.text: The material content of words seems to be determined of itself by the objects of thought.

segments.label: §96, sol source block2
segments.text: A comparative study of several languages shows the contrary, and this must necessarily be so, since the word depends on the apprehension of the object rather than directly on the object itself, and many objects are formed in the first place by the soul.

segments.label: §96, sol source block3
segments.text: The first law that prevails here is that language must divide the material of thought correctly. In other words, the object of the word must be marked off by fixed boundaries and contain everything that goes to complete its concept and nothing that belongs to it merely incidentally and is inessential to it.

segments.label: §96, sol source block4
segments.text: Even the meanings of expressions for corporeal objects do not always correspond to the fixed boundaries in nature, but fluctuate between them. This indeterminacy occurs still more frequently in intellectual designations. In the languages with which we are primarily concerned here, it is quite common to find determinations mixed in with the concept that impair its generality and that it must carry about with it to the detriment of clarity.

segments.label: §96, sol source block5
segments.text: Several languages, however, also have new and excellently formed concepts that must count as genuine extensions of thinking.

segments.label: §96, sol source block6
segments.text: For having a word for a concept never before thought within these boundaries is of immeasurable benefit if it concerns a body of material that can enter into thinking in such a way as to help it attain broader views.

segments.label: §96, sol source block7
segments.text: This distribution of concepts among words reveals, first of all, the nation's sense for a correct and sharply defined apprehension of nature and for logical precision. In higher respects, however, from it emerges the mind's fortunate capacity for creation.

segments.label: §96, sol source block8
segments.text: We should certainly very seldom picture this as the giving of a new word to a concept thought in its purity. Usually it is simply a matter of restamping a word hitherto used in a lower or less determinate sense.

segments.label: §96, muse source block1
segments.text: The material content of words seems to be determined of itself by the objects of thinking.

segments.label: §96, muse source block2
segments.text: Comparative investigation of several languages, however, shows the opposite, and since the word depends not immediately on the object but on the apprehension of it, indeed many objects are only first formed by the soul, it must necessarily be so.

segments.label: §96, muse source block3
segments.text: The first law prevailing here is now that of a correct division of the thought-material by language, or, expressed otherwise, that the object of the word should be circumscribed by firm boundaries, should contain everything that belongs to the completion of its concept, and nothing that is not essential to it but only attaches to it accidentally.

segments.text: Even with expressions for corporeal objects, their meanings are not always appropriate to the firm boundaries in nature, but waver about among them; this indeterminateness is found still more frequently with intellectual designations; and it is quite usual, in the languages with which we are here immediately concerned, to find determinations mixed in with the concept that disturb its generality and that it must carry about with it only to the detriment of distinctness.

segments.label: §96, muse source block5
segments.text: On the other hand, however, there are also in several languages new and excellently formed concepts, which must count as genuine enlargements of thinking.

segments.label: §96, muse source block6
segments.text: For the possession of a word for a concept not hitherto thought within these boundaries is of immeasurable gain, when it concerns a mass of thought-material that can intervene in thinking so as to promote the winning of enlarged views.

segments.label: §96, muse source block7
segments.text: In this distribution of concepts over words there is now revealed, in the first instance, the nation's sense for correct and sharp apprehension of nature and for logical exactness; but in higher respects there emerges from it the fortunate creative capacity of the mind.

segments.label: §96, muse source block8
segments.text: Certainly, however, one must picture this to oneself only very rarely as if a new word were given to a purely thought concept; ordinarily only a word hitherto taken in a lower or more indeterminate meaning is re-stamped.

segments.label: §97, de source block1
segments.text: Das zweite Gesetz in Absicht des Inhaltes der Wörter ist, dass das Wort nicht zu viele und durch zu lockere VerwandtschaftsBande mit einander verknüpfte Bedeutungen in sich fasse.

segments.label: §97, de source block2
segments.text: Es findet sich dies in einigen Sprachen mehr als in andren, namentlich führt man darüber im Chinesischen und Sanskrit Klage.

segments.label: §97, de source block3
segments.text: Doch sollte man nicht vergessen, dass diese grösstentheils nur die Mangelhaftigkeit der Wörterbücher trifft, die, ohne Ordnung und Nachdenken, alle Bedeutungen, in welchen sich das Wort in einzelnen Stellen findet, auf einander folgen lassen, und aus jeder Stelle gerade die bestimmteste Bedeutung herausheben, zu welcher der Zusammenhang der Begriffe den natürlichen und einfachen Sinn des Worts hinüberzwängt.

segments.label: §97, de source block4
segments.text: Würde dies gehörig gewürdigt, und unterschiede man die Zeiten und Gattungen des Gebrauchs, so würde jene, jetzt allerdings, vorzüglich den Anfänger störende Vieldeutigkeit sehr zusammenschmelzen.

segments.label: §97, de source block5
segments.text: Wo sie jedoch nicht abgeläugnet werden kann, da fällt sie auf der einen Seite mit der oben (96.) gerügten Unbestimmtheit zusammen, die mehr als Eine Bestimmung des Begriffs, und mithin mehrere Begriffe zulässt, kann aber auf der andren auch aus zu scharfsinniger Ausspinnung eines Begriffs in alle von ihm ausgehende Fäden, oder aus Vorliebe zu allzu kühnen Metaphern entstehen, und mithin gerade den Sprachen sehr geistreicher Nationen eigen seyn.

segments.label: §97, de source block6
segments.text: Mit der Vieldeutigkeit der Wörter darf man jedoch nicht den vielumfassenden Umfang ihrer Bedeutung verwechseln.

segments.label: §97, de source block7
segments.text: Bei ihm bleibt diese doch einfach, und eine das Nachdenken wahrhaft befördernde Sprache muss gerade auch auf den höchsten Stufen der Abstraction, oder den niedrigsten der individualisirenden Bestimmung (da solche Wörter auf beiden entstehen können) den Gedanken geheftet haben.

segments.label: §97, de source block8
segments.text: Nur die Vielfachheit neben einander stehender concreter Bedeutungen, und die willkührliche Anwendung allgemeiner auf einen der vielen unter ihnen begriffenen stört die Bestimmtheit des Ausdrucks und die leichte Verständlichkeit.

segments.label: §97, sol source block1
segments.text: The second law concerning the content of words is that a word should not encompass too many meanings whose ties of kinship with one another are too loose.

segments.label: §97, sol source block2
segments.text: This is found more in some languages than in others. It is a complaint made particularly about Chinese and Sanskrit.

segments.label: §97, sol source block3
segments.text: Yet we should remember that the complaint mostly applies to the shortcomings of dictionaries. Without order or reflection, they list one after another all the meanings in which a word occurs in particular passages, singling out from each passage precisely the most specific meaning into which the connection among the concepts forces the word's natural and simple sense.

segments.label: §97, sol source block4
segments.text: If this were duly taken into account and distinctions were drawn between periods and kinds of usage, that multiplicity of meanings, which at present is indeed troublesome especially to beginners, would shrink considerably.

segments.label: §97, sol source block5
segments.text: Where it cannot be denied, however, it coincides on the one hand with the indeterminacy criticised above (96), which admits more than one determination of the concept and hence more than one concept. On the other hand, it may also arise from spinning out a concept with excessive ingenuity into all the threads that issue from it, or from a fondness for overbold metaphors, and may thus be characteristic precisely of the languages of highly ingenious nations.

segments.label: §97, sol source block6
segments.text: The multiplicity of meanings of words must, however, be distinguished from the wide scope of their meaning.

segments.label: §97, sol source block7
segments.text: However wide its scope, the meaning remains single, and a language that genuinely fosters reflection must have found a way to give thought a foothold even at the highest stages of abstraction or the lowest stages of individualising determination, since such words can arise at either.

segments.label: §97, sol source block8
segments.text: Only the coexistence of multiple concrete meanings and the arbitrary application of general meanings to one of the many concepts they encompass impair precision of expression and ease of understanding.

segments.label: §97, muse source block1
segments.text: The second law with respect to the content of words is that the word should not comprehend in itself too many meanings, and meanings connected with one another by too loose bonds of kinship.

segments.label: §97, muse source block2
segments.text: This is found in some languages more than in others; complaint is made of it in particular in Chinese and Sanskrit.

segments.label: §97, muse source block3
segments.text: Yet one should not forget that this complaint mostly hits only the defectiveness of dictionaries, which, without order and reflection, let all the meanings in which the word is found in individual passages follow one upon another, and from every passage single out precisely the most determinate meaning to which the connexion of the concepts constrains the natural and simple sense of the word over.

segments.label: §97, muse source block4
segments.text: If this were duly appreciated, and the periods and kinds of use were distinguished, that ambiguity, which at present admittedly disturbs the beginner in particular, would melt down a great deal.

segments.label: §97, muse source block5
segments.text: Where it cannot, however, be denied, it coincides on the one side with the indeterminateness censured above (96.), which allows more than one determination of the concept, and consequently several concepts, but on the other side it can also arise from too ingenious a spinning-out of a concept into all the threads issuing from it, or from a predilection for all too bold metaphors, and consequently be peculiar precisely to the languages of very ingenious nations.

segments.label: §97, muse source block6
segments.text: With the ambiguity of words, however, one must not confuse the widely comprehending scope of their meaning.

segments.label: §97, muse source block7
segments.text: With the latter, the meaning nonetheless remains simple, and a language that truly promotes reflection must precisely have fixed thought even at the highest levels of abstraction, or the lowest of individualizing determination (since such words can arise at both).

segments.label: §97, muse source block8
segments.text: Only the manifoldness of concrete meanings standing side by side, and the arbitrary application of general meanings to one of the many things comprehended under them, disturbs the determinateness of expression and ease of intelligibility.

On the other hand, it may also arise from spinning out a concept with excessive ingenuity into all the threads that issue from it, or from a fondness for overbold metaphors, and may thus be characteristic precisely of the languages of highly ingenious nations.

segments.label: §97, revised source block6
segments.text: The multiplicity of meanings of words must, however, be distinguished from the wide scope of their meaning.

segments.label: §97, revised source block7
segments.text: However wide its scope, the meaning remains single, and a language that genuinely fosters reflection must have found a way to give thought a foothold even at the highest stages of abstraction or the lowest stages of individualizing determination, since such words can arise at either.

segments.label: §97, revised source block8
segments.text: Only the coexistence of multiple concrete meanings and the arbitrary application of general meanings to one of the many concepts they encompass impair precision of expression and ease of understanding.

segments.label: §98, de source block1
segments.text: Unter der Art der Bezeichnung des Begriffes im Wort verstehe ich hier nicht die durch den Ton, obgleich diejenige, von der hier die Rede ist, den Ton bestimmt, und bisweilen mit ihm zusammenfällt.

segments.label: §98, de source block2
segments.text: Sonst aber ist vom Tone allgemein (73 — 82.) und besonders in Beziehung auf die Bedeutung (83.) schon im Vorigen gesprochen worden.

segments.label: §98, de source block3
segments.text: Hier ist von dem Inhalt des Wortes, also dem Begriffe, die Rede.

segments.label: §98, de source block4
segments.text: Allein der Begriff kann weder in seiner Definition, noch, wenn er einem körperlichen Gegenstand angehört, in dem ganzen Wesen desselben gegeben werden; das Wort muss ihn in Einheit gestalten (88.), das also, wodurch es ihn dem Geiste des Hörenden andeutet, ist, auch als Begriff, seine Bezeichnung.

segments.label: §98, de source block5
segments.text: Ursprünglich liegt diese Bezeichnung (die eigentlich nur in Beziehung auf den Hörenden eine solche, von Seiten des Sprechenden aber eine Auffassung ist) in jedem Wort, bei den den Naturlauten nachgebildeten in dem Tönen der Gegenstände, bei andren für körperliche Dinge in andren ihrer Eigenschaften, bei intellectuellen in den zu ihrer Andeutung gewählten Metaphern.

segments.label: §98, de source block6
segments.text: Denn indem der Begriff in einen Ton gekleidet wurde, musste sich die Zunge doch durch etwas bei der Wahl desselben bestimmen lassen, und dies konnte nur diese, den ganzen Begriff in Einem Punkte zusammenfassende Anschauungsweise seyn.

segments.label: §98, de source block7
segments.text: Diese selbst aber kann man sich nur sinnlich denken, theils weil sie zur Wahl des Tons leiten soll, theils weil die ganze Wortbildung (89.) in der Sphäre der Einbildungskraft schwebt.

segments.label: §98, de source block8
segments.text: In den meisten Fällen ist jedoch diese sinnliche Auffassungsweise des Gegenstandes, welche dem Tone vorausgieng, oder mit ihm zugleich, doch immer ihn bestimmend, entstand, nicht mehr aufzuspüren, und dann hängt sie noch bloss an der auf den Ton ausgeübten Wirkung, bisweilen auch nicht einmal mehr an dieser auf eine erkennbare Weise.

segments.label: §98, de source block9
segments.text: Im ersteren Fall ist der Lautcharakter des Worts (seine Härte oder Sanftheit, seine Helligkeit oder Dumpfheit u. s. f.), im letzteren bloss der Schall der articulirten Töne selbst die Bezeichnung des Wortinhalts.

segments.label: §98, de source block10
segments.text: Beispiele geben die drei deutschen Wörter: Fliege, Krähe, Gans.

segments.label: §98, de source block11
segments.text: Bei dem ersten ist die Bezeichnung des Begriffs das unaufhörlich wiederkehrende Fliegen, wodurch das Thier so vorzüglich lästig wird; bei dem zweiten das Geschrei des Vogels; bei dem dritten das blosse, aus dem Indischen stammende, und auch da nicht zu erklärende Wort.

segments.label: §98, de source block12
segments.text: Aehnliche Beispiele gewähren die Wörter für geistige Begriffe mit und ohne erkennbare Metaphern.

segments.label: §98, sol source block1
segments.text: In speaking here of the way the concept is designated in the word, I do not mean designation by sound, although the mode of designation under discussion determines the sound and sometimes coincides with it.

segments.label: §98, sol source block2
segments.text: Sound has already been discussed above, both generally (73–82) and with special reference to meaning (83).

segments.label: §98, sol source block3
segments.text: Here we are concerned with the content of the word, that is, the concept.

segments.label: §98, sol source block4
segments.text: But the concept cannot be given in its definition or, if it belongs to a corporeal object, in the whole being of that object. The word must shape it into a unity (88). What the word uses to indicate the concept to the hearer's mind therefore constitutes its designation, even though it too is a concept.

segments.label: §98, sol source block5
segments.text: This designation, which is properly a designation only in relation to the hearer and on the speaker's side is an apprehension, is originally present in every word. In words modelled on natural sounds it lies in the sounds the objects make, in other words for corporeal things it lies in other properties of those things, and in words for intellectual concepts it lies in the metaphors chosen to indicate them.

segments.label: §98, sol source block6
segments.text: For when the concept was clothed in a sound, something had to guide the tongue in choosing that sound, and this could only have been the mode of intuition that brings the entire concept together at a single point.

segments.label: §98, sol source block7
segments.text: This mode of intuition itself can only be conceived as sensory, partly because it is to guide the choice of sound, and partly because word formation as a whole hovers in the sphere of the imagination (89).

segments.label: §98, sol source block8
segments.text: In most cases, however, this sensory mode of apprehending the object, which preceded the sound or arose together with it but always determined it, can no longer be traced. It then survives only in the effect it had on the sound, and sometimes it is no longer recognisable even there.

segments.label: §98, sol source block9
segments.text: In the former case, the sound character of the word, its harshness or softness, its brightness or dullness and so on, is the designation of the word's content. In the latter case, the designation is simply the audible sound of the articulated sounds themselves.

segments.label: §98, sol source block10
segments.text: The three German words *Fliege* ‘fly’, *Krähe* ‘crow’ and *Gans* ‘goose’ furnish examples.

segments.label: §98, sol source block11
segments.text: In the first, the designation of the concept is the incessant flying that makes the animal so particularly troublesome. In the second, it is the bird's cry. In the third, it is simply the word itself, which comes from Indian and cannot be explained there either.

segments.label: §98, sol source block12
segments.text: Words for concepts of the mind, with and without recognisable metaphors, furnish similar examples.
