segments.label: §99, de source block1
segments.text: Diese Art der Begriffsbezeichnung könnte man die Selbstbedeutung der Wörter nennen.

segments.label: §99, de source block2
segments.text: Denn sie unterscheiden sich wirklich durch sie von andren, demselben Gegenstande gewidmeten.

segments.label: §99, de source block3
segments.text: Es ist in vielen Rücksichten wichtig nachzuforschen, ob in einer Sprache vielen Wörtern eine solche Selbstbedeutung eigen ist? und auch den schon (91.) angedeuteten Fall zu unterscheiden, ob dieselbe noch allgemein von dem Volke gefühlt wird, oder nur noch dem Forscher erkennbar da liegt ?

segments.label: §99, de source block4
segments.text: Da man das Vorherrschen der Selbstbedeutungen wohl mit Recht als das Ursprünglichere in den Sprachen ansehen muss, so lassen sich daraus Folgerungen auf die in ihr vorgegangenen Umänderungen ziehen.

segments.label: §99, de source block5
segments.text: Sie selbst aber, soweit sie sich mit Zuverlässigkeit offenbaren, sind wichtig zu untersuchen, weil sie die Richtung zeigen, nach welcher ein Volk die Natur aufgefasst, und das Geistige in sinnlicher Umhüllung der Sprache angeeignet hat.

segments.label: §99, de source block6
segments.text: Da man sich aber hier auf einem geschichtlichen Gebiete befinden soll, so muss man sich wohl hüten, dem Scharfsinn und der Einbildungskraft hierbei zuviel einzuräumen, und sich nur auf dasjenige beschränken, worauf sichere Spuren der Bildung führen.

segments.label: §99, sol source block1
segments.text: This mode of designating concepts might be called the self-meaning of words.

segments.label: §99, sol source block2
segments.text: For it is indeed by this that they differ from other words devoted to the same object.

segments.label: §99, sol source block3
segments.text: It is important in many respects to investigate whether many words in a language possess such a self-meaning, and also to make the distinction already indicated (91) between cases in which it is still generally felt by the people and those in which it remains discernible only to the investigator.

segments.label: §99, sol source block4
segments.text: Since the predominance of self-meanings must presumably be regarded as a more original condition of languages, conclusions can be drawn from it about the changes that have taken place in a language.

segments.label: §99, sol source block5
segments.text: The self-meanings themselves, insofar as they can be identified reliably, are important to study because they show the direction in which a people has apprehended nature and made what belongs to the mind its own in the sensory clothing of language.

segments.label: §99, sol source block6
segments.text: Since the inquiry here is meant to be historical, however, we must take care to give ingenuity and imagination no more scope than is warranted, and restrict ourselves to what reliable traces of word formation lead us to.

segments.label: §100, de source block1
segments.text: Der sinnliche Stoff des Wortes, von dem wir hier reden, ist die Handhabe, an welcher der Geist die intellectuellen Begriffe auffasst, und wenn man dem Gange der Natur getreu bleiben will, muss man sich die Bezeichnung derselben in der Sprache nicht als vom Begriff zur Bezeichnung herab-, sondern, umgekehrt, zu ihm hinaufsteigend denken.

segments.label: §100, de source block2
segments.text: Es ist überall in der Menschheit so, dass sich aus Erscheinungen, die durch die blosse Fruchtbarkeit zeugender Kräfte, wie zufällig, ins Daseyn treten, sich ein Ganzes aufbaut, aus dem nachher dem beobachtenden Geiste die Einheit einer Idee entgegenstrahlt, und nicht anders ist es auch in der Sprache.

segments.label: §100, de source block3
segments.text: In der bunten Mannigfaltigkeit der Töne, welche die Wahrnehmung der Natur, das Bedürfniss der Mittheilung, und die gesellschaftliche Geschwätzigkeit hervorlockt, entdeckt die Seele, und in dem Grade häufiger und genievoller, in dem ihr selbst höhere intellectuelle Kraft und feinerer Sprachsinn beiwohnt, die geistigen Beziehungen, und prägt die vorhandenen Wörter in ihnen entsprechenden Bedeutungen aus.

segments.label: §100, de source block4
segments.text: Nicht durch ein gleichsam dumpfes, mit Eintheilen und Zergliedern beschäftigtes Brüten über dem Ideenstoff, sondern durch die Befruchtung der Naturmasse der Töne durch einen regen, immer auf das Höhere gerichteten Geist, entsteht in den Sprachen reicher und tiefer Ideengehalt in geistvoll ihm angeeigneten Wörtern.

segments.label: §100, sol source block1
segments.text: The sensory material of the word that we are discussing here is the handle by which the mind apprehends intellectual concepts. If we wish to follow the course of nature, we must think of their designation in language as ascending to the concept, reversing the imagined descent from concept to designation.

segments.label: §100, sol source block2
segments.text: Throughout human life, phenomena that come into existence seemingly by chance, through the mere fertility of generative forces, build up into a whole from which the unity of an idea later shines forth to the observing mind. So it is with language too.

segments.label: §100, sol source block3
segments.text: In the colourful variety of sounds drawn forth by the perception of nature, the need to communicate and social talkativeness, the soul discovers relations of the mind and stamps existing words with corresponding meanings. It does so more often and with greater genius in proportion to its own intellectual power and the refinement of its sense of language.

segments.label: §100, sol source block4
segments.text: A rich and deep content of ideas arises in languages, in words ingeniously adapted to that content, when an active mind, ever directed towards higher things, fertilises the natural mass of sounds, and not by a kind of dull brooding over the material of ideas, occupied with dividing and dissecting it.

segments.label: §100, muse source block1
segments.text: The sensible material of the word, of which we are speaking here, is the handle by which the mind grasps intellectual concepts, and if one wishes to remain true to the course of nature, one must think of their designation in language not as descending from concept to designation, but, conversely, as ascending up to it.

segments.label: §100, muse source block2
segments.text: It is everywhere in mankind as follows: out of appearances that step into existence, as it were accidentally, through the mere fruitfulness of generating powers, a whole builds itself up, out of which afterwards the unity of an idea radiates towards the observing mind, and it is no different in language.

segments.label: §100, muse source block3
segments.text: In the colourful manifoldness of tones which the perception of nature, the need of communication, and social talkativeness entice forth, the soul discovers — and the more frequently and the more full of genius, the more higher intellectual power and finer linguistic sense is present in it itself — the mental relations, and stamps out the words that are present in meanings corresponding to them.

segments.label: §100, muse source block4
segments.text: Not through a sort of dull brooding over the idea-material, occupied with dividing and dissecting, but through the fertilization of the natural mass of tones by a lively mind, always directed towards what is higher, there arises in languages a rich and deep idea-content in words ingeniously appropriated to it.

segments.label: §101, de source block1
segments.text: Das Wort, als Bezeichnung des Begriffs, ist verwandt mit dem Zeichen und dem Symbol.

segments.label: §101, de source block2
segments.text: Es ist aber hier der Ort diese drei Begriffe genau festzustellen, und zu zeigen, dass das Wort zwar mit den beiden andren Eigenschaften theilt, aber, seiner innersten Natur nach, von beiden verschieden ist.

segments.label: §101, de source block3
segments.text: Insofern es den Begriff durch seinen Laut hervorruft, erfüllt es allerdings den Zweck eines Zeichens, aber es geht dadurch gänzlich aus der Classe der Zeichen heraus, dass das Bezeichnete ein von seinem Zeichen unabhängiges Daseyn hat, der Begriff aber erst selbst seine Vollendung durch das Wort erhält, und beide nicht von einander getrennt werden können.

segments.label: §101, de source block4
segments.text: Dies zu verkennen, und die Wörter als blosse Zeichen anzusehen, ist der Grundirrthum, der alle Sprachwissenschaft und alle richtige Würdigung der Sprache zerstört.

segments.label: §101, de source block5
segments.text: Insofern das Wort den Begriff in einen sinnlichen Stoff vor der Einbildungskraft verwandelt, gleicht es dem Symbol.

segments.label: §101, de source block6
segments.text: Denn es schiebt der Idee eine Gestalt unter, und abstrahirt bei dem körperlichen Gegenstand von der Totalität seiner Wirklichkeit, indem es ihn an Einem Merkmale fest hält, und ihn in diesem durch etwas, ihm fremdes, einen Ton, bezeichnet.

segments.label: §101, de source block7
segments.text: Der Laut schliesst also, auf diese Weise einer Hieroglyphe gleich, den Begriff in sich.

segments.label: §101, de source block8
segments.text: Im Symbol wird Sinnliches und Unsinnliches, einander gegenseitig durchdringend, als Eins angesehen, dieses sich in jenem offenbarend, jenes sich zu diesem erweiternd; Idee und Körperstoff fallen zusammen.

segments.label: §101, de source block9
segments.text: Bei dem Worte lässt sich der Begriff auch nicht rein abscheiden vom Laute, nicht an sich, da er nicht ohne Sprache gedacht werden kann, nicht von dem ihm bestimmt in einer Sprache eignen, weil er zugleich dessen Individualitaet an sich trägt.

segments.label: §101, de source block10
segments.text: Dennoch ist das Wort durchaus vom Symbole verschieden.

segments.label: §101, de source block11
segments.text: Dieses verlangt eine vollständige, für sich bestehende Naturform, die auch ohne alle Beziehung auf eine inwohnende Idee betrachtet werden kann, aus der aber, so wie sie sich als Symbol darthut, die Idee aus allen Theilen hervorstrahlt.

segments.label: §101, de source block12
segments.text: Der Laut im Wort (als dessen jener Naturform entsprechender sinnlicher Stoff) ist hingegen nichts ohne Beziehung auf den Begriff, da er ausschliesslich die Bestimmung hat, diesen gestaltet hervorzurufen.

segments.label: §101, de source block13
segments.text: Es ist daher ein ganz verschiedenes Zusammenfallen des Sinnlichen und Unsinnlichen im Symbol und im Worte ; in diesem sind Laut und Begriff, ohne nur eine Trennung zuzulassen, und jeder für sich unvollständig, Eins und machen Ein Wesen aus, aber der Laut weicht gewissermassen dem Begriff, den er nur hervorrufen und gestalten soll.

segments.label: §101, de source block14
segments.text: Im Symbol ist die Naturform selbständig zugleich mit der sie durchdringenden Idee, und behauptet vorzugsweise ihre Rechte, beide sind dasselbe, da aus jedem Punkte der einen die andere vorstrahlt, aber sie sind nicht Eins.

segments.label: §101, de source block15
segments.text: Die Naturform bleibt auch ohne in ihr gedachte Idee, in Allem, wodurch sie im Symbol galt, wie der Körper, wenn ihn die Seele verlässt.

segments.label: §101, de source block16
segments.text: Wörter und Wortlaute können aber, wie alle andren Gegenstände, in ihrer Beschaffenheit und Zahl und in Zusammenhang mit ihrer Bedeutung, als Symbole behandelt werden, und so mag es wohl zu verstehen seyn, wenn von den Aegyptischen Priestern erzählt wird, dass sie die Götter durch das an einander gereihte Austönen der sieben Vocale feierten.

segments.label: §101, sol source block1
segments.text: The word, as the designation of the concept, is akin to the sign and the symbol.

segments.label: §101, sol source block2
segments.text: This is the place to establish these three concepts precisely and to show that although the word shares properties with the other two, in its innermost nature it differs from both.

segments.label: §101, sol source block3
segments.text: Insofar as the word evokes the concept through its sound, it does indeed fulfil the purpose of a sign. Yet what takes it altogether out of the class of signs is that what a sign designates has an existence independent of its sign, whereas the concept itself attains completion only through the word, and the two cannot be separated.

segments.label: §101, sol source block4
segments.text: To fail to recognise this and to regard words as mere signs is the fundamental error that destroys all science of language and all proper appreciation of language.

segments.label: §101, sol source block5
segments.text: Insofar as the word transforms the concept into sensory material before the imagination, it resembles the symbol.

segments.label: §101, sol source block6
segments.text: For it supplies the idea with a shape and, in the case of a corporeal object, abstracts from the entirety of its reality by holding it fast by a single feature and designating it in that feature by something foreign to it, a sound.

segments.label: §101, sol source block7
segments.text: The sound thus contains the concept within itself, like a hieroglyph.

segments.label: §101, sol source block8
segments.text: In the symbol, the sensory and the non-sensory interpenetrate and are regarded as one. The non-sensory reveals itself in the sensory and the sensory expands into the non-sensory. Idea and corporeal material coincide.

segments.label: §101, sol source block9
segments.text: In the word, too, the concept cannot be cleanly separated from sound, whether from sound as such, since the concept cannot be thought without language, or from the particular sound that belongs to it in a given language, since it also bears that sound's individuality.

segments.label: §101, sol source block10
segments.text: Nevertheless, the word differs entirely from the symbol.

segments.label: §101, sol source block11
segments.text: The symbol requires a complete, self-subsisting natural form that can be considered quite apart from any idea dwelling within it, but from every part of which the idea shines forth once the form manifests itself as a symbol.

segments.label: §101, sol source block12
segments.text: The sound in the word, as its sensory material corresponding to that natural form, is in contrast nothing apart from its relation to the concept, since its sole function is to evoke the concept in a definite shape.

segments.label: §101, sol source block13
segments.text: The sensory and the non-sensory therefore coincide in quite different ways in the symbol and in the word. In the word, sound and concept are inseparable and each is incomplete on its own. They are one and constitute a single being, but the sound in a sense gives way to the concept, which it is meant only to evoke and shape.

segments.label: §101, sol source block14
segments.text: In the symbol, the natural form stands independently alongside the idea that permeates it and has the stronger claim to its own rights. The two are the same, since from every point of the one the other shines forth, but they are not one.

segments.label: §101, sol source block15
segments.text: Even when no idea is thought within it, the natural form remains in all the respects in which it had import in the symbol, like the body when the soul leaves it.

segments.label: §101, sol source block16
segments.text: Words and word sounds, however, like all other objects, may be treated as symbols with regard to their character and number and in connection with their meaning. This may be how we should understand the account that the Egyptian priests celebrated the gods by sounding out the seven vowels in succession.

segments.label: §101, muse source block7

segments.label: §101, muse source block9

segments.label: §101, muse source block10
segments.text: Nevertheless the word is thoroughly different from the symbol.

segments.label: §101, muse source block11
segments.text: The latter demands a complete natural form, subsisting for itself, which can also be considered without any relation to a indwelling idea, but from which, as soon as it shows itself as symbol, the idea radiates forth from all its parts.

segments.label: §101, muse source block12
segments.text: The sound in the word (as the word's sensible material, corresponding to that natural form), by contrast, is nothing without relation to the concept, since it has exclusively the determination to call the latter forth in shaped form.

segments.label: §101, muse source block13
segments.text: It is therefore a quite different coinciding of the sensible and the non-sensible in symbol and in word; in the latter, sound and concept, without even admitting a separation, and each incomplete for itself, are one and make up one being, but the sound in a certain measure yields to the concept, which it is only to call forth and to shape.

segments.label: §101, muse source block14
segments.text: In the symbol the natural form is independent at the same time as the idea interpenetrating it, and maintains its rights pre-eminently; both are the same, since from every point of the one the other radiates forth, but they are not one.

segments.label: §101, muse source block15

segments.label: §101, muse source block16

segments.text: Das Symbol verlangt ausdrücklich die Verschmelzung des Unsinnlichen mit dem Sinnlichen ; der Körper soll nicht bloss Körper, die Idee nicht bloss Idee seyn.

segments.label: §102, de source block2
segments.text: Die Sprache dagegen ist ein rein geistiges Streben, gehend (24.) vom Denken zum Denken, nur auf diesem Wege gezwungen Körperstoff annehmend, und nur so wenig, als möglich, nur den leichten, gleich verhallenden Ton, und von diesem nur den articulirten, den mit möglichster Abschneidung alles Geräusches zum bloss hörbaren Verhältniss zurückgeführten.

segments.label: §102, de source block3
segments.text: Der symbolisirende Verstand und der Sinn und das Genie zur Sprache stehen daher in natürlichem Gegensatz mit einander.

segments.label: §102, de source block4
segments.text: Sie gewöhnen auch den Geist an eine ganz verschiedene Weile in der Folge der Vorstellungen, was in der Bildung der Köpfe bei Individuen und Nationen einer der hauptsächlichsten Punkte ist.

segments.label: §102, de source block5
segments.text: Das Symbolisiren führt zur Vertiefung in den einzelnen Gegenstand, dessen Schaale gleichsam durchdrungen werden muss, um die sie durchstrahlende Idee wahrzunehmen ; der Sprachsinn reisst den Geist in unaufhaltsam lebendiger Bewegung fort.

segments.label: §102, de source block6
segments.text: Denn er folgt der Flüchtigkeit des Gedanken und strebt nach seiner Unendlichkeit.

segments.label: §102, de source block7
segments.text: Da Jedes Wort zu einer Reihe gehört, und keines seinen Begriff vollkommen erschöpft, so geht er von einem zum anderen über, und durchläuft die sich nach und nach entwickelnde Gedankenfolge, nur die leichtesten, den unterbrochnen Zusammenhang am wenigsten durch Pausen störenden Einschnitte hinter sich lassend.

segments.label: §102, sol source block1
segments.text: The symbol expressly requires the fusion of the non-sensory with the sensory. The body is to be more than merely body, and the idea more than merely idea.

segments.label: §102, sol source block2
segments.text: Language, by contrast, is a purely mental striving that proceeds from thinking to thinking (24). Only on this passage is it compelled to take on corporeal material, and it takes on as little as possible, merely the light sound that fades as soon as it is heard, and of that only the articulated sound, reduced to a merely audible relation by cutting away as much noise as possible.

segments.label: §102, sol source block3
segments.text: The understanding that symbolises thus stands in natural opposition to the sense and genius for language.

segments.label: §102, sol source block4
segments.text: They also accustom the mind to very different lengths of pause in the succession of presentations, a matter of the first importance in the education of minds, whether of individuals or of nations.

segments.label: §102, sol source block5
segments.text: Symbolising leads to absorption in the individual object, whose shell must, as it were, be penetrated to perceive the idea shining through it. The sense of language sweeps the mind along in an irrepressibly lively movement.

segments.label: §102, sol source block6
segments.text: For it follows the fleeting movement of thought and strives towards thought's infinity.

segments.label: §102, sol source block7
segments.text: Since every word belongs to a series and none fully exhausts its concept, the sense of language passes from one to the next and runs through the gradually unfolding succession of thoughts, leaving behind only the slightest breaks, whose pauses disturb the continuity they interrupt as little as possible.

segments.label: §103, de source block1
segments.text: Wo in den Ton des Worts das dunkle Gefühl der Beschaffenheit des Gegenstandes gelegt ist, wie in Stärke die Festigkeit, in Wolke, Wolle, Wald die schwankende Unbestimmtheit der Begränzung und des Zusammentretens der Theile vor dem Auge, da liegt in der That etwas Symbolisches in demselben.

segments.label: §103, de source block2
segments.text: Denn diese Beschaffenheit leuchtet alsdann aus dem Tone hervor, und dieser wirkt wie ein Bild derselben auf das Gefühl.

segments.label: §103, de source block3
segments.text: Aber der Wortlaut selbst kann darum doch kein Symbol genannt werden.

segments.label: §103, de source block4
segments.text: Denn seine Bedeutung, auf welche dieser sein symbolischer Theil nur mitwirkt, wird nicht daraus erkannt, sondern auf dem ganz verschiedenen Wege, welchen die Sprache überhaupt nimmt.

segments.label: §103, de source block5
segments.text: Noch bestimmter und häufiger liegt das Symbolische in dem Begriffe der Wörter, und gerade in dem, wovon wir hier reden, der sinnlichen Bezeichnung derselben.

segments.label: §103, de source block6
segments.text: Es ist dies bei allen metaphorischen Ausdrücken der Fall.

segments.label: §103, de source block7
segments.text: Aber auch dies ändert die Natur des Wortes nicht ab.

segments.label: §103, de source block8
segments.text: Dies unläugbare Symbolisiren der Sprache beweist, dass die glückliche Anlage dazu den Sprachsinn wohlthätig unterstützt, es wird aber nun auch vollständig deutlich, in welchem Verhältniss beide zu einander stehen.

segments.label: §103, de source block9
segments.text: Es muss Gäbe und Drang vorhanden seyn, das Sinnliche und Unsinnliche in einander aufzusuchen und einzuhüllen, aber die helle und klare Richtung auf das Geistige muss vorherrschen, und durch die lebendige Stärke der Denkkraft die Neigung niederdrücken, gerade bei dem dunkeln und geheimnissvollen Zusammenhange beider zu verweilen.

segments.label: §103, sol source block1
segments.text: Where an obscure feeling for the character of the object has been put into the sound of a word, there is indeed something symbolic in that sound. Thus in *Stärke* ‘strength’ there is firmness, and in *Wolke* ‘cloud’, *Wolle* ‘wool’ and *Wald* ‘forest’ there is the wavering indefiniteness of the boundaries and of how the parts come together to the eye.

segments.label: §103, sol source block2
segments.text: For in such cases this character shines forth from the sound, which acts upon feeling like an image of it.

segments.label: §103, sol source block3
segments.text: Yet this does not make the word sound itself a symbol.

segments.label: §103, sol source block4
segments.text: For its symbolic part merely contributes to its meaning, which is apprehended by the quite different route that language takes in general.

segments.label: §103, sol source block5
segments.text: The symbolic is present still more distinctly and frequently in the concepts of words, precisely in what we are discussing here, their sensory designation.

segments.label: §103, sol source block6
segments.text: This is the case with all metaphorical expressions.

segments.label: §103, sol source block7
segments.text: Yet this, too, leaves the nature of the word intact.

segments.label: §103, sol source block8
segments.text: This undeniable symbolising activity of language shows that a natural gift for it benefits the sense of language. The relation between the two now also becomes completely clear.

segments.label: §103, sol source block9
segments.text: There must be both a gift and an impulse to seek the sensory and the non-sensory in one another and to wrap each in the other. But the bright and clear orientation towards what belongs to the mind must predominate and, by the living strength of the power of thought, suppress the inclination to linger on the very obscurity and mystery of the connection between them.

segments.label: §103, muse source block1
segments.text: Where the obscure feeling of the constitution of the object is laid into the tone of the word, as in *Stärke* firmness, in *Wolke*, *Wolle*, *Wald* the wavering indeterminateness of delimitation and of the coming-together of the parts before the eye, there there does in fact lie something symbolic in it.

segments.label: §103, muse source block2
segments.text: For this constitution then shines forth from the tone, and the latter acts like an image of it on feeling.

segments.label: §103, muse source block3
segments.text: But the word-sound itself can nonetheless not on that account be called a symbol.

segments.label: §103, muse source block4
segments.text: For its meaning, on which this its symbolic part only co-operates, is not recognized from it, but on the quite different path which language in general takes.

segments.label: §103, muse source block5
segments.text: Still more determinately and more frequently, what is symbolic lies in the concept of words, and precisely in that of which we are speaking here, their sensible designation.

segments.label: §103, muse source block6
segments.text: This is the case with all metaphorical expressions.

segments.label: §103, muse source block7
segments.text: But this, too, does not alter the nature of the word.

segments.label: §103, muse source block8
segments.text: This undeniable symbolizing of language proves that the fortunate disposition for it beneficially supports linguistic sense, but now it also becomes fully clear in what relation the two stand to one another.

segments.label: §103, muse source block9
segments.text: Gift and urge must be present to seek out the sensible and the non-sensible in one another and to wrap the one in the other, but the bright and clear direction towards what is mental must predominate, and through the living strength of the power of thought suppress the inclination to tarry precisely with the obscure and mysterious connexion of the two.

segments.text: This undeniable symbolizing on the part of language proves that a happy aptitude for it beneficially supports the linguistic sense; but it now also becomes completely clear in what relation the two stand to one another.

segments.label: §104, de source block1
segments.text: Da hier von der in dem Wort liegenden sinnlichen Vorstellung und von seiner Selbstbedeutung die Rede ist, so entsteht die Frage, was sich eigentlich die Seele bei dem Wort sinnlich vorstellt? ob den Gegenstand im Ganzen? oder die in dem Wort daran aufgefassten Eigenschaften ? oder etwas dem durch das Wort erregten Gefühle entsprechendes Unbestimmtes ? oder bei Völkern, die schon lang ein Alphabet besitzen, die Schriftzüge ?

segments.label: §104, de source block2
segments.text: Dies durch Selbstbeobachtung zu erforschen dürfte schwierig seyn.

segments.label: §104, de source block3
segments.text: Schon die Absicht verändert den Gegenstand der Beobachtung, und gewiss wechselt auch die Vorstellung selbst nach der Individualitaet und den Umständen durch alle jene Fälle durch.

segments.label: §104, de source block4
segments.text: Was dagegen, nicht bloss als gewiss, sondern auch als entscheidend für das Erkennen der wahren Natur der Sprache festgehalten werden muss, ist dass das Wort den Gegenstand nie anders in die Vorstellung bringt, und diese nie länger bei ihm verweilen lässt, als es die jedesmalige Gedankenverknüpfung erfordert, der es ihn unterordnet, und in die es ihn, als ein Glied, einflicht.

segments.label: §104, de source block5
segments.text: Dies liegt in der Natur des Worts, das ja nur darum an die Stelle der wirklichen Gegenstände Töne setzt, um dieselben durch diese Vermittlung in Gedanken zu verwandeln; es liegt ferner darin, dass die durch mehrere Worte ausgedrückte Gedankenreihe, genau genommen,

segments.label: §104, de source block6
segments.text: Eins, und die Rede ein Ganzes ist, wo die Einschnitte immer zugleich den Zweck haben, den Bau, als Ganzes, vorzugsweise sichtbar zu machen.

segments.label: §104, de source block7
segments.text: Es ist daher eine der wichtigsten Eigenschaften des Worts, gerade das und nicht mehr in der Vorstellung anzuregen, als der Gebrauch bedarf.

segments.label: §104, de source block8
segments.text: Dies wird nun zwar grossentheils bewirkt durch die angemessene Verbindung mit andren bestimmenden Worten und durch die ganze der Seele des Hörenden gegebene Richtung.

segments.label: §104, de source block9
segments.text: Aber es liegt zum Theil auch in der Bildung des Worts, welches in dieser Hinsicht Reinheit, Schärfe, Nüchternheit in der Bestimmung des Begriffs, und volle Angemessenheit zu einem klar gedachten Zwecke besitzen muss.

segments.label: §104, de source block10
segments.text: Hieraus entsteht zugleich die Nothwendigkeit mehrerer Ausdrücke für denselben Gegenstand nach der Verschiedenheit des Gebrauchs, in verschiedener Andeutung der an ihm herausgehobenen Seiten, und in verschiedenen Seelenstimmungen.

segments.label: §104, de source block11
segments.text: Denn auch diese kommen hier in Betrachtung neben dem logischen Zweck der Rede, und wirken vorzugsweise auf die Art der im Worte liegenden sinnlichen Vorstellung.

segments.label: §104, de source block12
segments.text: Denn dasselbe Wort ist offenbar von verschiedenen in einem dichterischen, und in einem wissenschaftlichen Vortrage begleitet.

segments.label: §104, de source block13
segments.text: Auch hier schafft aber die Sprache mehr zufällig, als absichtlich, und die sinnverwandten Wörter sind oft nur Wörter, aus andren Dialecten mit darin aufgenommenem Nebenbegriff übergetragen.

segments.label: §104, sol source block1
segments.text: Since we are concerned here with the sensory presentation contained in the word and with its self-meaning, the question arises of what the soul actually presents to itself in sensory terms when it encounters the word. Is it the object as a whole? The properties of the object apprehended in the word? Something indefinite corresponding to the feeling aroused by the word? Or, among peoples that have long had an alphabet, the written characters?

segments.label: §104, sol source block2
segments.text: This would probably be difficult to ascertain by self-observation.

segments.label: §104, sol source block3
segments.text: The very intention to observe changes the object of observation, and the presentation itself surely varies across all those possibilities according to the individual and the circumstances.

segments.label: §104, sol source block4
segments.text: One point must be held to be both certain and decisive for recognising the true nature of language. The word brings the object into presentation only in the way required by the particular connection of thoughts to which it subordinates the object and into which it weaves it as a component. The word allows the presentation to dwell on the object only as long as that connection requires.

segments.label: §104, sol source block5
segments.text: This lies in the nature of the word, which substitutes sounds for actual objects only to turn them into thoughts through that mediation. It lies further in the fact that the sequence of thoughts expressed by several words is, strictly speaking,

segments.label: §104, sol source block6
segments.text: one, and that discourse is a whole whose divisions always serve at the same time to make the structure as a whole especially apparent.

segments.label: §104, sol source block7
segments.text: It is therefore one of the most important properties of the word that it should evoke in presentation exactly what its use requires and no more.

segments.label: §104, sol source block8
segments.text: This is indeed achieved largely by combining the word appropriately with other words that determine it and by the overall direction given to the hearer's soul.

segments.label: §104, sol source block9
segments.text: But it also depends in part on the formation of the word, which in this respect must have purity, sharpness and sobriety in the determination of the concept and be fully suited to a clearly conceived purpose.

segments.label: §104, sol source block10
segments.text: This also accounts for the need for several expressions for the same object, according to differences of use, differences in the indication of the aspects singled out in the object, and differences in the states of mind in which the expressions are used.

segments.label: §104, sol source block11
segments.text: For these states of mind must be considered here alongside the logical purpose of discourse, and they bear chiefly on the kind of sensory presentation contained in the word.

segments.label: §104, sol source block12
segments.text: For the same word is plainly accompanied by different words in poetic and in scientific discourse.

segments.label: §104, sol source block13
segments.text: Here too, however, language creates more by chance than by design, and words akin in sense are often simply words adopted from other dialects together with a subsidiary concept acquired there.

segments.label: §104, muse source block1
segments.text: Since what is at issue here is the sensible presentation lying in the word and its self-meaning, the question arises: what, properly, does the soul sensibly present to itself with the word? the object as a whole? or the properties apprehended in it in the word? or something indeterminate corresponding to the feeling excited through the word? or, in peoples that have long possessed an alphabet, the written characters?

segments.label: §104, muse source block2
segments.text: To investigate this through self-observation would probably be difficult.

segments.label: §104, muse source block3
segments.text: The intention alone already alters the object of observation, and certainly the presentation itself, too, changes according to individuality and circumstances through all those cases.

segments.label: §104, muse source block4
segments.text: What, by contrast, must be held fast not only as certain but also as decisive for recognizing the true nature of language is that the word never brings the object into presentation otherwise, and never lets the latter tarry with it longer, than the connexion of thoughts of the moment requires — the connexion to which it subordinates it and into which it interweaves it as a member.

segments.label: §104, muse source block5
segments.text: This lies in the nature of the word, which indeed puts tones in the place of real objects only in order, through this mediation, to transform the latter into thoughts; it lies further in the fact that the series of thoughts expressed through several words is, strictly taken,

segments.label: §104, muse source block6
segments.text: one, and speech is a whole, in which the incisions always at the same time have the purpose of making the structure, as a whole, pre-eminently visible.

segments.label: §104, muse source block7
segments.text: It is therefore one of the most important properties of the word to excite in presentation precisely that, and no more, than use requires.

segments.label: §104, muse source block8
segments.text: This is indeed effected for the most part through the appropriate connexion with other determining words and through the whole direction given to the hearer's soul.

segments.label: §104, muse source block9
segments.text: But it lies in part also in the formation of the word, which in this respect must possess purity, sharpness, sobriety in the determination of the concept, and full appropriateness to a clearly thought purpose.

segments.label: §104, muse source block10
segments.text: From this there arises at the same time the necessity of several expressions for the same object according to the difference of use, in different indication of the sides singled out in it, and in different moods of soul.

segments.label: §104, muse source block11
segments.text: For these, too, come into consideration here alongside the logical purpose of speech, and act pre-eminently on the kind of sensible presentation lying in the word.

segments.label: §104, muse source block12
segments.text: For the same word is manifestly accompanied by different ones in a poetic delivery and in a scientific one.

segments.label: §104, muse source block13
segments.text: Here, too, however, language creates more accidentally than intentionally, and the words akin in sense are often only words transferred from other dialects with the subsidiary concept taken up in them there.

segments.label: §104, claude source block1
segments.text: Since the sensuous presentation lying in the word and its self-meaning are here in question, the question arises what the soul actually presents to itself sensuously with the word: the object as a whole? or the properties apprehended in it in the word? or something indeterminate corresponding to the feeling aroused by the word? or, among peoples that have long possessed an alphabet, the written characters?

segments.label: §104, claude source block2
segments.text: To explore this by self-observation would probably be difficult.

segments.label: §104, claude source block3
segments.text: The intention already alters the object of observation, and certainly the presentation itself also varies, according to individuality and circumstances, through all those cases.

segments.label: §104, claude source block4
segments.text: What, on the other hand, must be held fast not merely as certain but also as decisive for recognizing the true nature of language is that the word never brings the object into presentation otherwise, and never lets presentation dwell on it longer, than is required by the connection of thought of the moment, to which it subordinates the object and into which it weaves it as a link.

segments.label: §104, claude source block5
segments.text: This lies in the nature of the word, which after all puts tones in the place of actual objects only in order to transform these, by this mediation, into thoughts; it lies further in the fact that the series of thoughts expressed by several words is, strictly taken,

segments.label: §104, claude source block6
segments.text: one, and discourse a whole, in which the breaks always at the same time have the purpose of making the structure, as a whole, pre-eminently visible.

segments.label: §104, claude source block7
segments.text: It is therefore one of the most important properties of the word to stimulate in presentation exactly that, and no more, which the use requires.

segments.label: §104, claude source block8
segments.text: This is indeed brought about in large part by the appropriate connection with other determining words and by the whole orientation given to the soul of the hearer.

segments.label: §104, claude source block9
segments.text: But it also lies in part in the formation of the word, which in this respect must possess purity, sharpness and sobriety in the determination of the concept, and full appropriateness to a clearly thought purpose.

segments.label: §104, claude source block10
segments.text: From this there arises at the same time the necessity of several expressions for the same object according to the difference of use, in differing indication of the sides brought out in it, and in different moods of the soul.

segments.label: §104, claude source block11
segments.text: For these too come into consideration here beside the logical purpose of discourse, and act pre-eminently on the kind of sensuous presentation lying in the word.

segments.label: §104, claude source block12
segments.text: For the same word is evidently accompanied by different presentations in a poetic and in a scientific exposition.

segments.label: §104, claude source block13
segments.text: Here too, however, language creates more by chance than by design, and the words of kindred sense are often only words carried over from other dialects with an accessory concept taken up into them.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block1
segments.text: We have been discussing the sensory presentation in the word and its motivating meaning. What, then, does the soul actually present to itself in sensory terms when it encounters a word? The object as a whole? The properties of the object apprehended in the word? Something indefinite corresponding to the feeling the word arouses? Or, among peoples who have long had an alphabet, the written characters?

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block2
segments.text: This would probably be difficult to ascertain by self-observation.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block3
segments.text: The very intention to observe changes the object of observation, and the presentation itself surely varies across all those possibilities according to the individual and the circumstances.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block4
segments.text: One point must be held to be both certain and decisive for recognizing the true nature of language. The word brings the object into presentation only in the way required by the particular connection of thoughts to which it subordinates the object and into which it weaves it as a component. The word allows the presentation to dwell on the object only as long as that connection requires.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block5
segments.text: This follows from the nature of the word, which substitutes sounds for actual objects precisely to transform them into thoughts through that mediation. It follows also from the fact that the succession of thoughts expressed through several words is, strictly speaking,

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block6
segments.text: a unity, and that discourse is a whole whose divisions serve above all to make its structure as a whole apparent.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block7
segments.text: It is therefore one of the most important properties of the word that it should evoke in presentation exactly what its use requires and no more.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block8
segments.text: This is indeed achieved largely by combining the word appropriately with other words that determine it and by the overall direction given to the hearer’s soul.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block9
segments.text: But it also depends in part on the formation of the word, which in this respect must have purity, sharpness and sobriety in the determination of the concept and be fully suited to a clearly conceived purpose.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block10
segments.text: This also accounts for the need for several expressions for the same object, according to differences of use, differences in the indication of the aspects singled out in the object, and differences in the states of mind in which the expressions are used.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block11
segments.text: For these states of mind must be considered here alongside the logical purpose of discourse, and they bear chiefly on the kind of sensory presentation contained in the word.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block12
segments.text: What accompanies the same word in a poetic exposition plainly differs from what accompanies it in a scientific one.

segments.label: §104, synthesis source block13
segments.text: Here too, however, language creates more by chance than by design, and words akin in sense are often simply words adopted from other dialects together with a subsidiary concept acquired there.

segments.label: §105, de source block1
segments.text: Das begleitende Gefühl (95.) wirkt auf die Wörter entweder als einzelne Empfindung des Gemüths, oder als Gesammtstimmung der verbundenen intellectuellen und Gemüthskräfte, wo jene zwar herrschen, aber die Farbe dieser annehmen.

segments.label: §105, de source block2
segments.text: Aus jenem entstehen die liebkosenden, ehrenden, feierlichen, scheltenden, verächtlichen, spöttischen, scherzhaften, aus diesem die dichterischen, philosophischen, ermahnend rührenden Ausdrücke u. s. f. Es wird eigentlich kein Wort ohne eine dieser, wenn gleich im Einzelnen unbemerkbaren Nuancen der Empfindungen ausgesprochen, da die dadurch angeklungenen Saiten immer gespannt im Gemüthe da liegen.

segments.label: §105, de source block3
segments.text: Hier ist aber nur von den besondren Wörtern die Rede, in deren Bildung diese Bestimmungen des Gefühls so übergegangen sind, dass sie nun immer dieselben erregen, und wo diese nicht an ihrem Ort sind, nicht gebraucht werden können.

segments.label: §105, de source block4
segments.text: In den einzelnen Sprachen nimmt man an diesen Ausdrücken eine doppelte merkwürdige Erscheinung wahr.

segments.label: §105, de source block5
segments.text: Die Sprachen ungebildeter Völker enthalten eine grosse Anzahl solcher, die einzelne Gemüthsempfindung verrathen.

segments.label: §105, de source block6
segments.text: Die Sprache vergeistigt immer den Menschen, führt ihn erst zu reiner Intellectualitaet hinauf, dann aber, wenn kein Gegengewicht eintritt, zu trockner, sophistischer und spielender über den Gipfelpunkt hinüber; allein sie thut dies nur allmählich.

segments.label: §105, de source block7
segments.text: Alle Volksdialecte bedienen sich häufiger der liebkosenden, verkleinernden, vergrössernden, verschlechternden Wörter, als die höhere gereinigte Mundart.

segments.label: §105, de source block8
segments.text: Dagegen darf man da nicht nach besondren dichterischen suchen ; alles ist noch gewissermassen dichterisch, und wird, ohne Bewusstseyn des Gegensatzes, so aufgenommen.

segments.label: §105, de source block9
segments.text: In den Sprachen einiger hochgebildeten Nationen ist auf der andren Seite dies Bewusstseyn so fein und lebendig, und der Vortrag so keusch, dass niemals ein dichterisches Wort in der fesselfreien Rede geduldet wird.

segments.label: §105, de source block10
segments.text: Dies entspringt nur mittelbar aus dem dichterischen Gefühl der Nation, unmittelbar aber aus dem, einen viel höher gesteigerten und feiner geläuterten Sprachsinn voraussetzenden für die Prosa, als eigene Gattung der Rede.

segments.label: §105, de source block11
segments.text: Man trifft dies daher nur in den edelsten, und am geistvollsten bearbeiteten Sprachen an.

segments.label: §105, de source block12
segments.text: Bei den philosophischen Wörtern muss man die nur logischen, durch den Verstand construirten, die bloss zu den technisch wissenschaftlichen gehören, unterscheiden von den aus tieferem Nachdenken oder höherer Offenbarung, durch die synthetisirende Vernunft entstandenen.

segments.label: §105, de source block13
segments.text: Wo, wie im Indischen, abgezogene Philosophie mit der höchsten Dichtung eine grossartige Verbindung eingegangen ist, da finden sich diese Ausdrücke in vorzüglicher Stärke und Schönheit.

segments.label: §105, sol source block1
segments.text: The accompanying feeling (95) acts on words either as a particular feeling of the heart or as an overall attunement of the intellectual and affective powers working together, in which the former predominate but take on the colouring of the latter.

segments.label: §105, sol source block2
segments.text: From the former arise endearing, honorific, solemn, scolding, contemptuous, mocking and jocular expressions. From the latter arise poetic and philosophical expressions, expressions that move by exhortation, and so on. Strictly speaking, no word is uttered without one of these nuances of feeling, though it may be imperceptible in a particular case, since the strings that such nuances set resonating are always stretched taut in the heart.

segments.label: §105, sol source block3
segments.text: Here, however, we are concerned only with particular words into whose formation these determinations of feeling have entered so thoroughly that the words now always arouse the same feelings and cannot be used where those feelings are out of place.

segments.label: §105, sol source block4
segments.text: In individual languages these expressions exhibit a remarkable twofold phenomenon.

segments.label: §105, sol source block5
segments.text: The languages of uncultivated peoples contain a great many such expressions that betray particular feelings of the heart.

segments.label: §105, sol source block6
segments.text: Language continually spiritualises human beings, leading them first upwards to pure intellectuality and then, if no counterweight intervenes, beyond the summit to a dry, sophistical and playful intellectuality. It does this only gradually.

segments.label: §105, sol source block7
segments.text: All popular dialects use endearing, diminutive, augmentative and pejorative words more frequently than the higher, refined idiom.

segments.label: §105, sol source block8
segments.text: In those dialects, however, one should not look for specifically poetic words. Everything is still in a sense poetic and is received as such without awareness of the contrast.

segments.label: §105, sol source block9
segments.text: In the languages of some highly cultivated nations, on the other hand, this awareness is so refined and lively, and expression so chaste, that a poetic word is never tolerated in discourse free of metrical constraints.

segments.label: §105, sol source block10
segments.text: This arises only indirectly from the nation's feeling for poetry. It arises directly from its feeling for prose as a distinct kind of discourse, which presupposes a sense of language developed to a much higher degree and more finely refined.

segments.label: §105, sol source block11
segments.text: It is therefore found only in the noblest languages, those that have been cultivated with the greatest ingenuity.

segments.label: §105, sol source block12
segments.text: Among philosophical words we must distinguish those that are merely logical, constructed by the understanding and belonging solely to technical scientific vocabulary, from those that arise out of deeper reflection or higher revelation through the synthesising power of reason.

segments.label: §105, sol source block13
segments.text: Where abstract philosophy has entered into a grand union with the highest poetry, as in Indian, these expressions are found in exceptional strength and beauty.

segments.label: §106, de source block1
segments.text: Ich habe in dem Bisherigen die Natur und die Erfordernisse der Wörter, jedes einzeln für sich betrachtet, zu zergliedern versucht, um zu zeigen, wie die Sprache den einzelnen Begriff bezeichnet.

segments.label: §106, de source block2
segments.text: Jetzt ist es nothwendig, den ganzen Vorrath der Wörter Einer Sprache in den Verhältnissen ihrer Bedeutung zu einander, und in Beziehung auf den Umfang der Gegenstände und Begriffe zu untersuchen, um zu zeigen, wie die Sprache verfährt, um passende Ausdrücke für jeden Redegebrauch zu schaffen, und die ganze Masse der vorkommenden Begriffe zu bezeichnen.

segments.label: §106, sol source block1
segments.text: So far I have tried to analyse the nature of words and the requirements they must meet, considering each word individually, in order to show how language designates the individual concept.

segments.label: §106, sol source block2
segments.text: We must now examine the entire vocabulary of a single language, both in the relations of the words’ meanings to one another and in relation to the range of objects and concepts, in order to show how language creates suitable expressions for every use in speech and designates the whole body of concepts that arise.

segments.label: §106, muse source block1
segments.text: In what has gone before I have tried to analyse the nature and requirements of words, each considered singly by itself, in order to show how language designates the individual concept.

segments.label: §106, muse source block2
segments.text: It is now necessary to examine the whole stock of the words of one language in the relations of their meaning to one another, and in relation to the extent of objects and concepts, in order to show how language proceeds to create fitting expressions for every use in speech, and to designate the whole mass of concepts that occur.

segments.label: §106, claude source block1
segments.text: In the foregoing I have tried to analyse the nature and the requirements of words, each considered singly by itself, in order to show how language designates the single concept.

segments.label: §106, claude source block2
segments.text: It is now necessary to investigate the whole stock of the words of a single language in the relations of their meaning to one another, and with reference to the compass of objects and concepts, in order to show how language proceeds so as to create fitting expressions for every use in discourse, and to designate the whole mass of the concepts that occur.

segments.label: §107, de source block1
segments.text: Jede Sprache, welche sie seyn möge, trägt in jedem Zeitpunkt ihres Daseyns den Ausdruck aller Begriffe, die sich jemals in der Nation entwickeln können, in ihrem Schooss.

segments.label: §107, de source block2
segments.text: Jede ist ferner in dem jedesmaligen Zeitpunkte ihres Lebens genau dem jedesmaligen Gedankenumfang der Nation gleich.

segments.label: §107, de source block3
segments.text: Jede endlich in jedem ihrer Zustände bildet das Ganze einer Weltansicht, indem sie Ausdruck für alle Vorstellungen enthält, welche die Nation sich von der Welt macht, und für alle Empfindungen, welche die Welt in ihr hervorbringt.

segments.label: §107, sol source block1
segments.text: Every language, whatever it may be, carries in its womb, at every moment of its existence, the expression of all the concepts that can ever develop in the nation.

segments.label: §107, sol source block2
segments.text: Moreover, at each moment of its life, every language exactly matches the range of the nation’s thought at that moment.

segments.label: §107, sol source block3
segments.text: Finally, in each of its states, every language forms a complete view of the world, since it contains expressions for all the presentations the nation forms of the world and all the feelings the world evokes in it.

segments.label: §107, muse source block1
segments.text: Every language, whatever it may be, bears in its bosom at every moment of its existence the expression of all concepts that can ever develop in the nation.

segments.label: §107, muse source block2
segments.text: Every language, moreover, at the particular moment of its life in question, is exactly equal to the particular extent of thought of the nation at that moment.

segments.label: §107, muse source block3
segments.text: Every language, finally, in each of its states forms the whole of a view of the world, in that it contains expression for all presentations which the nation forms of the world, and for all sensations which the world produces in it.

segments.label: §107, claude source block1

segments.label: §107, claude source block2

segments.label: §107, claude source block3
segments.text: Each, finally, in every one of its states forms the whole of a world-view, in that it contains expression for all the presentations which the nation forms for itself of the world, and for all the sentiments which the world produces in it.

segments.label: §108, de source block1
segments.text: Diese Sätze beruhen auf der Identität des Denkens und Sprechens.

segments.label: §108, de source block2
segments.text: Was der Mensch denken kann, das vermag er auch zu sagen.

segments.label: §108, de source block3
segments.text: Das Denken einer Nation entwickelt sich bisweilen durch Mischung mit einer andren, wo dann auch die Sprache fremden Zuwachs empfängt, aber es kann sich auch ganz aus sich selbst ausbilden, und seinen ganzen Lauf in sich vollenden, und Nation und Sprache gedeihen, wenn es gelingt, dabei besser und eigenthümlicher.

segments.label: §108, de source block4
segments.text: Das Denken der Nation, bestehend aus dem Denken jedes Einzelnen, muss in jedem Augenblick ein Ganzes seyn.

segments.label: §108, de source block5
segments.text: Denn es ist die Art, wie der Mensch in jedem Augenblick sein geistiges Daseyn in dessen Stellung gegen die Welt geltend macht, und da sich in jedes einzelne Denken nothwendig dies ganze Daseyn, das nur in dieser Thätigkeit besteht, zusammenzieht ;so kann dies nicht theilweise, nicht verstümmelt geschehen.

segments.label: §108, sol source block1
segments.text: These propositions rest on the identity of thinking and speaking.

segments.label: §108, sol source block2
segments.text: Whatever a human being can think, they can also say.

segments.label: §108, sol source block3
segments.text: A nation’s thinking sometimes develops through mingling with another nation, in which case its language also receives additions from outside. But its thinking can also develop entirely from within and complete its whole course within itself, and where this succeeds, both nation and language flourish more and develop a more distinctive character.

segments.label: §108, sol source block4
segments.text: The thinking of the nation, made up of the thinking of each individual, must be a whole at every moment.

segments.label: §108, sol source block5
segments.text: For thinking is how a human being at every moment asserts their mental existence in relation to the world. Since this whole existence, which consists solely in this activity, necessarily comes together in each individual act of thinking, this cannot take place piecemeal or in a mutilated form.

segments.label: §108, muse source block1
segments.text: These propositions rest on the identity of thinking and speaking.

segments.label: §108, muse source block2
segments.text: What man can think, that he is also able to say.

segments.label: §108, muse source block3
segments.text: The thinking of a nation sometimes develops through mixture with another, in which case language too receives foreign increment, but it can also form itself wholly out of itself, and complete its whole course within itself, and nation and language thrive better and more peculiarly thereby, if it succeeds.

segments.label: §108, muse source block4
segments.text: The thinking of the nation, consisting of the thinking of each individual, must at every moment be a whole.

segments.label: §108, muse source block5
segments.text: For it is the way in which man at every moment asserts his mental existence in its position in relation to the world, and since this whole existence, which consists only in this activity, necessarily contracts itself into each individual act of thinking; this cannot happen partially, not in mutilated fashion.

segments.label: §108, claude source block1
segments.text: These propositions rest on the identity of thinking and speaking.

segments.label: §108, claude source block2
segments.text: Whatever human beings can think, that they are also able to say.

segments.label: §108, claude source block3
segments.text: The thinking of a nation sometimes develops through mixture with another, in which case the language too receives foreign accretions; but it can also form itself entirely out of itself, and complete its whole course within itself, and nation and language, if this succeeds, thrive thereby the better and with a character more peculiarly their own.

segments.label: §108, claude source block4
segments.text: The thinking of the nation, consisting of the thinking of each single person, must at every moment be a whole.

segments.label: §108, claude source block5
segments.text: For it is the way in which human beings at every moment assert their mental existence in its stance towards the world; and since this whole existence, which consists only in this activity, necessarily contracts itself into every single act of thinking, this cannot happen piecemeal, nor in mutilated form.

segments.label: §109, de source block1
segments.text: Es sind aber jene Sätze von der höchsten Wichtigkeit für die richtige Würdigung der Sprache.

segments.label: §109, de source block2
segments.text: Denn es beruhet auf ihnen, dass man die Sprache in keinem Augenblick ihres Lebens als abgeschlossen, sondern immer als fortschreitend, alles in ihr Enthaltene als Keim neuer Entwicklung betrachtet, und ihr Fortschreiten nicht mechanisch, als Ansetzung von Theilen, sondern wahrhaft organisch, als ein Entfalten eines Ganzen aus einem Ganzen ansieht.

segments.label: §109, de source block3
segments.text: Die Möglichkeit dieser Natur der Sprache liegt in dem, wovon schon im Vorigen geredet worden ist, in der Fähigkeit der articulirten Laute zu Versetzungen und Verbindungen aller Art, wo durch Hervorbringung kleiner Unterschiede, bei bleibender allgemeiner Aehnlichkeit, aus Einem Grundlaut ganze Geschlechter von Wortklängen (79.) entstehen, und durch die Abbeugung desselben Worts zu verwandten Bedeutungen, durch die Festsetzung der allgemein gleichbedeutenden Wörter, und durch neue Stempelung sonst anders gebrauchter.

segments.label: §109, de source block4
segments.text: Es ist ein Schaffen von Tönen und ein Schaffen von Begriffen, durch welches die Sprache in sich selbst wächst, das letztere geht ins Unendliche, allein das erstere hat, wie alle Erfahrung zeigt, eine Gränze.

segments.label: §109, de source block5
segments.text: Die Sprache erreicht einen Punkt, wo der Reichthum der Klänge nicht mehr aus dem eignen Schoosse, sondern höchstens noch durch Aufnahme fremder Wörter vermehrt wird.

segments.label: §109, de source block6
segments.text: Die weitere Bearbeitung wird dann gewissermassen innerlicher, und beschränkt sich auf die Fixirung und Modificirung der Bedeutungen.

segments.label: §109, de source block7
segments.text: Der Mangel aller geschichtlichen Erfahrung verbietet über diesen Scheidepunkt etwas Näheres zu sagen.

segments.label: §109, de source block8
segments.text: Soviel aber siehet man wohl, dass er da liegt, wo das Zusammentreten und Mengen der Stämme untereinander entweder selbst, oder in seiner Einwirkung auf die Sprache aufhört.

segments.label: §109, de source block9
segments.text: Denn alle innere Erweiterung der Sprache in ihren Tönen lässt sich doch nur füglich so denken, dass mehrere die nemliche Redende, durch Eigenthümlichkeit oder Trennung, Verschiedenheiten in sie bringen, die dann in das Ganze übergehen, schon von Verschiedenheiten auch der Bedeutung begleitet, oder sie erst dort erhaltend.

segments.label: §109, de source block10
segments.text: Dadurch dass jeder eigentlich, um verstanden zu werden, so sprechen will, als der andre, jeder aber doch, weil er nun einmal physisch und geistig ein andrer ist, wirklich etwas verschieden redet, dies etwas Verschiedene aber doch verstanden und wieder aufgenommen wird, kann in einer Sprache, wenn man sich dies unter Individuen, Familien und Stämmen Jahrhunderte lang fortgehend denkt, eine grosse Mannigfaltigkeit der Wortklänge entstehen.

segments.label: §109, de source block11
segments.text: Dass ein Dialect den andern und die allgemeine Sprache bereichert, erfahren wir ja oft selbst.

segments.label: §109, sol source block1
segments.text: Those propositions are of the utmost importance for a proper appreciation of language.

segments.label: §109, sol source block2
segments.text: For they are the basis for regarding language as always developing and at no moment of its life complete, and for seeing everything it contains as the seed of further development. Its advance is truly organic, the unfolding of one whole out of another, rather than the mechanical addition of parts.

segments.label: §109, sol source block3
segments.text: What makes this character of language possible is what has already been discussed: articulated sounds can be rearranged and combined in all sorts of ways, so that entire families of word sounds (§79) arise from a single basic sound through small differences that leave the general resemblance intact. It is also made possible by shifting the same word towards related meanings, fixing the meanings of broadly synonymous words, and giving a new stamp to words previously used in other ways.

segments.label: §109, sol source block4
segments.text: Language grows from within through the creation of sounds and the creation of concepts. The creation of concepts goes on without limit, but the creation of sounds, as all experience shows, has a limit.

segments.label: §109, sol source block5
segments.text: Language reaches a point at which its wealth of sounds no longer increases from its own womb and can at most be increased by taking in foreign words.

segments.label: §109, sol source block6
segments.text: Its further elaboration then becomes, in a sense, more inward and is confined to fixing and modifying meanings.

segments.label: §109, sol source block7
segments.text: The complete lack of historical evidence prevents us from saying anything more precise about this dividing point.

segments.label: §109, sol source block8
segments.text: We can see this much, however: it comes when the coming together and mingling of tribes ceases, either in itself or in its effect on language.

segments.label: §109, sol source block9
segments.text: For the only plausible way to conceive of any internal expansion of a language in its sounds is that different speakers of the same language introduce variations into it through their distinctiveness or separation. These then pass into the language as a whole, either already accompanied by differences of meaning or acquiring them only there.

segments.label: §109, sol source block10
segments.text: Everyone really wants to speak as others do in order to be understood, yet each person does in fact speak somewhat differently because each is physically and mentally different. This slight variation is still understood and taken up again. If we imagine this continuing for centuries among individuals, families and tribes, a great variety of word sounds can arise in a language.

segments.label: §109, sol source block11
segments.text: We often experience for ourselves how one dialect enriches another and the language at large.

segments.label: §109, muse source block1
segments.text: Those propositions are, however, of the highest importance for the correct appreciation of language.

segments.label: §109, muse source block2
segments.text: For it rests upon them that one regards language at no moment of its life as closed off, but always as advancing, everything contained in it as a germ of new development, and regards its advance not mechanically, as an attaching of parts, but truly organically, as an unfolding of a whole out of a whole.

segments.label: §109, muse source block3
segments.text: The possibility of this nature of language lies in what has already been spoken of above, in the capacity of articulated sounds for transpositions and combinations of all kinds, whereby, through production of small differences while general similarity remains, whole families of word-sounds (79.) arise from one basic sound, and through the deflection of the same word to kindred meanings, through the fixing of words generally synonymous, and through the new stamping of words otherwise used differently.

segments.label: §109, muse source block4
segments.text: It is a creating of sounds and a creating of concepts through which language grows within itself; the latter goes on to infinity, but the former has, as all experience shows, a limit.

segments.label: §109, muse source block5
segments.text: Language reaches a point where the richness of sounds is no longer increased from its own bosom, but at most still through the taking up of foreign words.

segments.label: §109, muse source block6
segments.text: Further working then becomes in a certain measure more inward, and restricts itself to the fixing and modifying of meanings.

segments.label: §109, muse source block7
segments.text: The lack of all historical experience forbids saying anything more precise about this dividing point.

segments.label: §109, muse source block8
segments.text: So much, however, one does see, that it lies where the coming together and mingling of tribes with one another ceases, either itself or in its effect upon language.

segments.label: §109, muse source block9
segments.text: For all inner enlargement of language in its sounds can after all be suitably conceived only on the supposition that several persons speaking the same language, through peculiarity or separation, bring differences into it which then pass into the whole, already accompanied by differences of meaning too, or only receiving them there.

segments.label: §109, muse source block10
segments.text: Through the fact that everyone properly, in order to be understood, wants to speak as the other does, but everyone nevertheless, because he is after all physically and mentally another, really speaks somewhat differently, but this something different is nevertheless understood and taken up again, a great manifoldness of word-sounds can arise in a language, if one conceives this as continuing for centuries among individuals, families and tribes.

segments.label: §109, muse source block11
segments.text: That one dialect enriches another and the general language, we indeed often experience ourselves.

segments.label: §109, claude source block1
segments.text: Those propositions, however, are of the highest importance for the right appraisal of language.

segments.label: §109, claude source block2
segments.text: For it rests on them that one regards language at no moment of its life as closed, but always as advancing, and everything contained in it as the germ of new development, and that one views its advance not mechanically, as an adding-on of parts, but truly organically, as an unfolding of a whole out of a whole.

segments.label: §109, claude source block3
segments.text: The possibility of this nature of language lies in that of which mention has already been made in the foregoing: in the aptitude of articulated sounds for transpositions and combinations of every kind, where, through the production of small differences while a general resemblance persists, whole families of word-sonorities (79.) arise from a single basic sound; and through the deflection of the same word to kindred meanings, through the settling of the words that are in general of like meaning, and through the new stamping of words otherwise differently used.

segments.label: §109, claude source block4
segments.text: It is a creating of tones and a creating of concepts through which language grows within itself; the latter goes on to infinity, but the former, as all experience shows, has a limit.

segments.label: §109, claude source block5
segments.text: Language reaches a point where the wealth of sonorities is no longer increased from its own womb, but at most still through the adoption of foreign words.

segments.label: §109, claude source block6
segments.text: The further elaboration then becomes, in a manner, more inward, and confines itself to the fixing and modifying of the meanings.

segments.label: §109, claude source block7
segments.text: The lack of all historical experience forbids saying anything more precise about this dividing point.

segments.label: §109, claude source block8
segments.text: This much, however, one can well see: that it lies where the coming together and mingling of the tribes with one another ceases, either in itself or in its influence upon language.

segments.label: §109, claude source block9
segments.text: For every inner enlargement of language in its tones can, after all, properly be conceived only thus: that several who speak the same language bring differences into it, through peculiarity or separation, which then pass over into the whole, either already accompanied by differences of meaning as well, or receiving them only there.

segments.label: §109, claude source block10
segments.text: Because everyone, in order to be understood, properly wants to speak as the other does, yet everyone, being after all physically and mentally another, in fact speaks somewhat differently, while this somewhat different speech is nevertheless understood and taken up again, a great variety of word-sonorities can arise in a language, if one imagines this going on for centuries among individuals, families and tribes.

segments.label: §109, claude source block11
segments.text: That one dialect enriches another and the general language is, after all, something we often experience ourselves.

segments.text: Those propositions are of the utmost importance for a proper appreciation of language.

segments.label: §109, revised source block9
segments.text: For the only plausible way to conceive of any internal expansion of a language in its sounds is that different speakers of the same language introduce variations into it through their distinctiveness or separation. These then pass into the language as a whole, either already accompanied by differences of meaning or acquiring them only there.

segments.label: §109, revised source block10
segments.text: Everyone really wants to speak as others do in order to be understood, yet each person does in fact speak somewhat differently because each is physically and mentally different. This slight variation is still understood and taken up again. If we imagine this continuing for centuries among individuals, families and tribes, a great variety of word sounds can arise in a language.

segments.label: §109, revised source block11
segments.text: We often experience for ourselves how one dialect enriches another and the language at large.

segments.label: §110, de source block1
segments.text: Insofern man unter dem Reichthum einer Sprache ihr Vermögen dem Bedürfniss des Ausdrucks zu genügen versteht, kann man alle gleich reich nennen.

segments.label: §110, de source block2
segments.text: Denn so wie man eine wahrhaft besitzt, kann es keinem Begriff und keiner Ideenwendung an der angemessnen Bezeichnung fehlen.

segments.label: §110, de source block3
segments.text: Darum ist aber die Prüfung des Reichthums einer Sprache keine müssige Untersuchung, wenn man sich nur recht über den Sinn des Ausdrucks versteht, und es giebt allerdings verschiedene Grade und Arten desselben.

segments.label: §110, de source block4
segments.text: Zuerst kommt es darauf an, dass jeder, sich als ein einzelner bestimmt absondernder Gegenstand oder Begriff auch in der Sprache ein einzelnes, ihn, ohne Umschreibung, bezeichnendes Wort finde ; so wie zweitens, dass es den Gegenständen ebensowenig an der gehörigen Verschiedenheit des Ausdrucks nach der Empfindung, mit der man spricht, und der Anschauungsweise, auf die man hinarbeitet, fehle.

segments.label: §110, de source block5
segments.text: Es kann aber auch drittens für denselben Gegenstand mehrere Wörter, ohne merkbare Verschiedenheit der Bedeutung oder Absicht, geben, und viertens endlich mehrere Formen desselben Worts.

segments.label: §110, sol source block1
segments.text: Insofar as the richness of a language means its ability to meet the need for expression, all languages may be called equally rich.

segments.label: §110, sol source block2
segments.text: For once one truly has command of a language, no concept or turn of thought can lack a suitable designation.

segments.label: §110, sol source block3
segments.text: Even so, examining the richness of a language is no idle inquiry, provided we are clear about what the term means. There are indeed different degrees and kinds of richness.

segments.label: §110, sol source block4
segments.text: What matters first is that every object or concept that stands out clearly as a distinct entity should find in the language a single word designating it without circumlocution. Second, objects should have the requisite variety of expression, according to the feeling with which one speaks and the mode of viewing them that one seeks to bring about.

segments.label: §110, sol source block5
segments.text: Third, there may also be several words for the same object without any perceptible difference in meaning or intention, and fourth, there may be several forms of the same word.

segments.label: §110, muse source block1
segments.text: Insofar as by the richness of a language one understands its capacity to satisfy the need for expression, one can call all languages equally rich.

segments.label: §110, muse source block2
segments.text: For as soon as one truly possesses a language, no concept and no turn of ideas can lack the appropriate designation.

segments.label: §110, muse source block3
segments.text: That is not to say, however, that examination of the richness of a language is an idle inquiry, if only one understands rightly the sense of the expression, and there are indeed different degrees and kinds of it.

segments.label: §110, muse source block4
segments.text: First it is a question of every object or concept that sets itself apart distinctly as an individual one also finding in the language an individual word designating it without circumlocution; as, secondly, of objects likewise not lacking the due diversity of expression according to the sensation with which one speaks, and the mode of intuition towards which one is working.

segments.label: §110, muse source block5
segments.text: But there can also, thirdly, be several words for the same object, without noticeable difference of meaning or intention, and, fourthly and finally, several forms of the same word.

segments.label: §110, claude source block1
segments.text: In so far as one understands by the wealth of a language its capacity to satisfy the need of expression, all may be called equally rich.

segments.label: §110, claude source block2
segments.text: For as soon as one truly possesses a language, no concept and no turn of ideas can lack its appropriate designation.

segments.label: §110, claude source block3
segments.text: The examination of the wealth of a language is not on that account an idle investigation, however, provided only that one is properly agreed about the sense of the expression; and there are indeed different degrees and kinds of this wealth.

segments.label: §110, claude source block4
segments.text: What matters first is that every object or concept that sets itself apart definitely as a single one should also find in the language a single word that designates it without circumlocution; and likewise, secondly, that the objects should just as little lack the due diversity of expression according to the sentiment with which one speaks and the mode of intuition towards which one is working.

segments.label: §110, claude source block5
segments.text: But, thirdly, there may also be several words for the same object without perceptible difference of meaning or intention, and fourthly, finally, several forms of the same word.
