segments.label: §111, de source block1
segments.text: Es ist in allen Sprachen der Fall, dass, was einige durch ein einzelnes Wort ausdrücken, von andern mit mehreren umschrieben wird, und die Klarheit und Bestimmtheit der Bezeichnung kann dennoch dieselbe seyn.

segments.label: §111, de source block2
segments.text: Indess ist es keinesweges gleichgültig, wenn eine Sprache oft zur Umschreibung ihre Zuflucht nehmen muss.

segments.label: §111, de source block3
segments.text: Die Mittheilung der Gedanken, der augenblickliche Zweck der Rede leidet dadurch allerdings nicht; allein der Unterschied liegt in der Form der Sprache, ihrer Rückwirkung auf das Denken überhaupt.

segments.label: §111, de source block4
segments.text: Denn man darf nie vergessen, dass die Beschaffenheit der Sprache, als eines Werkzeugs des Denkens, einen unmittelbaren Einfluss auf dasselbe ausübt, seine Klarheit, Bestimmtheit, Schnelligkeit, Schärfe erhöht, oder herabstimmt, ihm sinnliche Richtung nach aussen hin, oder geistige nach innen giebt, und dass dies bei weitem die wichtigste Seite in ihr ist.

segments.label: §111, de source block5
segments.text: Wo nun jeder Begriff sein ihm bestimmtes Wort findet, da regt dieser Reichthum den Geist an; die Sprache erscheint wie die Welt, in der auch Gegenstand sich an Gegenstand drängt, und wie eine Weltansicht soll sie sich ja zwischen die Natur und den Menschen stellen.

segments.label: §111, de source block6
segments.text: Ich werde auch in der Folge noch darauf zurückkommen, dass es höchst wichtig ist, dass die Sprache, die öde Abgezogenheit der Gedanken verlassend, in ihre Form die Form der äusseren Wirklichkeit aufnehme.

segments.label: §111, de source block7
segments.text: Dies beweist sich auch hier.

segments.label: §111, de source block8
segments.text: Auch eine wortarme Sprache kann eine Menge von Begriffen und Ideenreihen, sogar mit Klarheit und Bestimmtheit, ausdrücken; man sieht ein Beispiel davon an dem ärmlichen Gebrauch, den einige Missionsschriften von gewiss in sich reicheren ausser-Europaeischen Sprachen machen.

segments.label: §111, de source block9
segments.text: Dem Inhalte des Gedankens ist dann wohl Genüge geleistet.

segments.label: §111, de source block10
segments.text: Aber die Dürftigkeit der Sprache zieht den Geist herab, und es fehlt dem Denken in solcher Darstellung an Fülle, Frische und Lebendigkeit.

segments.label: §111, sol source block1
segments.text: It happens in all languages that what some express in a single word others express by a circumlocution of several words, and the designation may still be just as clear and precise.

segments.label: §111, sol source block2
segments.text: Yet it is by no means a matter of indifference if a language must often resort to circumlocution.

segments.label: §111, sol source block3
segments.text: The communication of thoughts, the immediate purpose of speech, certainly does not suffer thereby. The difference lies in the form of the language and its effect in turn on thinking as a whole.

segments.label: §111, sol source block4
segments.text: For we must never forget that the character of language as an instrument of thought has an immediate influence on thinking. It can heighten or diminish its clarity, precision, speed and sharpness, and turn it outwards towards the senses or inwards towards the mind. This is by far the most important aspect of language.

segments.label: §111, sol source block5
segments.text: Where every concept finds the word appointed for it, this richness stimulates the mind. Language appears like the world, where objects likewise crowd upon one another, and it is as a view of the world that language is meant to stand between nature and the human being.

segments.label: §111, sol source block6
segments.text: I shall return later to the point that it is of the utmost importance for language to leave behind the barren abstraction of thoughts and take up into its own form the form of external reality.

segments.label: §111, sol source block7
segments.text: This is borne out here as well.

segments.label: §111, sol source block8
segments.text: Even a language poor in words can express a host of concepts and sequences of ideas, and can do so clearly and precisely. An example is the impoverished use that some missionary writings make of non-European languages that are surely richer in themselves.

segments.label: §111, sol source block9
segments.text: The content of the thought may then have been adequately conveyed.

segments.label: §111, sol source block10
segments.text: But the impoverishment of the language drags down the mind, and thought so presented lacks fullness, freshness and vitality.

segments.label: §111, muse source block3

segments.label: §111, muse source block4

segments.label: §111, muse source block5
segments.text: Where now every concept finds its word appointed for it, there this richness stirs the mind; language appears like the world, in which object too presses upon object, and as a view of the world it is after all to place itself between nature and man.

segments.label: §111, muse source block6
segments.text: I shall also return later to the point that it is of the highest importance that language, abandoning the barren abstractedness of thoughts, should take up into its form the form of external actuality.

segments.label: §111, muse source block7
segments.text: This is proved here too.

segments.text: Even a language poor in words can express a multitude of concepts and series of ideas, even with clarity and determinateness; one sees an example of this in the meagre use which some mission writings make of non-European languages certainly richer in themselves.

segments.label: §111, muse source block9
segments.text: The content of the thought is then indeed satisfied.

segments.label: §111, muse source block10
segments.text: But the poverty of the language drags the mind down, and thinking in such representation lacks fullness, freshness and liveliness.

segments.label: §112, de source block1
segments.text: Aus denselben Gründen dürfen auch mehrere Wörter für denselben Begriff, selbst wenn sie kaum merkbare Unterschiede darböten, und mehrere Formen desselben Worts nicht als ein überflüssiger Luxus erscheinen.

segments.label: §112, de source block2
segments.text: Sie vermehren nicht nur die sinnliche Fülle der Sprache, sondern geben auch in der fortschreitenden geistigen Entwicklung der Nation Gelegenheit, die Begriffe, wenigstens durch den Gebrauch der verschiedenen Ausdrücke, wenn es sich auch nicht immer im Wörterbuch nachweisen lässt, feiner zu nuanciren und genauer zu bestimmen.

segments.label: §112, de source block3
segments.text: Sogar wenn Sprachen, wie die Englische, aus verschiedenen zusammengeflossen, für gewisse Begriffe zwei bloss durch ihren Ursprung verschiedene Ausdrücke, wie freedom und liberty, besitzen, so ist der Gebrauch derselben bei feinsinnigen und sprachkundigen Rednern doch nicht ganz gleichgültig.

segments.label: §112, de source block4
segments.text: Ueberhaupt ist keine Gattung des Reichthums der Sprachen geringzuschätzen.

segments.label: §112, de source block5
segments.text: Jede beweist, dass, sey es der Dauer ihres Bestehens, der Menge der Stämme und Individuen, die sie sprachen, oder der geistigen Regsamkeit der Nation zuzuschreiben, viel und mannigfach in ihr gesprochen wurde, mithin viele Gedanken und Empfindungen in sie übergiengen.

segments.label: §112, de source block6
segments.text: Je mehr aber dem Geiste einer Sprache Gehalt menschlichen Daseyns entgegenklingt, desto grösser, lebendiger und geistiger ist ihre anregende Kraft.

segments.label: §112, sol source block1
segments.text: For the same reasons, several words for the same concept, even if they offered scarcely perceptible differences, and several forms of the same word should not be regarded as a superfluous luxury.

segments.label: §112, sol source block2
segments.text: They increase the sensory fullness of the language and, as the nation’s mental life develops, make it possible to give concepts finer shades and more precise definition, at least through the use of the different expressions, even when the distinction cannot always be demonstrated in the dictionary.

segments.label: §112, sol source block3
segments.text: Even when languages such as English, formed by the convergence of several languages, have two expressions for certain concepts that differ only in origin, such as *freedom* and *liberty*, the choice between them is still not a matter of complete indifference to speakers with a fine and practised sense of language.

segments.label: §112, sol source block4
segments.text: In general, no kind of linguistic richness should be held in low esteem.

segments.label: §112, sol source block5
segments.text: Each kind shows that much was spoken in the language and in many different ways, and that many thoughts and feelings thus passed into it, whether this is due to the length of its existence, the number of tribes and individuals who spoke it, or the mental vigour of the nation.

segments.label: §112, sol source block6
segments.text: The more of the substance of human existence resounds in answer to the spirit of a language, the greater, livelier and more intellectual its power to stimulate the mind.

segments.label: §112, muse source block2

segments.label: §112, muse source block3

segments.label: §112, muse source block4
segments.text: In general no kind of richness of languages is to be slighted.

segments.label: §112, muse source block5
segments.text: Each proves that, whether it is to be ascribed to the duration of their existence, to the multitude of tribes and individuals who spoke them, or to the mental activity of the nation, much speaking in manifold ways went on in it, and consequently many thoughts and sensations passed into it.

segments.label: §112, muse source block6
segments.text: But the more content of human existence sounds back towards the mind from a language, the greater, livelier and more mental is its stimulating power.

segments.label: §112, revised source block4
segments.text: In general, no kind of linguistic richness should be held in low esteem.

segments.label: §112, revised source block5
segments.text: Each kind shows that much was spoken in the language and in many different ways, and that many thoughts and feelings thus passed into it, whether this is due to the length of its existence, the number of tribes and individuals who spoke it, or the mental vigour of the nation.

segments.label: §112, revised source block6
segments.text: The more of the substance of human existence resounds in answer to the spirit of a language, the greater, livelier and more intellectual its power to stimulate the mind.

segments.label: §113, de source block1
segments.text: Um die Beschaffenheit einer Sprache in Absicht ihres Wortvorraths vollständig zu beurtheilen, müsste man diesen mit der Masse der möglichen Begriffe, das Bezeichnete mit dem zu Bezeichnenden vergleichen.

segments.label: §113, de source block2
segments.text: Von den reinen Begriffen verstanden, ist dies unmöglich, da der Gedankenstoff sich nicht rein von dem Sprachstoff scheiden lässt, vielmehr die Bezeichnung erst das Entstehen des zu Bezeichnenden vor dem Geiste vollendet.

segments.label: §113, de source block3
segments.text: Selbst bei Naturgegenständen ist dies der Fall, da das Wort ja nicht sie überhaupt, sondern die in der Sprache gegründete Ansicht derselben bezeichnet.

segments.label: §113, de source block4
segments.text: Indess geht dies nur die strenge und ganz genaue Analyse an, sonst lässt sich allerdings fragen, welche in einer gegebenen Sprache ihr ursprünglich eigenthümliche Ausdrücke finden?

segments.label: §113, de source block5
segments.text: Allein bei unsinnlichen Begriffen ist diese Scheidung des Worts und Begriffs theils viel weniger, theils gar nicht zu versuchen.

segments.label: §113, de source block6
segments.text: Es giebt jedoch ein Analogon, durch welches sich wenigstens einigermassen zu dem beabsichteten Zwecke gelangen lässt.

segments.label: §113, de source block7
segments.text: Man kann nemlich an die Stelle der rein zu denkenden Begriffe die in einer Anzahl von Sprachen wirklich bezeichneten setzen, und die Masse dessen, was Bezeichnung zulässt und fordert, abmessen nach dem, was in den bekannten verschiedenen Sprachen etwa bezeichnet zu werden pflegt.

segments.label: §113, de source block8
segments.text: Insofern dient das Studium der vorhandenen Sprachen zur Prüfung des Umfangs des im Menschengeschlecht wirklich gewesenen Denkens und Empfindens.

segments.label: §113, de source block9
segments.text: Verbindet man nun diese Methode mit der Untersuchung des reinen, von einer bestimmten Sprache geschiedenen Gedankenstoffs vermittelst der Aufstellung allgemeiner Kategorien von Gegenständen und Begriffen, und immer herabsteigender Eintheilung, aber mit dem beständigen Bewusstseyn, dass, wo man in diesem Herabsteigen auf den individuellen Begriff kommt, eine bestimmte Sprache eintreten muss, so kann man, ohne in Irrthümer zu verfallen, doch den zu bezeichnenden Gedankenstoff, nicht rein und vollständig, aber genügend für die Sprachuntersuchung, mit dem Wörtervorrath einer Sprache zusammenhalten.

segments.label: §113, sol source block1
segments.text: To assess a language fully with respect to its vocabulary, one would have to compare that vocabulary with the whole body of possible concepts, comparing what is designated with what is to be designated.

segments.label: §113, sol source block2
segments.text: If what is meant is concepts in their purity, this is impossible, since the material of thought cannot be cleanly separated from the material of language. It is designation itself that completes the emergence before the mind of what is to be designated.

segments.label: §113, sol source block3
segments.text: This is true even of natural objects, for the word designates the view of them grounded in the language, rather than the objects simply as such.

segments.label: §113, sol source block4
segments.text: This difficulty, however, concerns only strict and fully precise analysis. Apart from that, one can certainly ask which natural objects have expressions originally peculiar to a given language.

segments.label: §113, sol source block5
segments.text: With non-sensory concepts, however, this separation of word and concept is much less feasible in some cases and cannot be attempted at all in others.

segments.label: §113, sol source block6
segments.text: There is, however, an analogue by which we can at least come somewhat closer to the intended aim.

segments.label: §113, sol source block7
segments.text: We can substitute the concepts actually designated in a number of languages for the concepts that would have to be thought in their purity, and gauge the body of what admits of and calls for designation by what tends to be designated in the various known languages.

segments.label: §113, sol source block8
segments.text: In this respect, the study of existing languages serves to examine the range of thinking and feeling that has actually existed among humankind.

segments.label: §113, sol source block9
segments.text: We can combine this method with an inquiry into the pure material of thought, considered apart from any particular language, by setting up general categories of objects and concepts and subdividing them into progressively narrower classes. If we constantly bear in mind that a particular language must come into play as soon as we descend to the individual concept, we can compare the material of thought to be designated with the vocabulary of a language without falling into error. Such a comparison is neither pure nor complete, but it is adequate for the study of language.

segments.label: §113, muse source block1
segments.text: In order to judge completely the character of a language with respect to its stock of words, one would have to compare this stock with the mass of possible concepts, what is designated with what is to be designated.

segments.label: §113, muse source block2
segments.text: Understood of pure concepts, this is impossible, since the material of thought cannot be purely separated from the material of language; rather designation first completes the arising, before the mind, of what is to be designated.

segments.label: §113, muse source block3
segments.text: Even with objects of nature this is the case, since the word after all designates not them in general, but the view of them grounded in the language.

segments.label: §113, muse source block4
segments.text: Yet this concerns only strict and wholly exact analysis; otherwise one can indeed ask, what finds in a given language expressions originally peculiar to it?

segments.label: §113, muse source block5
segments.text: But with non-sensuous concepts this separation of word and concept is in part much less, in part not at all, to be attempted.

segments.label: §113, muse source block6
segments.text: There is, however, an analogue by means of which one can at least to some extent attain the intended purpose.

segments.label: §113, muse source block7
segments.text: One can namely put in place of the concepts to be thought purely those actually designated in a number of languages, and measure the mass of what admits and requires designation by what is usually designated, as the case may be, in the various known languages.

segments.label: §113, muse source block8
segments.text: Insofar the study of existing languages serves to test the extent of thinking and feeling that has actually existed in the human race.

segments.label: §113, muse source block9
segments.text: If one now combines this method with investigation of the pure material of thought, separated from any particular language, by means of setting up general categories of objects and concepts, and division descending ever further, but with the constant consciousness that, where in this descent one comes to the individual concept, a particular language must enter, one can, without falling into errors, nevertheless hold together the material of thought to be designated, not purely and completely, but sufficiently for linguistic inquiry, with the stock of words of a language.

segments.label: §113, claude source block1
segments.text: In order to judge the constitution of a language completely with respect to its stock of words, one would have to compare this stock with the mass of possible concepts, what is designated with what is to be designated.

segments.label: §113, claude source block2
segments.text: Understood of the pure concepts, this is impossible, since the material of thought cannot be purely separated from the material of language; rather, it is the designation that first completes the coming-into-being, before the mind, of what is to be designated.

segments.label: §113, claude source block3
segments.text: This is the case even with natural objects, since the word, after all, designates not them as such, but the view of them that is grounded in the language.

segments.label: §113, claude source block4
segments.text: This, however, concerns only strict and wholly exact analysis; otherwise one can certainly ask: which of them find, in a given language, expressions originally peculiar to it?

segments.label: §113, claude source block5
segments.text: With non-sensuous concepts, however, this separation of word and concept is in part much less to be attempted, in part not to be attempted at all.

segments.label: §113, claude source block6
segments.text: There is, however, an analogue by which the intended purpose can be attained at least to some extent.

segments.label: §113, claude source block7
segments.text: One can, namely, put in the place of the concepts that are to be thought purely those actually designated in a number of languages, and measure the mass of what admits and demands designation by what, more or less, is usually designated in the various known languages.

segments.label: §113, claude source block8
segments.text: To this extent the study of the existing languages serves for the examination of the compass of the thinking and sensibility that have actually existed in the human race.

segments.label: §113, claude source block9
segments.text: If one now combines this method with the investigation of the pure material of thought, separated from any particular language, by means of the setting up of general categories of objects and concepts and of an ever-descending division, but with the constant consciousness that, where in this descent one arrives at the individual concept, a particular language must step in, then one can, without falling into errors, nevertheless hold the material of thought that is to be designated — not purely and completely, but sufficiently for the investigation of language — against the stock of words of a language.

segments.label: §114, de source block1
segments.text: Nach Kategorien geordnete Wörterbücher, wie Pollux und Amara's Cosha sind hierzu nützliche Hülfsmittel, und es war ein zweckmässiger Einfall Havestadts die Wörter der Sprache Chilis auch auf diese Weise zu ordnen.

segments.label: §114, de source block2
segments.text: Allein sehr vervollständigt müssen diese Arbeiten werden, und man sollte nicht versäumen, aus sovielen Sprachen, als zu vergleichen möglich ist, die Wörter zusammenzutragen, durch welche Gegenstände bezeichnet, oder Begriffe gestempelt werden, die in andren keinen erschöpfenden Ausdruck in einem eignen Worte finden.

segments.label: §114, de source block3
segments.text: Wiederholen muss ich zwar hier, dass, wenn man es scharf und genau nimmt, kein Wort einer Sprache völlig dem einer andern entspricht.

segments.label: §114, de source block4
segments.text: Hier aber ist nur von den Fällen die Rede, wo durch ein Wort für diejenigen, welche die Sprache bisher nicht kannten, wirklich ein neuer Begriff, oder eine neue wichtige Nuance eines Begriffes entsteht.

segments.label: §114, de source block5
segments.text: Denn es kommt hier auf die Auffindung des zu bezeichnenden Gedankenstoffs an, und zu dieser kann das blosse Vorschreiten nach Kategorien und logischen Definitionen nicht genügen, wenn man nicht das schon wirklich in Sprache Gedachte hinzunimmt.

segments.label: §114, sol source block1
segments.text: Dictionaries arranged by category, such as that of Pollux and Amara’s *Cosha*, are useful aids here, and it was a good idea of Havestadt’s to arrange the words of the language of Chile in the same way.

segments.label: §114, sol source block2
segments.text: These works must, however, be made much more comprehensive. From as many languages as can be compared, one should be sure to collect the words that designate objects or give concepts a definite stamp, where those objects or concepts find no fully adequate expression in a word of their own in other languages.

segments.label: §114, sol source block3
segments.text: I must repeat here that, strictly and precisely speaking, no word in one language corresponds completely to a word in another.

segments.label: §114, sol source block4
segments.text: Here, however, we are concerned only with cases in which a word actually brings a new concept or an important new shade of a concept into being for those who were previously unfamiliar with the language.

segments.label: §114, sol source block5
segments.text: For the aim here is to discover the material of thought to be designated, and simply proceeding by categories and logical definitions cannot suffice for this unless we also take into account what has already actually been thought in language.

segments.label: §114, muse source block1
segments.text: Dictionaries ordered by categories, such as Pollux and Amara's *Cosha*, are useful aids for this, and it was a purposeful idea of Havestadt's also to order the words of the language of Chile in this way.

segments.label: §114, muse source block2
segments.text: But these works must be very much completed, and one should not omit to bring together from as many languages as it is possible to compare the words by which objects are designated, or concepts stamped, which in other languages find no exhaustive expression in a word of their own.

segments.label: §114, muse source block3
segments.text: I must indeed repeat here that, if one takes it sharply and exactly, no word of one language corresponds completely to that of another.

segments.label: §114, muse source block4
segments.text: Here, however, only those cases are in question where through a word, for those who did not previously know the language, a really new concept, or a new important nuance of a concept, arises.

segments.label: §114, muse source block5
segments.text: For what is at issue here is the discovery of the material of thought to be designated, and for this mere advance by categories and logical definitions cannot suffice, if one does not add what has already actually been thought in language.

segments.label: §114, claude source block1

segments.text: For what matters here is the discovery of the material of thought that is to be designated, and for this the mere advance by categories and logical definitions cannot suffice unless one adds to it what has already actually been thought in language.

segments.label: §115, de source block1
segments.text: Es lässt sich daher angeben, und es muss angegeben werden, für welche Gegenstände und Begriffe eine Sprache Wörter besitzt, was sie auf Erden und am Himmel, von Leblosem und Lebendigem, an dem thierischen und menschlichen Körper, was endlich von Eigenschafts- und Verhältnissbegriffen, was von unsinnlichen mit Wörtern bezeichnet hat.

segments.label: §115, de source block2
segments.text: Wo mehrere Sprachen, sey es auch nur durch die gleiche Lage der sie redenden Nationen, etwas Gemeinsames haben, wie die Amerikanischen, da wird es wichtig zu sehen, ob ungefähr derselbe Kreis den Vorrath der in ihnen zu Wörtern gestempelten Begriffe umschliesst, und durch die Vergleichung vieler Sprachen dürfte man wohl, immer davon ausgehend, dass jede Sprache ein Ganzes der Weltansicht gewährt, auf einen gewissen gleichsam ursprünglichen, und in allen wiederkehrenden Kreis dieser Art gelangen.

segments.label: §115, de source block3
segments.text: Derselbe müsste sogar, da sich ja allen Nationen im Ganzen dieselbe Welt darstellt, bei allen derselbe seyn, wenn es nicht von der Kraft und Gelegenheit abhienge, wieviel von dieser Welt wirklich in Sprache verwandelt wird.

segments.label: §115, de source block4
segments.text: Dem Fortschreiten der Entdeckung und Benennung besonderer Gegenstände ist es hierbei leicht nachzugehen möglich, aber vorzüglich wichtig ist die Aufsuchung der Modificationen der geistigen Begriffe, die selbst in bekannten Sprachen noch bei weitem nicht genau genug verfolgt worden ist.

segments.label: §115, sol source block1
segments.text: We can and must therefore specify the objects and concepts for which a language has words. We must identify what it has designated in words on earth and in the heavens, among lifeless and living things, in animal and human bodies, and finally among concepts of qualities and relations and among non-sensory concepts.

segments.label: §115, sol source block2
segments.text: Where several languages have something in common, as the American languages do, even if only because the nations that speak them are similarly situated, it becomes important to see whether roughly the same domain encompasses the stock of concepts stamped into words in those languages. By comparing many languages, and always taking as our starting point that each offers a complete view of the world, we may well arrive at a domain of this kind that is, as it were, original and recurs in them all.

segments.label: §115, sol source block3
segments.text: Indeed, since on the whole the same world presents itself to all nations, this domain would have to be the same for them all, were it not that the amount of this world actually transformed into language depends on capacity and opportunity.

segments.label: §115, sol source block4
segments.text: Here it is easy to trace the progress of the discovery and naming of particular objects. It is especially important, however, to trace the modifications of concepts of the mind, a task that has still been pursued nowhere near precisely enough, even in familiar languages.

segments.label: §115, muse source block1
segments.text: It can therefore be stated, and it must be stated, for which objects and concepts a language possesses words, what on earth and in heaven, of lifeless and living things, on the animal and human body, what finally of concepts of quality and relation, what of non-sensuous things, it has designated with words.

segments.label: §115, muse source block2
segments.text: Where several languages, be it only through the same situation of the nations speaking them, have something in common, as the American languages do, it becomes important to see whether approximately the same circle encompasses the stock of concepts stamped into words in them, and through comparison of many languages one might well, always proceeding from the fact that every language affords a whole of a view of the world, arrive at a certain as it were original circle of this kind, recurring in all.

segments.label: §115, muse source block3
segments.text: It would even have to be the same in all, since on the whole the same world presents itself to all nations, if it did not depend on power and opportunity how much of this world is actually transformed into language.

segments.label: §115, muse source block4
segments.text: It is easy here to follow the advance of discovery and naming of particular objects, but what is especially important is the seeking out of the modifications of mental concepts, which even in known languages has still by far not been pursued exactly enough.

segments.text: Indeed, since on the whole the same world presents itself to all nations, this domain would have to be the same for them all, were it not that the amount of this world actually transformed into language depends on power and opportunity.

segments.label: §115, revised source block4
segments.text: It is easy here to follow the progress of discovering and naming particular objects. Of special importance, however, is tracing the modifications of intellectual concepts, which have by no means been followed precisely enough even in familiar languages.

segments.label: §116, de source block1
segments.text: Innerhalb des Wörtervorraths einer Sprache entsteht die fernere Frage : welche Gattungen von Gegenständen und Begriffen ein Uebergewicht in dem Reichthum ihrer Ausdrücke haben ? und es kommt daher auch in dieser Rücksicht auf eine Sonderung derselben nach Classen an.

segments.label: §116, de source block2
segments.text: Denn natürlich bringt nicht nur der allgemeine Bildungsstand der Nationen hierin Ungleichheiten hervor, sondern auch Gewohnheit, Sitte und Lebensart wenden bald diesem, bald jenem Zweige menschlicher Beschäftigung, und daher bald dieser, bald jener Classe von Gegenständen und Begriffen eine grössere Mannigfaltigkeit von Ausdrücken zu.

segments.label: §116, de source block3
segments.text: Die allgemeine Sprachuntersuchung muss nicht nur von den allgemeinsten Classen ausgehen, sondern auch ihre Eintheilung so anlegen, dass sich daraus die Weise ergiebt, wie die Sprache den Begriff sowohl vor dem Verstände (98.), als dem Ohre andeutet, was man die Technik ihrer Bezeichnung nennen kann.

segments.label: §116, sol source block1
segments.text: Within the vocabulary of a language a further question arises: which kinds of objects and concepts predominate in the richness of their expressions? Here too, then, it is important to distinguish them by class.

segments.label: §116, sol source block2
segments.text: For differences naturally arise in this respect from the general level of cultivation of nations, and also from habits, customs and ways of life, which give a greater variety of expressions to one branch of human activity or another, and thus to one class of objects and concepts or another.

segments.label: §116, sol source block3
segments.text: The general study of language must begin with the broadest classes and arrange its classification so as to show how language indicates the concept both to the understanding (§98) and to the ear. This may be called its technique of designation.

segments.label: §116, muse source block1
segments.text: Within the stock of words of a language there arises the further question: which kinds of objects and concepts have a preponderance in the richness of their expressions? and in this respect too it therefore depends on a separation of them into classes.

segments.label: §116, muse source block2
segments.text: For naturally not only the general state of cultivation of nations produces inequalities in this, but also habit, custom and way of life turn a greater manifoldness of expressions now to this, now to that branch of human occupation, and therefore now to this, now to that class of objects and concepts.

segments.label: §116, muse source block3
segments.text: General linguistic inquiry must not only proceed from the most general classes, but also lay out its division in such a way that from it there results the manner in which language indicates the concept both before the understanding (98.) and before the ear, which one may call the technique of its designation.

segments.label: §116, claude source block1
segments.text: Within the stock of words of a language there arises the further question: which genera of objects and concepts have a preponderance in the wealth of their expressions? and so in this respect too what matters is a sorting of them by classes.

segments.label: §116, claude source block2
segments.text: For naturally it is not only the general state of cultivation of the nations that produces inequalities here; habit, custom and way of life also bestow a greater variety of expressions now on this, now on that branch of human occupation, and hence now on this, now on that class of objects and concepts.

segments.label: §117, de source block1
segments.text: Da man hierzu ihrem eignen Gange nachgehen muss, und alles Bedürfniss der Bezeichnung im Denken ruht, so zerfallen in dieser Hinsicht alle Wörter in solche, welche die Materie, den Gegenstand, und solche, welche die Form, die Thätigkeit des Denkens betreffen.

segments.label: §117, de source block2
segments.text: Denn das Denken bedarf eigener, um die Begriffe zu verbinden, zu trennen, zu vergleichen und nach den ihm eigenthümlichen Operationen zu behandeln.

segments.label: §117, de source block3
segments.text: Man kann diese Wörter allgemein logische oder dialektische nennen, und ihre Eigenthümlichkeit besteht darin, dass sie, subjectiv betrachtet, durch innere Handlung Hervorgebrachtes bezeichnen, objectiv betrachtet aber nicht Gegenstände, noch Eigenschaften von Gegenständen, sondern nur Beziehungen und Verhältnisse der Begriffe und Dinge auf einander, und zu dem Verstände, durch den sie gedacht werden.

segments.label: §117, sol source block1
segments.text: Since this requires us to follow language’s own course, and every need for designation has its basis in thinking, all words fall in this respect into those that concern the matter of thinking, its object, and those that concern its form, its activity.

segments.label: §117, sol source block2
segments.text: For thinking needs words of its own to connect, separate and compare concepts, and to handle them according to its characteristic operations.

segments.label: §117, sol source block3
segments.text: These words may be called logical or dialectical in general. Their distinctive feature is that, viewed subjectively, they designate what is produced by an inner act. Viewed objectively, they designate only the connections and relations of concepts and things to one another and to the understanding that thinks them, rather than objects or properties of objects.

segments.label: §117, muse source block1
segments.text: Since for this one must follow its own course, and all need for designation rests in thinking, all words in this respect fall into those concerning the matter, the object, and those concerning the form, the activity of thinking.

segments.label: §117, muse source block2
segments.text: For thinking needs words of its own in order to combine, separate and compare concepts and to treat them according to the operations peculiar to it.

segments.label: §117, muse source block3
segments.text: These words may in general be called logical or dialectical, and their peculiarity consists in this, that, considered subjectively, they designate what is produced through inner action, but, considered objectively, not objects, nor qualities of objects, but only relations and relationships of concepts and things to one another, and to the understanding through which they are thought.

segments.label: §117, claude source block1

segments.label: §117, claude source block2

segments.label: §118, de source block1
segments.text: In der Materie des Denkens bildet natürlich das Gebiet des Körperlichen und Unkörperlichen die hauptsächlichste Abtheilung.

segments.label: §118, de source block2
segments.text: In Rücksicht der Technik der Bezeichnung muss ihr aber eine in diesem Betracht wesentlichere, nemlich die der Wörter für Gegenstände, Beschaffenheiten und Handlungen vorausgehen.

segments.label: §118, de source block3
segments.text: Denn da die Gegenstände den Menschen immer durch hervorstechende Eigenthümlichkeit der Beschaffenheit oder Bewegung anregen, so veranlassen sie ihn auch, sie daran hauptsächlich zu bezeichnen, und Beschaffenheits- und Bewegungswörter schweben daher, als die obersten und allgemeinsten in der Sprache.

segments.label: §118, de source block4
segments.text: Es müssen hierhin auch die allgemeinen Verhältniss- und Beziehungswörter gezählt werden.

segments.label: §118, de source block5
segments.text: Denn obgleich dieselben eigentlich, da es der Verstand ist, welcher die Begriffe auf einander bezieht, in die Classe (117.) der, seine Thätigkeit bezeichnenden Ausdrücke fallen, so gehören sie, insofern man sie an den Gegenständen selbst vorhanden betrachtet, in dieser Rücksicht auch hierher.

segments.label: §118, de source block6
segments.text: Man könnte hier einwenden wollen, dass dieser Unterschied bloss ein grammatischer sey.

segments.label: §118, de source block7
segments.text: Er ist aber wirklich in allen Sprachen lexicalisch und grammatisch zugleich.

segments.label: §118, de source block8
segments.text: Denn in allen giebt es Wörter, die ursprünglich und ihrem Begriff nach, also lexicalisch, auch ohne alle grammatische Abzeichen, Substantiva, Adjectiva und Adverbia, oder Verba sind, und die hiernach Einer Gattung angehörenden bildet nachher die Grammatik in die beiden andren Gattungen um.

segments.label: §118, de source block9
segments.text: Es ist so wesentlich hierauf zu achten, dass in mehr als Einer Sprache nicht ursprüngliche Verba bloss durch Verbindung eines ursprünglichen mit einem gleichfalls ursprünglichen Stamm, also rein lexicalisch, und ohne alle Hülfe der Grammatik gebildet werden.

segments.label: §118, de source block10
segments.text: An diese Hauptabtheilungen schliessen sich nun alle besonderen an, die ich aber hier, wo ich nur einen möglichst kurzen Abriss des allgemeinen Sprachbaus zu geben bemüht bin, übergehe.

segments.label: §118, sol source block1
segments.text: The principal division in the matter of thought is naturally between the corporeal and the incorporeal.

segments.label: §118, sol source block2
segments.text: For the technique of designation, however, another division, more fundamental in this respect, must come first, namely the division into words for objects, qualities and actions.

segments.label: §118, sol source block3
segments.text: For objects always stimulate human beings through some salient feature of their quality or movement and thus prompt them to designate those objects chiefly by that feature. Hence words for qualities and movements stand highest in language as its most general words.

segments.label: §118, sol source block4
segments.text: General words for relations and connections must also be counted here.

segments.label: §118, sol source block5
segments.text: Strictly speaking, since it is the understanding that relates concepts to one another, these words fall into the class of expressions that designate its activity (§117). Yet insofar as the relations and connections are considered to be present in the objects themselves, the words belong here too.

segments.label: §118, sol source block6
segments.text: One might object at this point that the distinction is merely grammatical.

segments.label: §118, sol source block7
segments.text: In fact, it is both lexical and grammatical in all languages.

segments.label: §118, sol source block8
segments.text: For in all languages there are words that are originally and by virtue of their concepts, hence lexically, nouns, adjectives and adverbs, or verbs, even without any grammatical markers. Grammar can then recast words belonging on this basis to one of the three classes into the other two.

segments.label: §118, sol source block9
segments.text: It is essential to bear this in mind, for in more than one language non-original verbs are formed simply by combining an original verb with an equally original stem, hence by purely lexical means and without any help from grammar.

segments.label: §118, sol source block10
segments.text: All the more particular divisions follow from these main divisions. I pass over them here, since I am trying to give as brief an outline as possible of the general structure of language.

segments.label: §118, muse source block1
segments.text: In the matter of thinking, the domain of the corporeal and the incorporeal naturally forms the principal division.

segments.label: §118, muse source block2
segments.text: With respect to the technique of designation, however, there must precede it one more essential in this regard, namely that of words for objects, qualities and actions.

segments.label: §118, muse source block3
segments.text: For since objects always stimulate man through salient peculiarity of quality or movement, they also occasion him to designate them chiefly by that, and words for quality and for movement therefore hover, as the highest and most general, in language.

segments.label: §118, muse source block4
segments.text: The general words for relationship and relation must also be counted here.

segments.label: §118, muse source block5
segments.text: For although these properly, since it is the understanding which relates concepts to one another, fall into the class (117.) of expressions designating its activity, they nevertheless, insofar as one regards them as present on the objects themselves, belong in this respect here as well.

segments.label: §118, muse source block6
segments.text: One might wish to object here that this difference is merely a grammatical one.

segments.label: §118, muse source block7
segments.text: It is, however, in all languages really lexical and grammatical at once.

segments.label: §118, muse source block8
segments.text: For in all of them there are words which originally and according to their concept, thus lexically, even without any grammatical marks, are substantives, adjectives and adverbs, or verbs, and grammar afterwards transforms those belonging in this way to one kind into the two other kinds.

segments.label: §118, muse source block9
segments.text: It is so essential to attend to this that in more than one language non-original verbs are formed merely by combination of an original one with a likewise original stem, thus purely lexically, and without any help from grammar.

segments.label: §118, muse source block10
segments.text: To these main divisions all the particular ones now attach themselves, which, however, I pass over here, where I am endeavouring to give only the shortest possible outline of the general structure of language.

segments.label: §118, claude source block2

segments.label: §118, claude source block3

segments.label: §118, claude source block5

segments.label: §118, claude source block6

segments.label: §118, claude source block7
segments.text: But in all languages it is really lexical and grammatical at once.

segments.label: §118, claude source block8

segments.text: It is thus essential to note that in more than one language non-original verbs are formed merely by the combination of one original stem with another likewise original one — that is, purely lexically, and without any help from grammar.

segments.label: §119, de source block1
segments.text: Dieselbe Classificirung der Begriffe erleichtert und befördert nun auch die Einsicht in die Technik der Bezeichnung.

segments.label: §119, de source block2
segments.text: Ich will nemlich hier von dieser nicht in Beziehung auf die Töne reden, sondern (98.), im Gebiete des Denkens bleibend, von der Wahl der Wörter für Dinge und Begriffe nach andren an ihnen herausgehobnen, oder auf sie bezogenen Begriffen.

segments.label: §119, de source block3
segments.text: Diese Begriffe lassen sich bei weitem nicht immer an den Wörtern erkennen ; aber die erkennbaren aufzusuchen ist ungemein wichtig, da nicht allein daraus erst die individuelle, durch die Sprache gegebene Weltansicht recht deutlich hervorleuchtet, sondern auch überhaupt die ganze Bezeichnungsart durch Verwandtschaft der Begriffe, subjective und objective, eine der wundervollsten Seiten der Sprache ist.

segments.label: §119, de source block4
segments.text: Denn die Aufgabe ist keine geringere, als von den ersten und rohesten Bedürfnissen gegenseitiger Mittheilung zu der Gesammtheit der höchsten Ideen und ihrer feinsten Nuancen aufzusteigen, und das neue Wort, oder die neue Bedeutung immer an schon Vorhandenes anzuknüpfen, da die Sprache immer unter der allgemeinen Bedingung der Möglichkeit der Verständigung steht und der Redende also über das einmal Verstandene nicht weiter hinübergehen darf, als ihm der Hörende zu folgen im Stande ist.

segments.label: §119, sol source block1
segments.text: The same classification of concepts also makes it easier to understand the technique of designation and furthers that understanding.

segments.label: §119, sol source block2
segments.text: Here I shall stay within the domain of thinking (§98) and discuss this technique in terms of how words are chosen for things and concepts on the basis of other concepts singled out in them or brought into relation with them, leaving sounds aside.

segments.label: §119, sol source block3
segments.text: These concepts are far from always discernible in the words. But it is exceedingly important to seek out those that can be discerned, since only then does the distinctive view of the world afforded by the language shine out clearly. Moreover, the whole way of designating through affinities among concepts, subjective and objective alike, is one of the most remarkable aspects of language.

segments.label: §119, sol source block4
segments.text: For the task is nothing less than to rise from the earliest and crudest needs of mutual communication to the full range of the highest ideas and their finest shades, while always linking a new word or a new meaning to something already there. Language is always subject to the general condition that mutual understanding must be possible, so speakers may go beyond what is already understood only as far as their hearers can follow.

segments.label: §119, muse source block1
segments.text: The same classification of concepts now also facilitates and promotes insight into the technique of designation.

segments.label: §119, muse source block2
segments.text: I wish namely here to speak of this not in relation to sounds, but (98.), remaining in the domain of thinking, of the choice of words for things and concepts according to other concepts picked out on them, or referred to them.

segments.label: §119, muse source block3
segments.text: These concepts can by far not always be recognized on the words; but to seek out those that can be recognized is uncommonly important, since not only does the individual view of the world given through language first shine forth quite clearly from this, but also in general the whole manner of designation through kinship of concepts, subjective and objective, is one of the most wonderful sides of language.

segments.label: §119, muse source block4
segments.text: For the task is no lesser one than to ascend from the first and crudest needs of mutual communication to the totality of the highest ideas and their finest nuances, and always to attach the new word, or the new meaning, to what is already present, since language always stands under the general condition of the possibility of being understood and the speaker may therefore not go beyond what has once been understood further than the hearer is able to follow him.

segments.label: §119, claude source block1
segments.text: This same classification of concepts now also facilitates and furthers insight into the technique of designation.

segments.label: §119, claude source block2
segments.text: For I intend to speak of this here not with reference to the tones but (98.), remaining within the domain of thinking, of the choice of words for things and concepts according to other concepts singled out in them or referred to them.

segments.text: Here I shall stay within the domain of thinking (§98) and discuss this technique in terms of how words are chosen for things and concepts on the basis of other concepts singled out in them or brought into relation with them, leaving sounds aside.

segments.label: §119, synthesis source block3
segments.text: These concepts are far from always discernible in the words. But it is exceedingly important to seek out those that can be discerned, since only then does the distinctive view of the world afforded by the language shine out clearly. Moreover, the whole way of designating through affinities among concepts, subjective and objective alike, is one of the most remarkable aspects of language.

segments.label: §119, synthesis source block4
segments.text: For the task is nothing less than to rise from the earliest and crudest needs of mutual communication to the full range of the highest ideas and their finest shades, while always linking a new word or a new meaning to something already there. Language is always subject to the general condition that mutual understanding must be possible, so speakers may go beyond what is already understood only as far as their hearers can follow.

segments.label: §119, revised source block1
segments.text: The same classification of concepts also makes it easier to understand the technique of designation and furthers that understanding.

segments.label: §120, de source block1
segments.text: Die unkörperlichen Begriffe bezieht die Sprache auf körperliche, die Wesen der Körperwelt auf die allgemeinen Kategorien der Beschaffenheit und Bewegung, doch ist diese Regel nicht gleich durchgehend, als jene.

segments.label: §120, de source block2
segments.text: Aus beiden ergiebt sich, dass in der Sprache eine Anzahl allgemeiner körperlicher Beschaffenheitsund Bewegungsbegriffe vorhanden ist, welche den Hauptstoff zur Bezeichnung aller übrigen bilden, und auf die man daher bei der Untersuchung des Wörtervorraths einer Sprache vorzüglich ausgehen muss.

segments.label: §120, de source block3
segments.text: Man kann daher auch diese Untersuchung von zwei verschiedenen Seiten aus anstellen, von Seiten der bezeichnenden und der zu bezeichnenden Begriffe.

segments.label: §120, de source block4
segments.text: Die Vergleichung dieses doppelten Verfahrens zeigt alsdann theils die Angemessenheit der Bezeichnung, theils in der Wahl und Bestimmung der bezeichnenden Begriffe die in dem Volke vorherrschende Neigung zu dieser oder jener sinnlichen Anschauungsweise, und die Art der geistigen Auffassung, den Grad ihrer Klarheit, Bestimmtheit, Reinheit und Tiefe.

segments.label: §120, sol source block1
segments.text: Language relates incorporeal concepts to corporeal ones, and the entities of the corporeal world to the general categories of quality and movement, though the second rule applies less consistently than the first.

segments.label: §120, sol source block2
segments.text: It follows from both rules that language contains a number of general concepts of corporeal quality and movement that supply the principal material for designating all the others. These are therefore what one must particularly look for when investigating the vocabulary of a language.

segments.label: §120, sol source block3
segments.text: This inquiry can accordingly proceed from two sides, that of the designating concepts and that of the concepts to be designated.

segments.label: §120, sol source block4
segments.text: Comparing the results of these two procedures then shows the aptness of the designation and, in the selection and specification of the designating concepts, reveals the people’s prevailing inclination towards one mode of sensory viewing or another, as well as their mode of mental apprehension and its degree of clarity, precision, purity and depth.

segments.label: §120, muse source block1
segments.text: Language refers incorporeal concepts to corporeal ones, the beings of the corporeal world to the general categories of quality and movement, although this rule is not as universally pervasive as that one.

segments.label: §120, muse source block2
segments.text: From both it follows that there is present in language a number of general corporeal concepts of quality and movement which form the main material for designating all the rest, and from which one must therefore chiefly start out in investigating the stock of words of a language.

segments.label: §120, muse source block3
segments.text: One can therefore also carry out this investigation from two different sides, from the side of the designating and of the concepts to be designated.

segments.label: §120, muse source block4
segments.text: Comparison of this double procedure then shows partly the appropriateness of the designation, partly, in the choice and determination of the designating concepts, the inclination predominant in the people to this or that sensuous mode of intuition, and the kind of mental apprehension, the degree of its clarity, determinateness, purity and depth.

segments.label: §121, de source block1
segments.text: Es ist darum keinesweges nothwendig, dass eine Sprache eine Anzahl von Wurzelwörtern besitze, die man als den Ursprung aller übrigen ansehen könne.

segments.label: §121, de source block2
segments.text: Selbst wo solche vorhanden sind, werden doch auch, und am häufigsten, abgeleitete zur Bezeichnung neuer Begriffe gebraucht.

segments.label: §121, de source block3
segments.text: Aber die Betrachtung der Wurzelwörter kann hier nicht umgangen werden.

segments.label: §121, de source block4
segments.text: Sie haben nemlich offenbar eine doppelte, eine grammatische und lexicalische Geltung.

segments.label: §121, de source block5
segments.text: Sie können in der verbundenen Rede gar nicht, oder nur unter gewissen Bedingungen, ohne grammatische Veränderung, erscheinen, und sie dienen als Stammwörter zur Ableitung und Zusammensetzung.

segments.label: §121, de source block6
segments.text: Es giebt Sprachen, in denen es zur lexicographischen Sitte geworden ist, wie im Sanskrit und Wallisischen, jedes Wort auf eine der angenommenen Wurzeln zurückzuführen.

segments.label: §121, de source block7
segments.text: Allein es ist wohl keine dieses Baues, in der sich nicht an auffallenden Beispielen der Ungrund eines solchen Verfahrens zeigen liesse.

segments.label: §121, de source block8
segments.text: Neben der Mehrzahl willig und leicht aus den Wurzeln ableitbarer Wörter giebt es immer noch viele, die sich nur durch gewaltsame und spielende Künstelei unter sie bringen lassen.

segments.label: §121, sol source block1
segments.text: It is therefore by no means necessary for a language to possess a number of root words that can be regarded as the source of all the rest.

segments.label: §121, sol source block2
segments.text: Even where such words exist, derived words are also used, and used most frequently, to designate new concepts.

segments.label: §121, sol source block3
segments.text: But the root words cannot be passed over here.

segments.label: §121, sol source block4
segments.text: For they plainly have a twofold significance, grammatical and lexical.

segments.label: §121, sol source block5
segments.text: In connected speech they can appear without grammatical alteration either not at all or only under certain conditions, and they serve as base words for derivation and compounding.

segments.label: §121, sol source block6
segments.text: In some languages, such as Sanskrit and Welsh, it has become customary in lexicography to trace every word back to one of the posited roots.

segments.label: §121, sol source block7
segments.text: Yet there is probably no language of this structure in which striking examples could not be found to show how unfounded such a procedure is.

segments.label: §121, sol source block8
segments.text: Alongside the majority of words that lend themselves readily and easily to derivation from the roots, there are always many that can be brought under them only by forced and fanciful contrivance.

segments.label: §121, muse source block8

segments.label: §122, de source block1
segments.text: Die Sprache kennt aber auch noch ein andres Mittel zur Vermehrung ihres Wortreichthums, als die Bildung einzelner Ausdrücke.

segments.label: §122, de source block2
segments.text: Sie bezeichnet nemlich an ganzen Reihen von Wörtern ihnen allen gemeinschaftliche Bestimmungen, schafft Ausdrücke nicht durch neue Wortklänge, sondern durch nach Regeln bestimmte Umänderung der vorhandenen.

segments.label: §122, de source block3
segments.text: Dies geschieht oft durch blosse Zusammensetzung, allein auch durch Ableitung, und zwar sowohl durch Agglutination, als durch Inflexion.

segments.label: §122, de source block4
segments.text: Von dieser Art sind die Patronymica, Gentilitia, Abstracta, die Eigenthumswörter (eine fast durch alle Amerikanischen Sprachen gehende Gattung), die Causal- Volitiv-Verba u. s. f. Da man sich aus praktisch sehr zu billigenden Gründen einmal gewöhnt hat,

segments.label: §122, de source block5
segments.text: Alles, was sich auf Regeln bringen lässt, in die Grammatik aufzunehmen, und dem Wörterbuch nur das alphabetische Nachweisen des Einzelnen zu überlassen, so findet man diese Bezeichnungsmethoden jetzt gewöhnlich in den Grammatiken, aber sie gehören offenbar zu der Bildung des Wortvorraths, nicht zu der Verbindung der Rede.

segments.label: §122, de source block6
segments.text: Ihre genauere und tiefere Untersuchung ist aber wichtig, weil sich danach beurtheilen lässt, wie logisch genau und philosophisch richtig die Sprache dabei verfährt.

segments.label: §122, de source block7
segments.text: Denn da hier von nach Regeln gebildeten Gattungen die Rede ist, so kommt es darauf an, wie der Eintheilungsgrund aufgefasst, ob alle aus ihm fliessende Arten erschöpft, ja selbst ob in der Wahl, diese Begriffe durch Ableitung, also nach Gesetzen, die erlernt werden müssen, oder durch Zusammensetzung, also auf unmittelbar verständliche Weise, zu bezeichnen, der Zufall oder eine Regel gewaltet hat.

segments.label: §122, de source block8
segments.text: Denn der logischen Zweckmässigkeit wäre es gemässer die Bildung nach Gesetzen nur da vorzunehmen, wo die zu bezeichnenden Gattungen sich, der Zahl und Beschaffenheit nach, rein aus Begriffen ableiten lassen, nicht da, wo, wie bei dem Begriffe des Eigenthums, ein einzelnes factisches Verhältniss die Wortgattung bestimmt.

segments.label: §122, de source block9
segments.text: Es giebt auch noch einen andern Fall, an dem die logische Angemessenheit und Vollständigkeit der Sprachbezeichnung geprüft werden muss, nemlich an den Begriffen, die zusammen eine Sphäre ausfüllen, und wo es sich nun fragt, ob die Sprache für jeden derselben einen eignen Ausdruck besitzt, und ob an den Ausdrücken selbst die Wechselbeziehung dieser Begriffe bezeichnet ist.

segments.label: §122, de source block10
segments.text: Als Beispiele darf ich hier nur die Dimensionen des Raums und die Weltgegenden anführen.

segments.label: §122, de source block11
segments.text: Mehrere Sprachen fassen in jenen unter demselben Ausdruck zwei verschiedne wie schmal und eng, breit und gross zusammen, in diesen bewahrt in vielen Sprachen, wie im Deutschen und Sanskrit (in jenem in Bezug auf den den Tag theilenden Sonnenlauf, in diesem in Bezug auf einen angenommenen Standpunkt, nach dem man die Seiten bestimmt), der Ausdruck die Gleichförmigkeit der Begriffe, in andren, wie im Lateinischen, ist dieselbe gestört, oder gar keine vorhanden.

segments.label: §122, sol source block1
segments.text: Language has another means of increasing the richness of its vocabulary besides forming individual expressions.

segments.label: §122, sol source block2
segments.text: It marks features common to whole series of words and creates expressions by altering existing word sounds according to definite rules, without creating new word sounds.

segments.label: §122, sol source block3
segments.text: This often takes place through simple compounding, but also through derivation, whether by agglutination or by inflection.

segments.label: §122, sol source block4
segments.text: Examples include patronymics, names of clans or peoples, abstract nouns, words of possession (a class found in almost all American languages), causative and volitive verbs, and so forth. Since, for excellent practical reasons, it has become customary

segments.label: §122, sol source block5
segments.text: to include in the grammar everything that can be reduced to rules and leave the dictionary only to list individual items alphabetically, these methods of designation are now usually found in grammars. They plainly belong, however, to the formation of the vocabulary rather than to the combining of words in speech.

segments.label: §122, sol source block6
segments.text: A closer and deeper examination of them is important, for it allows us to judge how logically precise and philosophically sound the language’s procedure is.

segments.label: §122, sol source block7
segments.text: For since we are dealing here with classes formed according to rules, what matters is how the basis of classification is conceived, whether all the kinds that follow from it are covered, and even whether chance or a rule governed the choice between designating these concepts by derivation, according to laws that must be learnt, and by compounding, in a way that is immediately intelligible.

segments.label: §122, sol source block8
segments.text: For it would be more consonant with logical propriety to form words according to laws only where the kinds to be designated can be derived, in their number and character, from concepts alone, and to refrain from doing so where a particular factual relation determines the class of words, as with the concept of possession.

segments.label: §122, sol source block9
segments.text: There is another case in which the logical aptness and completeness of linguistic designation must be tested. Where a set of concepts together fills an entire domain, the question is whether the language has a distinct expression for each and whether the expressions themselves mark the interrelation of the concepts.

segments.label: §122, sol source block10
segments.text: Here I can give only the dimensions of space and the points of the compass as examples.

segments.label: §122, sol source block11
segments.text: For the dimensions of space, several languages bring two distinct concepts under a single expression, as in *schmal* ‘narrow’ and *eng* ‘tight’, or *breit* ‘broad’ and *gross* ‘large’. For the points of the compass, the expressions in many languages, such as German and Sanskrit, preserve the uniformity of the concepts. German does so by reference to the course of the sun that divides the day, and Sanskrit by reference to an assumed standpoint from which the sides are determined. In other languages, such as Latin, this uniformity is disrupted or altogether absent.

segments.label: §122, muse source block1
segments.text: Language knows, however, yet another means of increasing its richness in words besides the formation of individual expressions.

segments.label: §122, muse source block2
segments.text: It designates namely, on whole series of words, determinations common to them all, creates expressions not through new word-sounds, but through alteration of existing ones determined according to rules.

segments.label: §122, muse source block3
segments.text: This often happens through mere composition, but also through derivation, and indeed both through agglutination and through inflexion.

segments.label: §122, muse source block4
segments.text: Of this kind are the *Patronymica*, *Gentilitia*, *Abstracta*, the property words (a kind running through almost all American languages), the causal-volitive verbs, etc. Since one has once accustomed oneself, for reasons in practical respects much to be approved,

segments.label: §122, muse source block5
segments.text: to take into grammar everything that can be brought under rules, and to leave to the dictionary only the alphabetical listing of the individual item, one now usually finds these methods of designation in grammars, but they evidently belong to the formation of the stock of words, not to the combination of speech.

segments.label: §122, muse source block6
segments.text: Their more exact and deeper investigation is, however, important, because one can judge from it how logically exact and philosophically correct language proceeds therein.

segments.label: §122, muse source block7
segments.text: For since kinds formed according to rules are in question here, it depends on how the ground of division is apprehended, whether all species flowing from it are exhausted, indeed even whether in the choice of designating these concepts through derivation, thus according to laws that must be learnt, or through composition, thus in an immediately intelligible way, chance or a rule has prevailed.

segments.label: §122, muse source block8
segments.text: For it would be more in accordance with logical purposefulness to undertake formation according to laws only where the kinds to be designated can be derived purely from concepts, in number and quality, not where, as with the concept of property, an individual factual relation determines the kind of word.

segments.label: §122, muse source block9
segments.text: There is also another case by which the logical appropriateness and completeness of linguistic designation must be tested, namely by the concepts which together fill up a sphere, and where the question now is whether language possesses for each of them an expression of its own, and whether the reciprocal relation of these concepts is designated on the expressions themselves.

segments.label: §122, muse source block10
segments.text: As examples I need cite here only the dimensions of space and the points of the compass.

segments.label: §122, muse source block11
segments.text: Several languages in the former combine under the same expression two different ones, such as *schmal* 'narrow, slender' and *eng* 'narrow, tight', *breit* 'broad' and *gross* 'large'; in the latter, in many languages, as in German and Sanskrit (in the former in relation to the course of the sun dividing the day, in the latter in relation to an assumed standpoint according to which one determines the sides), the expression preserves the uniformity of the concepts; in others, as in Latin, this is disturbed, or there is none at all.

segments.label: §122, claude source block1
segments.text: Language, however, also knows another means of increasing its wealth of words besides the formation of single expressions.

segments.label: §122, claude source block2
segments.text: For it designates, on whole series of words, determinations common to them all; it creates expressions not through new word-sonorities but through alteration, determined according to rules, of those already present.

segments.label: §122, claude source block3
segments.text: This often takes place through mere compounding, but also through derivation, and indeed both through agglutination and through inflection.

segments.label: §122, claude source block4
segments.text: Of this kind are the patronymics, gentile nouns, abstract nouns, the ownership-words (a genus running through almost all the American languages), the causal and volitive verbs, and so forth. Since, for reasons very much to be approved in practice, one has by now become accustomed

segments.label: §122, claude source block5
segments.text: to admit into the grammar everything that can be reduced to rules, and to leave to the dictionary only the alphabetical registering of the particular item, these methods of designation are now usually found in the grammars; but they evidently belong to the formation of the stock of words, not to the connection of discourse.

segments.label: §122, claude source block6
segments.text: Their more exact and deeper investigation is important, however, because by it one can judge how logically exact and philosophically correct the language's procedure is in this.

segments.label: §122, claude source block7
segments.text: For since we are speaking here of genera formed according to rules, what matters is how the principle of division has been apprehended, whether all the species flowing from it have been exhausted, and indeed even whether, in the choice of designating these concepts by derivation — that is, according to laws that must be learnt — or by compounding — that is, in an immediately intelligible way — chance or a rule has prevailed.

segments.label: §122, claude source block8
segments.text: For it would be more in keeping with logical purposiveness to undertake formation according to laws only where the genera to be designated can, in number and constitution, be derived purely from concepts, not where, as with the concept of ownership, a single factual relation determines the genus of words.

segments.label: §122, claude source block9
segments.text: There is yet another case in which the logical appropriateness and completeness of linguistic designation must be examined, namely in the concepts which together fill a sphere, where the question then is whether the language possesses an expression of its own for each of them, and whether the reciprocal reference of these concepts is designated in the expressions themselves.

segments.label: §122, claude source block10
segments.text: As examples I need cite here only the dimensions of space and the cardinal points.

segments.label: §122, claude source block11
segments.text: In the former, several languages comprise under the same expression two different ones, such as *schmal* ['narrow'] and *eng* ['tight, close'], *breit* ['broad'] and *gross* ['large']; in the latter, in many languages, as in German and Sanskrit (in German with reference to the course of the sun that divides the day, in Sanskrit with reference to an assumed standpoint from which the sides are determined), the expression preserves the uniformity of the concepts; in others, as in Latin, this uniformity is disturbed, or none at all is present.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block1
segments.text: Language has another means of increasing the richness of its vocabulary besides forming individual expressions.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block2
segments.text: It marks features common to whole series of words and creates expressions by altering existing word sounds according to definite rules, without creating new word sounds.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block3
segments.text: This often takes place through simple compounding, but also through derivation, whether by agglutination or by inflection.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block4
segments.text: Examples include patronymics, names derived from those of peoples, abstract nouns, words of possession (a class found through almost all American languages), causative and volitive verbs, and so forth. For good practical reasons, it has become customary

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block5
segments.text: to include in the grammar whatever can be brought under rules, and to leave the dictionary to list individual cases alphabetically. That is why these methods of designation are now generally found in grammars. They clearly belong to the formation of vocabulary rather than to the combining of words in discourse.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block6
segments.text: A closer and deeper examination of them is important, for it allows us to judge how logically precise and philosophically sound the language’s procedure is.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block7
segments.text: For since we are dealing here with classes formed according to rules, what matters is how the basis of classification is conceived, whether all the kinds that follow from it are covered, and even whether chance or a rule governed the choice between designating these concepts by derivation, according to laws that must be learnt, and by compounding, in a way that is immediately intelligible.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block8
segments.text: For it would be more consonant with logical propriety to form words according to laws only where the kinds to be designated can be derived, in their number and character, from concepts alone, and to refrain from doing so where a particular factual relation determines the class of words, as with the concept of possession.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block9
segments.text: There is another case in which the logical aptness and completeness of linguistic designation must be tested. Where a set of concepts together fills an entire domain, the question is whether the language has a distinct expression for each and whether the expressions themselves mark the interrelation of the concepts.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block10
segments.text: Here I can give only the dimensions of space and the points of the compass as examples.

segments.label: §122, synthesis source block11
segments.text: For the dimensions of space, several languages bring two distinct concepts under a single expression, as in *schmal* ‘narrow’ and *eng* ‘tight’, or *breit* ‘broad’ and *gross* ‘large’. For the points of the compass, the expressions in many languages, such as German and Sanskrit, preserve the uniformity of the concepts. German does so by reference to the course of the sun that divides the day, and Sanskrit by reference to an assumed standpoint from which the sides are determined. In other languages, such as Latin, this uniformity is disrupted or altogether absent.

segments.label: §123, de source block1
segments.text: Die ganze hier nur im äussersten Umriss angedeutete Untersuchung des Wortvorraths der Sprachen geht darauf hinaus, das System der Bildung desselben möglichst genau und vollständig zu erkennen, damit man übersehe, wieviel, was unter dem gegebenen Möglichen, und auf welche Weise sie bezeichnet?

segments.label: §123, de source block2
segments.text: Darum muss das Gebiet des zu Bezeichnenden nach seinen verschiedenen Abtheilungen (113— 118.), der Vorrath der Begriffe, welche man zum Zweck der Bezeichnung auf andre bezieht (119 — 122.), und endlich der Umfang der Wortlaute, sowohl der Wurzelwörter als der abgeleiteten und zusammengesetzten, nach der Beschaffenheit und Behandlung der Töne (73 — 82.) durchgegangen werden.

segments.label: §123, sol source block1
segments.text: The aim of this entire investigation of the vocabulary of languages, indicated here only in the barest outline, is to understand the system by which it is formed as precisely and completely as possible, so that one can see how much and what, out of the given range of possibilities, each language designates, and in what way.

segments.label: §123, sol source block2
segments.text: One must therefore survey the domain of what is to be designated in its various divisions (§§113–118), the stock of concepts brought into relation with others for purposes of designation (§§119–122), and finally the range of word sounds in both root words and derived and compound words, with attention to the character and treatment of the sounds (§§73–82).

segments.label: §123, muse source block1
segments.text: The whole investigation of the stock of words of languages, here only indicated in the outermost outline, aims at recognising as exactly and completely as possible the system of its formation, so that one may survey how much, what among given possibilities, and in what manner it designates?

segments.label: §123, muse source block2
segments.text: For that reason the domain of what is to be designated according to its different divisions (113—118.), the stock of concepts which for the purpose of designation one refers to others (119—122.), and finally the extent of word-sounds, both of root-words and of derived and compound words, according to the character and treatment of the sounds (73—82.), must be gone through.

segments.text: The whole investigation of the stock of words of languages, here indicated only in barest outline, aims at recognizing the system of its formation as exactly and completely as possible, so that one may survey: how much, what among the given possibilities, and in what manner does the language designate?

segments.label: §123, claude source block2
