segments.label: §124, de source block1
segments.text: Ist dies geschehen, so besitzt man einen Begriff von dem Material, welches die Sprache der Rede darbietet, und hat nun nur noch (105.) das die Wörter begleitende Gefühl, ihre Rückwirkung auf die Seele zu betrachten.

segments.label: §124, de source block2
segments.text: Es war hiervon bisher nur als von einem Theile des Wortgehaltes die Rede, hier ist nun aber die Eigenthümlichkeit der Sprache in der Behandlung aller Wörter zusammenzufassen.

segments.label: §124, de source block3
segments.text: Wie in dem zu Bezeichnenden die Welt, so erscheint hier der Mensch, und beide so auf einander bezogen, wie sich beide in der nemlichen Sprache darstellen.

segments.label: §124, de source block4
segments.text: Die leichtere oder trägere Erregbarkeit des Gefühls, die hellere oder dunklere Farbe der Phantasie, die mehr prosaische oder poetische Richtung werden hier als Ursachen offenbar, wie man sie bei der objectiven Bildung der Wörter als Erfolge erkannt hat.

segments.label: §124, sol source block1
segments.text: Once this is done, one has a conception of the material that language offers to speech, and all that remains is to consider the feeling that accompanies words (§105), their effect in turn on the mind.

segments.label: §124, sol source block2
segments.text: So far this has been discussed only as part of the content of a word. Here we must consider together the distinctive way in which the language treats all its words.

segments.label: §124, sol source block3
segments.text: Just as the world appears in what is to be designated, so the human being appears here, and the two are related to one another as they present themselves in one and the same language.

segments.label: §124, sol source block4
segments.text: The greater or lesser readiness with which feeling is aroused, the lighter or darker colouring of the imagination, and the more prosaic or more poetic tendency emerge here as causes, just as they were recognized as effects in the objective formation of words.

segments.label: §124, muse source block1
segments.text: When this has been done, one possesses a concept of the material which language offers to speech, and now has only still (105.) to consider the feeling accompanying the words, their reaction upon the soul.

segments.label: §124, muse source block2
segments.text: This was hitherto spoken of only as a part of the content of the word; here, however, the peculiarity of language in the treatment of all words is now to be gathered together.

segments.label: §124, muse source block3
segments.text: As in what is to be designated the world appears, so here man appears, and both related to one another as both present themselves in the same language.

segments.label: §124, muse source block4
segments.text: The easier or more sluggish excitability of feeling, the brighter or darker colour of the imagination, the more prosaic or poetic direction become manifest here as causes, as one recognised them in the objective formation of words as results.

segments.label: §125, de source block1
segments.text: Es würde daher auch unnütz seyn, hier mehr ins Einzelne einzugehen.

segments.label: §125, de source block2
segments.text: Es genügt zu bemerken, dass es hier darauf ankommt, den bisher objectiv geprüften Wörtervorrath nunmehr subjectiv zu betrachten, um zu sehen, ob sich eine gewisse Gleichförmigkeit des Gefühls, das bei der Wortbildung vorgewaltet hat, entdecken lässt, und welche Art nationeller Eigenthümlichkeit sich darin offenbart?

segments.label: §125, de source block3
segments.text: Denn dies auf die Bildung einwirkende Gefühl ist dasselbe, das nachher das Wort auch im Gebrauche immer begleitet.

segments.label: §125, de source block4
segments.text: Ich nenne es aber Gefühl, theils um in dem allgemeinsten Wort alles zusammenzufassen, worin die Sprache die Spuren der menschlichen Art zu seyn an sich tragen kann, theils aber und besonders weil das, wovon wir hier reden, wirklich im Augenblick seiner Thätigkeit nur als Gefühl, nicht in klarem und deutlichem Bewusstseyn wirkt.

segments.label: §125, de source block5
segments.text: Denn sonst liegt ganz vorzüglich auch die rein intellectuelle Richtung darin, so wie die ganze subjective Wirkung, welche die Wörter einer Sprache darum, weil sie ihr angehören, anders, als die einer andren, hervorbringen.

segments.label: §125, de source block6
segments.text: Dass diese wieder auch auf die objective Darstellung der Welt durch die Sprache beiträgt, versteht sich von selbst.

segments.label: §125, de source block7
segments.text: Allein viele in der Sprachwissenschaft nothwendige Absonderungen und Abtheilungen führen nicht sowohl auf wirklich verschiedene Gegenstände, als bloss auf Betrachtung verschiedner Seiten desselben Gegenstands.

segments.label: §125, de source block8
segments.text: Wenn z. B. in der Wortbildung einer Sprache die Richtung liegt, den Geist vorzugsweise in der Sphäre leichter Ideenverknüpfung zu Zwecken des Lebens zu halten, so wird es diese intellectuelle Stimmung vorzüglich seyn, welche auch die unkörperlichen Ausdrücke der Sprache gewöhnlich begleitet.

segments.label: §125, de source block9
segments.text: Es wird aber zugleich daraus entstehen, dass diese Ausdrücke auch selbst in der Bezeichnung ihre Gegenstände mehr von der oberflächlichen Seite nehmen.

segments.label: §125, de source block10
segments.text: Dennoch wird, um die Sprache von dieser Seite vollständig zu kennen, immer die doppelte Zusammenstellung dieser objectiven Beschaffenheit und dieses subjectiven Einflusses auf dieselbe nothwendig bleiben.

segments.label: §125, de source block11
segments.text: Denn der letztere wird hernach auch in andren Theilen des Sprachbaues, namentlich z. B. in der Zusammenfügung der Rede gleichförmig erscheinen.

segments.label: §125, sol source block1
segments.text: It would therefore serve no purpose to go into greater detail here.

segments.label: §125, sol source block2
segments.text: It is enough to observe that the vocabulary examined objectively up to this point must now be considered subjectively, to see whether a certain uniformity can be discerned in the feeling that prevailed in word formation and what kind of national distinctiveness is revealed in it.

segments.label: §125, sol source block3
segments.text: For the feeling that acts on the formation of a word is the same feeling that always accompanies it afterwards in use.

segments.label: §125, sol source block4
segments.text: I call it feeling partly to gather under the most general term everything in which language can bear traces of the human way of being, but chiefly because, at the moment it is active, what we are discussing really operates only as feeling, outside clear and distinct consciousness.

segments.label: §125, sol source block5
segments.text: For in other respects it encompasses, most notably, the purely intellectual tendency, as well as the whole subjective effect that the words of a language produce by virtue of belonging to it and that differs from the effect produced by the words of another language.

segments.label: §125, sol source block6
segments.text: It goes without saying that this effect in turn contributes to the language’s objective portrayal of the world.

segments.label: §125, sol source block7
segments.text: Yet many distinctions and divisions that linguistic inquiry requires lead less to genuinely different objects than to the consideration of different aspects of the same object.

segments.label: §125, sol source block8
segments.text: If, for example, the word formation of a language tends chiefly to keep the mind within the sphere of readily associating ideas for the purposes of life, it will above all be this intellectual disposition that ordinarily accompanies the language’s expressions for incorporeal things as well.

segments.label: §125, sol source block9
segments.text: At the same time, this will lead those expressions themselves to apprehend their objects in designation from a more superficial aspect.

segments.label: §125, sol source block10
segments.text: Nevertheless, to know the language fully in this respect, one must always consider together both this objective character and the subjective influence upon it.

segments.label: §125, sol source block11
segments.text: For the latter will then appear in the same way in other parts of the structure of the language, notably in how words are joined in speech.

segments.label: §125, revised source block5
segments.text: For in other respects it encompasses, most notably, the purely intellectual tendency, as well as the whole subjective effect that the words of a language produce by virtue of belonging to it and that differs from the effect produced by the words of another language.

segments.label: §125, revised source block6
segments.text: It goes without saying that this effect in turn contributes to the language’s objective portrayal of the world.

segments.label: §125, revised source block7
segments.text: Yet many distinctions and divisions that linguistic inquiry requires lead less to genuinely different objects than to the consideration of different aspects of the same object.

segments.label: §125, revised source block8
segments.text: If, for example, the word formation of a language tends chiefly to keep the mind within the sphere of readily associating ideas for the purposes of life, it will above all be this intellectual disposition that ordinarily accompanies the language’s expressions for incorporeal things as well.

segments.label: §125, revised source block9
segments.text: This disposition will also have a further result. Even in designating their objects, these expressions will take them from a more superficial side.

segments.label: §125, revised source block10
segments.text: Nevertheless, to know the language fully in this respect, one must always consider together both this objective character and the subjective influence upon it.

segments.label: §125, revised source block11
segments.text: For the latter will then appear in the same way in other parts of the structure of the language, notably in the construction of discourse.

segments.label: §126, de source block1
segments.text: Die subjective Stimmung, welche bei der Wortbildung mitwirkt, und vom gebildeten Worte wieder hervorgebracht wird, da Ursach und Wirkung immer eine an die Stelle der andren treten, hängt bei weitem weniger fest an dem todten Wort, als die Bezeichnung des Gegenstandes.

segments.label: §126, de source block2
segments.text: Wenn also selbst diese, wie wir (84.) gesehen haben, im Laufe der Zeit Veränderungen ausgesetzt ist, so ist dies weit mehr bei dem subjectiven Eindruck der Fall.

segments.label: §126, de source block3
segments.text: Erhabene Wörter sinken zu gemeinen herab, poetische werden zu prosaischen, und umgekehrt, die ganze Richtung des Denkens und Empfindens einer Nation ändert sich unvermerkt ab, und indem dies wieder (125.) auf die Bezeichnung zurückwirkt, bleiben zwar Laut und Bedeutung scheinbar und im Ganzen dieselben, aber die veränderte Auffassung der letzteren zeigt der genaueren Prüfung doch etwas Verschiednes in ihr.

segments.label: §126, de source block4
segments.text: So schiebt sich besonders unkörperlichen Ausdrücken: Seele, Geist, Herz, Gemüth u. s. f. nach und nach durch die blosse Auffassung ein sehr verschiedener Sinn unter.

segments.label: §126, de source block5
segments.text: Umgekehrt aber ändert sich, wie dies, vielleicht durch den Einfluss einzelner Schriftsteller, in einigen hauptsächlichen Ausdrücken geschieht, allmählich die Geistesrichtung der Nation ab, und diese Aenderung wirkt alsdann in verstärktem Verhältniss auf die ganze Sprache zurück.

segments.label: §126, de source block6
segments.text: Von diesen Veränderungen in dem die Wörter begleitenden Gefühl, sie mögen nun Einfluss auf ihre Bedeutungen ausüben oder nicht, tragen die vereinzelten Wörter selten irgend kennbare Spuren an sich.

segments.label: §126, de source block7
segments.text: Nur wo literarische Denkmäler vorhanden sind, lässt sich denselben nachgehen.

segments.label: §126, de source block8
segments.text: Da die Ursachen dieser Veränderungen auch allein in der Auffassungsweise der Nation liegen, in dem Innern des Menschen aber sehr plötzliche und schroffe Uebergänge möglich sind, so erfahren die Sprachen diese gerade für ihr innerstes Wesen entscheidendsten Umwandlungen schneller, häufiger und stärker, als die durch Abbeugung auch der Bedeutungen im Ganzen, und durch Umformung der Töne.

segments.label: §126, de source block9
segments.text: Ihr Studium gehört hauptsächlich in die Geschichte der Geistesbildung, die Sprachkunde lässt sie oft ganz ausserhalb ihres Kreises liegen, und thut nicht Unrecht hieran, wenn sie sich bloss auf den materiellen, gewissermassen roheren Theil der Sprache beschränken will, muss ihn aber nothwendig in sich fassen, wenn diese, wie es hier der Zweck ist, in ihrem vollständigen Verhältniss zum Menschen dargestellt werden soll.

segments.label: §126, sol source block1
segments.text: The subjective disposition that plays a part in forming a word and is in turn produced by the word once formed, since cause and effect continually change places, adheres far less firmly to the dead word than does the designation of the object.

segments.label: §126, sol source block2
segments.text: If even the designation of the object is subject to change over time, as we have seen (§84), this holds far more strongly for the subjective impression.

segments.label: §126, sol source block3
segments.text: Elevated words sink to the level of common ones, poetic words become prosaic, and vice versa. The whole direction of a nation’s thinking and feeling changes imperceptibly. As this in turn acts upon designation (§125), sound and meaning seem to stay the same and do so on the whole, yet the altered apprehension of the meaning discloses a difference in it to closer scrutiny.

segments.label: §126, sol source block4
segments.text: In this way, expressions for incorporeal things in particular, such as *Seele* ‘soul’, *Geist* ‘spirit’, *Herz* ‘heart’ and *Gemüth* ‘mind in its affective aspect’, gradually acquire a very different sense simply through the way they are apprehended.

segments.label: §126, sol source block5
segments.text: Conversely, when this happens in a few principal expressions, perhaps through the influence of individual writers, the nation’s cast of mind gradually changes, and this change then acts back on the entire language with increased force.

segments.label: §126, sol source block6
segments.text: Individual words taken in isolation rarely bear any discernible traces of these changes in the feeling that accompanies them, whether or not the changes affect their meanings.

segments.label: §126, sol source block7
segments.text: Only where literary records exist can these changes be traced.

segments.label: §126, sol source block8
segments.text: Moreover, since the causes of these changes lie solely in the nation’s mode of apprehension, and very sudden and abrupt transitions are possible in a person’s inner life, languages undergo these transformations, the very ones most decisive for their innermost nature, more rapidly, more frequently and more intensely than they undergo the transformations that come from shifts in meanings themselves as a whole and from the reshaping of sounds.

segments.label: §126, sol source block9
segments.text: The study of these changes belongs chiefly to the history of intellectual cultivation. The study of language often leaves them entirely outside its scope and is justified in doing so if it means to confine itself to the material, in a sense coarser, part of language. But it must include them if language is to be presented in the full extent of its relation to the human being, as is the aim here.

segments.label: §126, muse source block1
segments.text: The subjective mood which cooperates in word-formation and is produced again by the formed word, since cause and effect always step into each other's place, is attached by far less firmly to the dead word than is the designation of the object.

segments.label: §126, muse source block2
segments.text: If, therefore, even the latter, as we have seen (84.), is exposed to changes in the course of time, this is far more the case with the subjective impression.

segments.label: §126, muse source block3
segments.text: Elevated words sink down to common ones, poetic words become prosaic, and vice versa, the whole direction of a nation's thinking and feeling alters imperceptibly, and as this in turn (125.) reacts upon designation, sound and meaning indeed remain apparently and on the whole the same, but the altered apprehension of the latter nevertheless shows closer examination something different in it.

segments.label: §126, muse source block4
segments.text: Thus especially to incorporeal expressions: *Seele* 'soul', *Geist* 'spirit, mind', *Herz* 'heart', *Gemüth* 'inner disposition, mind', etc., a very different sense gradually insinuates itself through mere apprehension.

segments.label: §126, muse source block5
segments.text: Conversely, however, as happens, perhaps through the influence of individual writers, in some principal expressions, the mental direction of the nation gradually alters, and this alteration then reacts upon the whole language in increased proportion.

segments.label: §126, muse source block6
segments.text: Of these changes in the feeling accompanying words, whether they exert influence on their meanings or not, isolated words seldom bear any recognisable traces on themselves.

segments.label: §126, muse source block7
segments.text: Only where literary monuments are extant can they be traced.

segments.label: §126, muse source block8
segments.text: Since the causes of these changes also lie solely in the nation's mode of apprehension, but very sudden and abrupt transitions are possible in the interior of man, languages undergo these transformations, precisely the most decisive for their innermost being, more quickly, frequently and strongly than those through deflection of meanings too as a whole, and through reshaping of sounds.

segments.label: §126, muse source block9
segments.text: Their study belongs chiefly to the history of mental formation; the study of language often leaves them wholly outside its circle, and does not do wrong in this if it wishes to restrict itself merely to the material, in a certain measure cruder, part of language, but must necessarily include it within itself if language, as is the purpose here, is to be represented in its complete relation to man.

segments.label: §126, claude source block1
segments.text: The subjective mood which co-operates in word-formation, and is produced again by the formed word, since cause and effect always step each into the other's place, clings far less firmly to the dead word than does the designation of the object.

segments.label: §126, claude source block2
segments.text: If, then, even the latter, as we have seen (84.), is exposed to changes in the course of time, this is far more the case with the subjective impression.

segments.label: §126, claude source block3
segments.text: Elevated words sink to common ones, poetic words become prosaic, and conversely; the whole direction of a nation's thinking and sensibility alters imperceptibly, and as this in turn (125.) reacts upon the designation, sound and meaning do indeed remain apparently and on the whole the same, but the altered apprehension of the latter nevertheless shows closer examination something different in it.

segments.label: §126, claude source block4
segments.text: Thus, through mere apprehension, a very different sense is gradually slipped beneath incorporeal expressions in particular: *Seele* ['soul'], *Geist* ['mind, spirit'], *Herz* ['heart'], *Gemüth* ['mind, temper'], and so forth.

segments.label: §126, claude source block5
segments.text: Conversely, however, as this happens in some principal expressions, perhaps through the influence of individual writers, the mental direction of the nation gradually alters, and this change then reacts in intensified proportion upon the whole language.

segments.label: §126, claude source block6
segments.text: Of these changes in the feeling that accompanies the words, whether or not they exert influence on their meanings, the isolated words seldom bear any recognizable traces.

segments.label: §126, claude source block7
segments.text: Only where literary monuments exist can they be traced.

segments.label: §126, claude source block8
segments.text: Since, moreover, the causes of these changes lie solely in the nation's mode of apprehension, while very sudden and abrupt transitions are possible within the human being, languages undergo these transformations — the most decisive precisely for their innermost essence — more quickly, more frequently and more strongly than those brought about through deflection even of the meanings as a whole, and through reshaping of the tones.

segments.label: §126, claude source block9
segments.text: Their study belongs chiefly to the history of the cultivation of the mind; the study of language often leaves them lying wholly outside its circle, and does no wrong in this if it wishes to confine itself merely to the material, as it were cruder, part of language, but must necessarily include it within itself if language, as is the aim here, is to be represented in its complete relation to the human being.

segments.label: note:chinese-tones, de source block1
segments.text: Es ist auffallend, dass die Chinesische Sprache, ihrer Armuth an gesprochenen Wörtern ungeachtet, doch nicht jedes der möglichen Wörter durch alle vorhandnen Betonungsarten durchführt. Noch weniger verbindet sie alle Endvocale mit jedem Anfangsconsonanten.

segments.label: note:chinese-tones, sol source block1
segments.text: [Author's note] It is striking that the Chinese language, despite its paucity of spoken words, does not run each possible word through all the available tones. Still less does it combine all final vowels with every initial consonant.

segments.label: note:chinese-tones, muse source block1
segments.text: Author's note: It is striking that the Chinese language, notwithstanding its poverty in spoken words, does not carry each of the possible words through all the existing modes of accentuation. Still less does it combine all final vowels with every initial consonant.

segments.label: note:chinese-tones, claude source block1
segments.text: It is striking that the Chinese language, its poverty in spoken words notwithstanding, nevertheless does not carry every one of the possible words through all the existing kinds of intonation. Still less does it combine all final vowels with every initial consonant.

segments.label: note:chinese-tones, synthesis source block1

segments.label: note:coptic-sanskrit, de source block1
segments.text: So könnte man das Coptische hrosch und Sanskritische rôsha, die beide Zorn bedeuten, für gleichartig halten, da das h hier ebenso ein blosser Hauch des r seyn könnte, wie es in hloili auch loili ist. Allein sorgfältigere Vergleichung zeigt, dass hrosch aus dem gleichbedeutenden horsch, wie hroyr aus hoyrooy und heri entstanden, und also jene Lautähnlichkeit mit dem Indischen Worte bloss zufällig ist.

segments.label: note:coptic-sanskrit, sol source block1
segments.text: [Author's note] One might thus take Coptic *hrosch* and Sanskrit *rôsha*, both meaning ‘anger’, to be of the same kind, since the *h* here might be a mere aspiration of the *r*, just as *hloili* also occurs as *loili*. Closer comparison, however, shows that *hrosch* arose from *horsch*, which has the same meaning, just as *hroyr* arose from *hoyrooy* and *heri*. The resemblance in sound to the Indian word is therefore merely accidental.

segments.label: note:coptic-sanskrit, muse source block1

segments.label: note:deleted-word-symbol, de source block1
segments.text: Nach „sich“ gestrichen: „Allein genauer untersucht, hat das Wort ganz und gar nicht die Natur eines Symbols, und der symbolisirende und der durch richtigen und feinen Sprachsinn geleitete Verstand sind vielmehr einander entgegengesetzt. Denn die Sprache sucht in dem Worte den Begriff selbst, rein und unmittelbar, den körperlichen Gegenstand oder die unkörperliche Idee, und bedient sich des scheinbaren Symbols, des Lautes, nur als eines Mittels.“

After *sich* (‘itself’), the following was deleted: "On closer examination, however, the word has altogether none of the nature of a symbol, and the understanding that symbolises and the understanding guided by a correct and refined sense of language are in fact opposed to one another. For language seeks in the word the concept itself, purely and immediately, the corporeal object or the incorporeal idea, and uses the apparent symbol, the sound, merely as a means."

segments.text: Man findet diese Begriffe mit grosser Klarheit und auf vorzüglich geistreiche Weise im 3. Kapitel des 1. Buchs der Creuzerschen Symbolik und Mythologie entwickelt. „Immer“, heisst es S. 57., „bleibt es wesentliche Eigenschaft dieser (der tropischen) Darstellungsart, dass sie ein Einziges, ein Ungetheiltes giebt.“ und S. 63. „Das Wesen durchdringt und belebt die Naturform. Jener Streit zwischen dem Unendlichen und dem Endlichen ist also aufgelöset, dadurch dass jenes, sich selbst begränzend, ein Menschliches ward.“

segments.label: note:creuzer, sol source block1
segments.text: Author's note. These concepts are developed with great clarity and exceptional insight in chapter 3 of book 1 of Creuzer's *Symbolik und Mythologie*. On p. 57 we read, "It always remains an essential property of this (tropical) mode of representation that it gives something single, something undivided." And on p. 63, "The essence permeates and animates the natural form. That conflict between the infinite and the finite is thus resolved by the infinite, in setting limits to itself, becoming something human."

segments.label: note:creuzer, muse source block1
segments.text: These concepts are found developed with great clarity and in a pre-eminently ingenious way in chapter 3 of book 1 of Creuzer's *Symbolik und Mythologie*. "Always", it is said on p. 57, "it remains the essential property of this (the tropical) mode of presentation, that it gives something single, something undivided", and on p. 63: "The being interpenetrates and enlivens the natural form. That conflict between the Infinite and the Finite is thus resolved, through the former, limiting itself, having become something human."

segments.label: note:creuzer, claude source block1
segments.text: These concepts are found developed with great clarity and in an eminently ingenious manner in the 3rd chapter of the 1st book of Creuzer's *Symbolik und Mythologie*. "It always remains", it says on p. 57, "an essential property of this (the tropical) mode of portrayal that it gives something single, something undivided." and on p. 63: "The essence permeates and animates the natural form. That conflict between the infinite and the finite is thus resolved, in that the former, limiting itself, became something human."

segments.label: note:creuzer, synthesis source block1

On p. 57 we read, “It always remains an essential property of this mode of representation (by tropes) that it gives a single, undivided thing.” On p. 63, “Essence permeates and animates the natural form. The conflict between the infinite and the finite is thus resolved when the former sets bounds to itself and becomes something human.”

segments.label: note:creuzer, revised source block1
segments.text: These concepts are developed with great clarity and exceptional insight in book 1, chapter 3 of Creuzer’s *Symbolik und Mythologie*. On p. 57 we read, “It always remains an essential property of this mode of representation (by tropes) that it gives a single, undivided thing.” On p. 63, “Essence permeates and animates the natural form. The conflict between the infinite and the finite is thus resolved through the former’s setting bounds to itself and becoming something human.”
