text_version.body: A word is a sound that designates a concept. A word therefore always has unity of sound, which is produced by accent where sounds are combined, and unity of concept. The simple word is the true individual in language. For it contains in full the entire operation of the understanding in language. It is even itself the form in which the mind sets outside itself again, as an object, what it has transformed into its own subjectivity (§39). What one obtains by analysing the word itself, however, the syllable and the letter, consists merely of elements of language and is no longer language. All words, including compound words, are the constituents and material of speech, and the vocabulary of a language therefore contains the entire material of a nation's thought. The word shares in the whole nature of language as developed above. It has the same objectivity and subjectivity (§40), exercises the same power over the human being (§42), and is likewise subject to human freedom (§51). It shapes objects into an ideal world of its own, which in language as a whole takes the place of the actual world (§39). The distinctive way in which language apprehends things consists chiefly in this, that individual subjectivity, remaining constant, takes and treats all the constituents of language in the same way and attaches itself to each of them. This way of apprehending things arises more from the ideal than from the material part of languages, more from the mode of presentation they provide than from the sounds used in them. Words that pass from generation to generation and from nation to nation, with little change in sound and designating definite objects, can therefore bear this distinctive character only faintly on their face. It emerges only in their use and in the way they supplement, limit, and determine one another. Where this use is known only from scanty samples, as with the languages of uncultivated nations, mere knowledge of the words, which for that very reason is also incomplete, is insufficient to get to the bottom of what is distinctive about the language in its most important respect.

text_version.body: A word is a sound which designates a concept. There always lies in the word, therefore, unity of sound — which, where sounds are combined, is effected by the accent — and unity of concept. The simple word is the true individual in language. For it contains completely the whole act of the understanding performed by language; it is indeed itself the form in which the mind places outside itself again, as such, the Object transformed into its subjectivity (39.); but that which results when it is itself in turn analysed — the syllable and the letter — is no longer language, but only an element of it. All words, even compound words, are the constituents, the material of discourse, and in the stock of words of a language there therefore lies the entire thought-material of a nation. The word shares the whole nature of language developed in what precedes; it has the same objectivity and subjectivity (40.), exercises the same power over man (42.), and is equally subject to his freedom (51.); it forms objects into its own ideal world, which in language in general takes the place of the real one (39.). The distinctive apprehension of things through language lies principally in this, that individual subjectivity, always remaining the same as itself, takes and treats all the constituents of language in the same way, attaching itself to each one; and it derives more from the ideal than from the material part of languages, more from the mode of presentation given through language than from the sounds used in it. Words which pass, in little-changed tones and designating determinate objects, from generation to generation and from nation to nation can therefore bear this distinctiveness visibly upon them only to a slight extent; it is revealed only in their use and in the way in which they mutually supplement, limit, and determine one another. Where, therefore, as with the languages of uncultivated nations, this use is known only from scanty specimens of language, mere knowledge of words, incomplete for that very reason, does not suffice to fathom the distinctiveness of the language precisely in its most important aspect.

Bestimmen lässt sich dieselbe füglich nur da, wo sie verhältnissmässig gering ist, und durch die Sprache ganz oder grösstentheils wirklich erschöpft wird. Dies kann beinahe nur bei den Sprachen mit einsylbigen Wörtern der Fall seyn.

text_version.body: The number of possible words in a language depends on the number of possible syllables in it (§62.a) and on its particular rules and habits of word formation (§62.b). This number can readily be determined only where it is relatively small and the language actually makes use of all or most of the possibilities. This can occur almost exclusively in languages with monosyllabic words.

text_version.body: Wenn man aber diese Sprachen als eine eigne Gattung zusammenfasst, so muss man wohl verstehen, in welcher Art dies geschieht. Rein factisch kann diese Abtheilung nicht genannt werden. Denn ein grosser Theil aller, auch noch so vielsylbiger Sprachen lässt sich auf einsylbige Wurzeln durch Zergliederung zurückführen, und geht man in Gedanken auf den Ursprung der Sprachen zurück, so ist das Natürlichste, dem einfachen Begriff auch nur einen einfachen Laut zu widmen. Doch darf man dies nicht so verstehen, als müsste nothwendig jedes Stammwort einsylbig seyn. Denn in unsrer Sprachuntersuchung, in der wir nie bis auf den Anfang zurückzugehen vermögen, ist der Begriff des Stammworts selbst nur ein Verhältnissbegriff, und jede unsrer Sprachen kann mit vielen mehrsylbigen Wörtern, neben einsylbigen, begonnen haben. Dagegen besitzen auch die einsylbigen Sprachen diese Eigenschaft nicht rein, und wenn in ihnen zwei Wörter zu einem zusammengesetzten Begriff zusammenkommen, so hängt es nur von dem Accent ab, der dieselben verbindet, oder doch noch, jedes einzeln hervorstossend, trennt. Nun zu entscheiden, ob diese Trennung auch im Verstände die Begriffe weiter auseinander hält, oder ob die Verknüpfung der Begriffe die Eigenthümlichkeit der Aussprache nur als solche, nicht als Wortscheidung ansehen lässt, dürfte wohl an Unmöglichkeit gränzen. Dagegen lässt sich wohl mit Grunde behaupten, dass die Spaltung der Töne da, wo die nahe Verbindung die Begriffe zu Eins macht, den Einfluss stört, welchen die Abtheilung der Rede in richtige und angemessene Wortganze auf den Geist hervorbringt. In jedem einzelnen Fall mag es gleichgültig seyn, ob die Lautabtheilung mit der Gedankenabtheilung gleichen Schritt hält oder nicht. Aber in der Masse ist die Wichtigkeit unverkennbar, und die durchgängige Zerschneidung der Laute in einzelne Sylben muss auf den Fluss der Gedanken unvortheilhaft einwirken. Indess hat man wohl nie in China selbst die Untersuchung auf diese feineren geistigen Einflüsse der Sprache gerichtet, und in der Natur stellt sich ein Misverhältniss gewöhnlich immer wieder durch andre daneben eintretende Umstände her, so dass im Ganzen wieder dieselbe Erscheinung, als wo es nicht vorhanden ist, hervorkommt.

text_version.body: When these languages are grouped together as a class of their own, however, one must be clear about the basis on which this is done. This classification can hardly be called purely factual. For a large proportion of languages, however polysyllabic they may be, can be traced back by analysis to monosyllabic roots, and if one goes back in thought to the origin of languages, the most natural thing is to assign just one simple sound to a simple concept. This should not, however, be taken to mean that every stem word must necessarily be monosyllabic. For in our investigation of language, in which we can never go back to the very beginning, the concept of a stem word is itself only a relative concept, and any of our languages may have begun with many polysyllabic words alongside its monosyllabic ones. Conversely, even monosyllabic languages do not exhibit this property in its pure form. When two words in them come together to form a compound concept, it is solely the accent that either binds them together or still keeps them apart by bringing each out separately. It would probably be all but impossible to decide whether this separation also keeps the concepts further apart in the understanding, or whether their connection leads one to regard the peculiarity of pronunciation as merely that, without taking it to mark a division between words. There is good reason, however, to maintain that keeping the sounds separate where the close connection makes the concepts one interferes with the effect on the mind of dividing speech into proper and appropriate units, each forming a whole word. In any individual case it may make no difference whether the division of sounds keeps pace with the division of thought. Taken together, however, the cases are unmistakably important, and the systematic breaking up of sounds into separate syllables must adversely affect the flow of thought. Yet these subtler effects of language on the mind have probably never been investigated in China itself, and in nature an imbalance generally rights itself through other circumstances that come into play alongside it, so that the overall result is the same as where no imbalance exists.

text_version.body: But if these languages are grouped together as a distinct genus, one must properly understand in what way this is done. This division cannot be called purely factual. For a large part of all languages, however polysyllabic they may be, can be traced back by analysis to monosyllabic roots; and if one goes back in thought to the origin of languages, the most natural thing is to assign to the simple concept likewise only a simple sound. Yet this must not be understood as if every stem-word must necessarily be monosyllabic. For in our investigation of language, in which we are never able to go back to the beginning, the concept of the stem-word is itself only a relative concept, and any of our languages may have begun with many polysyllabic words alongside monosyllabic ones. On the other hand, the monosyllabic languages, too, do not possess this property in purity; and when in them two words come together to form a composite concept, it depends only on the accent whether it connects them or, thrusting each forth singly, still separates them. To decide now whether this separation also holds the concepts further apart in the understanding, or whether the linking of the concepts makes the peculiarity of pronunciation appear only as such, not as a division between words, would probably border on impossibility. On the other hand, it may well be asserted with good reason that the splitting of the tones, where close combination makes the concepts into one, disturbs the influence which the division of discourse into correct and appropriate word-wholes produces on the mind. In each individual case it may be indifferent whether the division of sound keeps pace with the division of thought or not. But in the aggregate the importance is unmistakable, and the thoroughgoing cutting up of the sounds into individual syllables must act disadvantageously on the flow of thoughts. Meanwhile, investigation has probably never in China itself been directed to these finer mental influences of language; and in nature a disproportion is ordinarily always redressed by other circumstances that intervene alongside it, so that on the whole the same phenomenon emerges again as where it is not present.

In each individual case it may be indifferent whether the division of sound keeps pace with the division of thought or not. But in the mass the importance is unmistakable, and the thoroughgoing cutting up of the sounds into single syllables must act unfavourably on the flow of thoughts. However, in China itself inquiry has probably never been directed to these subtler mental influences of language, and in nature a disproportion usually rights itself again and again through other circumstances arising alongside it, so that on the whole the same phenomenon emerges once more as where the disproportion is not present.

text_version.body: When these languages are grouped together as a class of their own, however, one must be clear about the basis on which this is done. This classification can hardly be called purely factual. For a large proportion of languages, however polysyllabic they may be, can be traced back by analysis to monosyllabic roots, and if one goes back in thought to the origin of languages, the most natural thing is to assign just one simple sound to a simple concept. This should not, however, be taken to mean that every stem word must necessarily be monosyllabic. For in our investigation of language, in which we can never go back to the very beginning, the concept of a stem word is itself only a relative concept, and any of our languages may have begun with many polysyllabic words alongside its monosyllabic ones. Conversely, even monosyllabic languages do not exhibit this property in its pure form. When two words in them come together to form a compound concept, it is solely the accent that either binds them together or still keeps them apart by bringing each out separately. It would probably be all but impossible to decide whether this separation also keeps the concepts further apart in the understanding, or whether their connection leads one to regard the peculiarity of pronunciation as merely that, without taking it to mark a division between words. There is good reason, however, to maintain that keeping the sounds separate where the close connection makes the concepts one interferes with the effect on the mind of dividing speech into proper and appropriate units, each forming a whole word. In any individual case it may make no difference whether the division of sounds keeps pace with the division of thought. Taken together, however, the cases are unmistakably important, and the systematic breaking up of sounds into separate syllables must adversely affect the flow of thought. Yet these subtler effects of language on the mind have probably never been investigated in China itself, and in nature an imbalance generally rights itself through other circumstances that come into play alongside it, so that the overall result is the same as where no imbalance exists.

text_version.body: Schon der Begriff einsylbiger Sprachen muss daher mit gewisser Einschränkung verstanden werden, und die mehrsylbigen können ursprünglich einsylbig gewesen seyn. Die Wortabtheilung, die dieser Classification zum Grunde liegt, beruht sogar in Absicht der Laute auf Umständen, die, wie eben gezeigt worden, um so schwieriger zu beurtheilen sind, als sie keine genaue Kenntniss des lebendigen Vortrags der Rede voraussetzen. Dennoch bleibt der einsylbige Bau einer kleinen Anzahl von Sprachen eine höchst merkwürdige Erscheinung, die, gerade ihrer Seltenheit wegen, die aufmerksamste Betrachtung verdient. Durchaus falsch ist die Vorstellungsweise, diese Sprachen, gleichsam wie Kindersprachen, als auf einer Stufe ursprünglicher Unvollkommenheit stehen geblieben anzusehen. Die Ursachen der Einsylbigkeit müssen gewiss ganz anders und viel tiefer aufgesucht werden. Da aber diese Eigenschaft den Amerikanischen Sprachen fremd ist, so habe ich ihr nur hier im Gebäude der Sprache überhaupt ihre passende Stelle anweisen wollen.

text_version.body: The very concept of monosyllabic languages must therefore be understood with some qualification, and polysyllabic languages may originally have been monosyllabic. Even as regards the sounds, the division into words underlying this classification depends on circumstances that, as we have just seen, are all the harder to judge because no precise knowledge of how speech is delivered in actual use can be taken for granted. Nevertheless, the monosyllabic structure of a small number of languages remains a highly remarkable phenomenon, deserving the closest attention precisely because of its rarity. It is altogether mistaken to regard these languages as children’s languages, as it were, that have remained at a stage of original imperfection. The causes of monosyllabism must surely be sought in quite a different way and at a much deeper level. Since this property is foreign to the American languages, however, my aim here has simply been to assign it its proper place in the structure of language in general.

text_version.body: Wo die Wortbildung an keine so feste Form gebunden ist, da bleibt die Anzahl der möglichen Wörter unbestimmt, und eine Menge von zusammentretenden Umständen, von denen sich nur selten Rechenschaft geben lässt, bestimmt, welche davon wirklich ins Daseyn gerufen werden. Aber immer muss man annehmen, dass jedes durch ein andres, vor ihm vorhandenes entstanden ist. Denn alle Veränderungen in der Sprache geschehen (43.) allmählich, und immer wird nur das schon ganz oder zum Theil Gehörte nachgesprochen. Die Untersuchung der Wortlaute befindet sich daher überall an der Mitte einer Kette, deren Anfang ihr unzugänglich bleibt. Es bedarf aber kaum der verwahrenden Bemerkung, dass darum nicht alle noch vorhandene Sprachen Theile der nemlichen Kette zu seyn brauchen, da es (46.) verschiedene, lange oder niemals mit einander in Verbindung getretene Wörterentwicklungen geben könnte. Da jedoch die Gleichheit der Sprachwerkzeuge und ihrer Gesetze überall dieselben und nur eine gewisse Anzahl von Wortlauten möglich macht, so kann (47.) die blosse Einerleiheit oder Verwandtschaft des Tons für sich nicht über ihren historischen oder physiologischen Unterschied entscheiden. Die Verwandtschaft lässt sich auf zwiefache Weise denken, durch Ableitung, indem der einfachere durch Anhängung, Vorschlag oder Einschiebung zum mehr oder minder Zusammengesetzten wird, und durch Anklang, indem der einfache Ton, auch einfach, aber verändert, wiederklingt, oder eine verwandte Idee durch einen verwandten bezeichnet wird. Von dieser Entstehung jedes Worts aus einem andren Wort dürften höchstens die Naturlauten nachgeahmten auszunehmen seyn, die zwar gewöhnlich gleichfalls von Geschlecht zu Geschlecht und Nation zu Nation übergehen, aber auch plötzlich entstehen können, obgleich sie auch in diesem Fall sich immer der Lautanalogie der übrigen Sprache anschliessen werden.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §77 — checked German

text_version.body: Where word formation is not bound to so fixed a form, the number of possible words remains indeterminate, and which of them are actually called into being is determined by a host of converging circumstances that can rarely be accounted for. One must always assume, however, that each word arose through another that existed before it. For all changes in language occur gradually (§43), and what is repeated in speech has invariably been heard before, in whole or in part. The investigation of word sounds therefore always finds itself in the middle of a chain whose beginning remains inaccessible to it. It scarcely needs pointing out, however, that the languages still in existence need not therefore all be parts of the same chain, since there could have been separate lines of development of words that came into contact only after a long time, or never did so at all (§46). Since, however, the sameness of the organs of speech and of the laws governing them makes the same limited set of word sounds possible everywhere, mere identity or affinity of sound cannot in itself decide the distinction between the historical and physiological grounds of that resemblance (§47). The affinity can be conceived in two ways, through derivation, when the simpler sound becomes more or less composite by the addition of something at the end, at the beginning, or within it, and through echo, when the simple sound recurs, still simple but altered, or when a kindred idea is designated by a kindred sound. The only possible exceptions to this emergence of each word from another are words that imitate natural sounds. These too usually pass from generation to generation and from nation to nation, but they can also arise suddenly, in which case they will still conform to the sound analogies of the rest of the language.

text_version.body: Where word-formation is bound to no such fixed form, the number of possible words remains indeterminate, and a multitude of concurring circumstances, of which an account can only rarely be given, determines which of them are actually called into existence. But it must always be assumed that each one has arisen through another that existed before it. For all changes in language take place gradually (43.), and what is repeated in speaking is always only what has already been heard, wholly or in part. The investigation of word-sounds therefore finds itself everywhere in the middle of a chain whose beginning remains inaccessible to it. There is, however, hardly any need for the cautionary remark that not all languages still in existence need on that account be parts of the same chain, since (46.) there could be different developments of words that have never, or for a long time have not, entered into connection with one another. Since, however, the sameness of the organs of speech and of their laws makes the same word-sounds, and only a certain number of them, possible everywhere, mere identity or affinity of tone cannot by itself decide (47.) concerning their historical or physiological difference. Affinity can be conceived in two ways: by derivation, in that the simpler sound becomes, by addition at the end, addition at the beginning, or insertion, the more or less composite one; and by similarity of sound, in that the simple tone sounds again, still simple but changed, or a related idea is designated by a related tone. From this origin of every word from another word, at most those imitated from sounds of nature might be excepted; they ordinarily pass likewise from generation to generation and from nation to nation, but can also arise suddenly, although even in this case they will always conform to the sound-analogy of the rest of the language.

text_version.body: Hier, wo nur dem Gange der Wortbildung in einer gegebenen Sprache nachgeforscht werden soll, kommt es bloss darauf an, die zusammengesetzten Wortlaute in immer einfachere, soweit dies möglich ist, zu zergliedern, die Analogie dieser Zusammensetzung zu entwickeln, und die gefundenen einfachsten Wörter wiederum unter sich in ihren Lautverhältnissen zu vergleichen. Daraus ergeben sich nun auf der einen Seite die Gesetze und Gewohnheiten der Wortbildung der Nationen, auf der andren der Umfang, die Vollständigkeit und die Alterthümlichkeit ihres Wortbaus. Zu den ersteren gehören die Veränderungen der Wörter durch die Vocalreihe, die Einschiebungen und Veränderungen der Consonanten, die Erweiterungen der Wörter durch Vor- und Nachklänge, die Sylbenwiederholungen und Versetzungen. An diesem Allem lässt sich sehr oft der rohere oder feinere Sprachsinn der Nationen erkennen.

text_version.body: Here, where the question is simply how word formation proceeds in a given language, all that is required is to analyse compound word sounds into progressively simpler ones as far as possible, to work out the analogy governing their composition, and then to compare the simplest words thus found with one another in respect of their sound relationships. This reveals both the laws and habits of word formation among nations and the extent, completeness, and antiquity of their word structure. The laws and habits include changes to words by variation along the vowel series, the insertion and alteration of consonants, the extension of words by sounds added at the beginning or end, and the repetition and transposition of syllables. All this very often reveals how coarse or refined a nation's sense of language is.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §78 — sol English, vocabulary

text_version.body: Here, where only the course of word-formation in a given language is to be investigated, the sole concern is to analyse composite word-sounds into ever simpler ones, as far as this is possible, to develop the analogy of this composition, and in turn to compare the simplest words thus found with one another in their sound-relations. From this there result, on the one side, the laws and customs of the word-formation of nations and, on the other, the extent, completeness, and archaic character of their word-structure. To the former belong the alterations of words through the vowel-series, the insertions and alterations of consonants, the extensions of words by sounds placed before and after, repetitions of syllables, and transpositions. In all this the cruder or finer sense for language of nations can very often be recognized.

text_version.body: Je näher eine Sprache aus einer schon vollständig geformten entnommen ist, desto weniger steigt sie zu einfachen Lauten auf, die in dem Wörtervorrath mehrerer von diesen kaum überhaupt angetroffen werden. Nur da wo bedeutende Stämme Jahrhunderte hindurch, in grosser Freiheit von fremder Vermischung, ihre Sprache von Geschlecht zu Geschlecht fortgetragen haben, und der Ursprung sich in Dunkel verliert, erscheint der weite und alterthümliche Bau, in dem sich lange Geschlechtsreihen von Wörtern auf ihre Grundlaute zurückführen lassen, diese noch in ihrer Einfachheit Bedeutung haben, jede Analogie sich an zahlreichen Beispielen erweist, jede mit andren in derselben Sphäre oder Gattung befindliche Lautbeschaffenheit mehrere dieser oder alle neben sich findet, und in welchem mithin strenge Analogie den Geist durch ein vielumfassendes System von Wortklängen führt. Dies wirkt nun, ausser dem Einfluss einer solchen Fülle und Regelmässigkeit auf den Gebrauch, auch in sich, im klaren Bewusstseyn, wie in dunklem Gefühl auf die Nation zurück, und die Spracherzeugung in ihr wird fruchtbarer für Alles, womit sie in Berührung steht, wenn sich der Welt von Ideen auch eine sich selbst leicht und wundervoll ordnende Welt von Tönen zur Seite stellt. Der Bau einer solchen Sprache knüpft jeden Einzelnen an viel entferntere Zeiten, an einen viel ursprünglicheren Zustand des Menschengeschlechts, an eine unendlich erscheinende Masse einmal da gewesener, und sich doch immer auf irgend eine Weise berührender und wieder hervorrufender Gedanken und Empfindungen an.

text_version.body: The more directly a language is drawn from one already fully formed, the less far it goes back to simple sounds, which are hardly to be found at all in the vocabularies of several such languages. It is only where major tribes have handed down their language from generation to generation for centuries, largely free from admixture from outside, and where its origin is lost in obscurity, that this extensive and ancient structure appears. In it long genealogies of words can be traced back to their basic sounds, and these still have meaning in their simplicity. Each analogy can be demonstrated by numerous examples, and each sound feature that shares a sphere or class with others is found alongside several or all of them. Strict analogy thus guides the mind through a comprehensive system of word sounds. Beyond the influence of such abundance and regularity on usage, this structure also acts in its own right upon the nation, both in clear consciousness and in obscure feeling. The production of language among its people becomes more fruitful for everything it comes into contact with when alongside the world of ideas there stands a world of sounds that orders itself with ease and in a wondrous way. The structure of such a language connects each individual with far more distant times, with a far more original state of humankind, and with a seemingly infinite mass of thoughts and sensations that once existed and yet continually, in one way or another, touch and call forth one another again.

text_version.body: Hierin liegt (55.) das Regelsystem der Wortbildung, das man, auch bei der bloss lexikalischen Vergleichung der Sprachen, von den Tönen selbst zu unterscheiden hat. Die Grundlage desselben ist das Lautsystem. Denn je feiner und geistiger sich das Gehör und der Sprachsinn in diesem erweist, desto sorgfältiger wird jede, vielleicht anfangs nur zufällig, durch Einschiebung eines Hauchs, eines Vocals, eines Nasenlauts, entstehende Abänderung des Tones beachtet, und durch die ähnlichen Fälle durchgeführt, und desto analogischer werden ihr andre gleichartige Veränderungen angebildet. Von verwandten Nationen gehen die Grundzüge dieses Systems in verwandte Sprachen über, und die Gleichartigkeit der Sprachen lässt sich in vieler Hinsicht richtiger an der lexikalischen Analogie, als an der grammatischen erkennen. Denn sie beruht nicht, wie diese auf allgemeinen Denkgesetzen, sondern heftet sich unmittelbar an den Ton. Je individueller aber eine Gleichartigkeit ist, desto sichrer weist sie auf einen geschichtlichen Zusammenhang hin. Doch müssen die Fälle wohl beachtet werden, wo Wörter, in deren Bau Analogien dieser Art angedeutet sind, in andre Sprachen ohne diese Analogien selbst, d. h. ohne das Gefühl derselben bei der andren Nation, und daher ohne Fortbildung durch sie, übergegangen sind, und nun Theile einer Sprache werden, in welcher gar kein solcher Bau in solcher Vollkommenheit, oder ein andres System desselben vorhanden ist.

text_version.body: Herein lies the system of rules of word formation (§55), which must be distinguished from the sounds themselves even in a purely lexical comparison of languages. Its foundation is the sound system. For the more refined and discerning the ear and the sense of language prove to be in the sound system, the more carefully each modification of sound, arising perhaps at first by mere chance through the insertion of an aspiration, a vowel, or a nasal sound, is attended to and carried through similar cases, and the more closely other changes of the same kind are modelled on it by analogy. From kindred nations the main features of this system pass into kindred languages, and in many respects the similarity in kind between languages can be discerned more accurately from lexical analogy than from grammatical analogy. For lexical analogy attaches directly to sound, whereas grammatical analogy rests on general laws of thought. The more individual the similarity in kind, however, the more surely it points to a historical connection. Careful attention must be paid, however, to cases where words whose structure shows traces of analogies of this kind have passed into other languages without the analogies themselves. The other nation has no sense of those analogies, and consequently no further development takes place by their means. The words thus become parts of a language where such a structure is nowhere developed to the same degree of perfection, or where that structure follows a different system.

text_version.body: Herein lies (55.) the system of rules of word-formation, which, even in the merely lexical comparison of languages, must be distinguished from the tones themselves. Its basis is the sound-system. For the finer and more intellectual the hearing and the sense for language prove themselves to be in this system, the more carefully is every modification of the tone — arising perhaps at first only by chance, through insertion of a breath, a vowel, a nasal sound — attended to and carried through in similar cases, and the more analogically are other changes of the same kind formed after it. From related nations the fundamental features of this system pass over into related languages, and the sameness of kind of languages can in many respects be recognized more correctly from lexical analogy than from grammatical analogy. For it does not rest, as the latter does, on general laws of thought, but attaches itself immediately to the tone. The more individual a sameness of kind is, however, the more surely it points to a historical connection. Care must, however, be taken to note the cases where words in whose structure analogies of this kind are indicated have passed into other languages without these analogies themselves — that is, without the feeling for them in the other nation, and therefore without further development by it — and now become parts of a language in which no such structure exists in such perfection, or in which a different system of it exists.

text_version.body: Aus diesem inneren Zusammenhange der Wörter, auch in ihren Lauten, folgt nunmehr von selbst, dass die Wörter mehrerer Sprachen zum Behuf der Auffindung ihrer Gleichartigkeit nicht dürfen unmittelbar mit einander verglichen werden, sondern erst eine Vergleichung derselben in jeder einzeln vorausgehen muss. Die alphabetische Nebeneinanderstellung der Wörter verschiedener Sprachen reisst jede von diesen aus ihrem natürlichen Zusammenhang. Wenn aber die Vergleichung der Wörter einer Sprache unter einander geschehen ist, so ergeben sich für die mit einer andren zwei Gegenstände: die Regeln der lexikalischen Analogie und die Grundlaute, und mit den ersteren die von einer Sprache in die andre übergegangenen wirklich nach diesen Regeln geformten zusammengesetzten Wörter. Eine Vergleichung, die ihre Gewähr in sich selbst trägt, kann nur auf diese Weise geschehen. Wenn man aber, wie es sehr oft der Fall ist, aus Mangel an Hülfsmitteln, oder weil eine Sprache gar keinen so einsichtlich ausgeführten inneren Bau hat, und weil man auch den vorhandenen doch nie ganz vollständig erkennt, auf die unmittelbare Wörtervergleichung zurückgewiesen wird, so muss man doch die beiden zu vergleichenden Wörter erst möglichst genau jedes in seiner Sprache, ihrer Entstehung nach, erforschen, um nicht wirklich verschiedene wegen bloss scheinbarer Lautähnlichkeit, als gleichartig, anzusehen.

text_version.body: It now follows from this internal connectedness of words, extending even to their sounds, that to discover similarities in kind between languages one must first compare the words within each language before comparing them across languages. Setting the words of different languages side by side in alphabetical order tears each of those languages out of its natural context. Once the words of one language have been compared with one another, two objects of comparison with another language emerge, the rules of lexical analogy and the basic sounds. With the rules come the compound words that actually were formed according to them and passed from one language into the other. Only in this way is a comparison possible that carries its own warrant. Very often, however, one is thrown back on direct comparison of words, either for want of resources or because a language has no internal structure worked out with such clarity, and also because one never fully grasps even the structure that is there. One must still investigate the origin of each word to be compared as precisely as possible in its own language, lest one take genuinely different words to be of the same kind on the strength of a merely apparent resemblance in sound.

The alphabetical placing side by side of the words of different languages tears each of these languages out of its natural context. But when the comparison of the words of one language with one another has been made, two objects result for comparison with another language: the rules of lexical analogy and the fundamental sounds, and, together with the former, the composite words that have passed from one language into the other and are actually formed according to these rules. A comparison that carries its guarantee in itself can be made only in this way. But if, as very often happens, from lack of aids, or because a language has no inner structure executed in so intelligible a manner, and because even that which exists is never known quite completely, one is thrown back on immediate comparison of words, the two words to be compared must nevertheless first be investigated as exactly as possible, each in its own language, as to their origin, so as not to regard words that are really different as of the same kind on account of merely apparent similarity of sound.

Setting the words of different languages side by side in alphabetical order tears each of those languages out of its natural context. With the rules come the complex words that actually were formed according to them and passed from one language into the other. Only in this way is a comparison possible that carries its own warrant. Very often, however, one is thrown back on direct comparison of words, either for want of resources or because a language has no internal structure worked out with such clarity, and also because one never fully grasps even the structure that is there. One must still investigate the origin of each word to be compared as precisely as possible in its own language, lest one take genuinely different words to be of the same kind on the strength of a merely apparent resemblance in sound.

text_version.body: In allen hier betrachteten Beziehungen ist nur auf die Abhängigkeit der Wortbildung von der Tonbehandlung der Nation gesehen worden, auf die Art, wie sie dem Vorrath ihrer Wortlaute Umfang und Mannigfaltigkeit giebt. Es gesellt sich aber der Wortbildung auch hauptsächlich Rücksicht auf die Bedeutung zu, und wenn z. B. die Entstehung von λαμβάνω aus λάβω blosse Tonveränderung ist, so führt die von legen aus liegen eine Nuance des Sinnes mit sich. Ganz auf der Bedeutung beruht die Wortbildung durch Zusammensetzung, in welcher immer mehrere Begriffe verbunden werden, entweder zu einem neuen dritten, oder, wie bei der Bildung durch Vor- und Nachsilben, bloss zu verschiedner Bestimmung des Hauptbegriffs. Die Lautverhältnisse wirken dabei nur gelegentlich auf untergeordnete Weise mit.

text_version.body: In all the respects considered here, attention has been confined to the dependence of word formation on a nation's treatment of sound, to the way it gives scope and variety to its stock of word sounds. Consideration of meaning, however, also plays a principal role in word formation. For example, while the formation of *λαμβάνω* from *λάβω* is a mere change of sound, the formation of *legen* from *liegen* brings with it a shade of difference in sense. Word formation by compounding rests entirely on meaning. Several concepts are always combined, either to form a new, third concept or, as in formation by prefixes and suffixes, simply to give the principal concept a different determination. Sound relationships enter into this only occasionally and in a subordinate way.

text_version.body: In der Wahl der Laute für die Begriffe lässt sich die Sprache natürlich durch die klareren und dunkleren Beziehungen leiten, welche das Gefühl und die Einbildungskraft, der Individualität der Nationen gemäss, unter ihnen findet. Geschichtlich verliert sich dies aber in die Zeiten der Spracherfindung, an welche keine Untersuchung mehr reicht, und durch die allmähliche Sprachumänderung, wo bald der Ton von dem Grundton, bald der Begriff von dem Grundbegriff nach und nach weiter abgebeugt wird, erleidet dies Verhältniss zwischen Ton und Bedeutung sehr oft eine gänzliche Abänderung. Auch ist das, seiner Natur nach, unbestimmtere Gefühl, auf dem es beruht, in verschiedenen Völkern verschieden, und gerade die Nationen, die ursprünglichere, d. h. weniger Spuren grosser Umwälzungen an sich tragende Sprachen besitzen, dulden in ihren Silben weniger zusammenstossende Consonanten, und entbehren mithin ein Mittel mehr, den Charakter des Wortlauts zu bestimmen. Es ist also eine gar nicht ungewöhnliche Erscheinung, starke und selbst widrige Begriffe mit sanften und weichen Lauten und umgekehrt gepaart zu sehen, und in geschichtlichen Sprachuntersuchungen ist auf diese Analogie durchaus kein Gewicht zu legen. Phantasie und Scharfsinn finden darin einen weiten, aber höchst unsichren Boden, und für zehn, solche Uebereinstimmung des Tons mit der Bedeutung beweisende Beispiele geräth man auf eine viel grössere Anzahl, in welchen sie fehlt. Dagegen wäre es gleich unrichtig, die Aufmerksamkeit ganz davon abzuwenden. Denn es ist nicht zu läugnen, dass in Sprachen von hohem Alter und weitem und mannigfaltigem Wortbau sich das Gefühl einer solchen unverkennbaren Uebereinstimmung häufiger aufdringt, als in andren. Wo sie aber in einer unvermischt gebliebenen Muttersprache Jahrhunderte hindurch auf dieselbe Nation fortwirkt, da erhöht und verstärkt sie den Einfluss der Sprache, bei der Alles darauf ankommt, durch die engste Verschmelzung des Tons mit dem Begriff aus dem Wort ein eignes, zwischen dem Menschen und der Welt, zugleich abhängig und unabhängig von beiden, schwebendes Wesen zu machen. Vorzüglich sichtbar ist dies im Deutschen, und den von ihm abhängenden Sprachen.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §83 — checked German

text_version.body: In choosing sounds for concepts, language is naturally guided by the clearer and more obscure relations that feeling and imagination, in keeping with the individuality of nations, find between them. Historically, however, this goes back into the lost ages in which language was invented, beyond the reach of any inquiry. As language gradually changes, now the sound diverges progressively from the basic sound, now the concept from the basic concept, and this relation between sound and meaning very often changes altogether. The feeling on which this relation rests, being by nature less determinate, also varies from one people to another. And precisely those nations with more original languages, that is, languages bearing fewer traces of great upheavals, tolerate fewer consonants coming together in their syllables and thus lack a further means of shaping the character of the word sound. It is therefore by no means unusual to see strong and even disagreeable concepts paired with gentle and soft sounds, and vice versa, and no weight whatever should be placed on this analogy in historical investigations of language. Fancy and acumen find ample but highly uncertain ground here, and for every ten examples that demonstrate such agreement between sound and meaning, one comes upon a far greater number in which it is absent. It would, however, be equally mistaken to disregard it altogether. For there is no denying that in languages of great antiquity and of extensive and varied word structure, the feeling of such unmistakable agreement forces itself upon us more often than in others. Where this agreement continues to act for centuries on the same nation in a mother tongue that has remained unmixed, it heightens and strengthens the influence of language. For language, everything depends on making the word, through the closest fusion of sound with concept, into a being in its own right, suspended between the human being and the world, at once dependent on and independent of both. This is especially apparent in German and in the languages that depend on it.

text_version.body: In the choice of sounds for concepts, language naturally allows itself to be guided by the clearer and obscurer relations which feeling and imagination, in accordance with the individuality of nations, find among them. Historically, however, this is lost in the times of the invention of language, which no investigation can any longer reach; and through gradual alteration of language, in which now the tone is gradually deflected further from the fundamental tone, now the concept from the fundamental concept, this relation between tone and meaning very often undergoes a complete alteration. Moreover, the feeling, by its nature more indeterminate, on which it rests, is different in different peoples; and precisely those nations which possess more original languages — that is, languages bearing fewer traces of great upheavals — tolerate fewer colliding consonants in their syllables, and consequently are without one more means of determining the character of the word-sound. It is therefore a by no means unusual phenomenon to see strong and even repugnant concepts paired with gentle and soft sounds, and vice versa; and in historical investigations of language no weight at all is to be placed on this analogy. Fantasy and acumen find in this a wide but highly uncertain field; and for ten examples proving such agreement of tone with meaning, one comes upon a far greater number in which it is absent. On the other hand, it would be equally incorrect to turn attention wholly away from it. For it cannot be denied that in languages of great age and of broad and manifold word-structure the feeling of such an unmistakable agreement presents itself more frequently than in others. But where it continues to act for centuries in a mother tongue that has remained unmixed, upon the same nation, it heightens and strengthens the influence of language, in which everything depends on making the word, through the closest fusion of tone with concept, into a distinctive being hovering between man and the world, at once dependent on and independent of both. This is especially visible in German and in the languages dependent on it.

text_version.body: Die Wortlaute gehen zwar zugleich mit ihren Bedeutungen von Geschlecht zu Geschlecht und von Stamm zu Stamm über; da aber der Begriff beweglicher ist, als der sinnlich wahrnehmbare Laut, und nach Verhältnissen, die bald in ihm, bald im Individuum, bald auch in den äussern Umständen liegen, leichtere Uebergänge bildet, so entstehen häufigere Abbeugungen der Bedeutungen, als des Tons. Man kann daher die Wortlaute als Formen ansehen, die aus grauem Alterthume her sich bis auf uns erhalten, und in sich einen mehr oder minder wechselnden Gehalt aufbewahrt haben, durch den sich jedoch immer ein, wenn gleich oft nur lose verknüpfender Faden hindurchschlingt. Schon insofern wird in der Untersuchung des Sprachbaus eine, in der Natur allerdings nicht vorhandene, Trennung des Wortes als Laut und als Begriff nothwendig. Denn die stätige Reihe der Vorstellungen erfordert, ebenso als die stätige Reihe der Töne, Eintheilung in den Wortlauten entsprechende Gedankeneinheiten, durch welche ideale Objecte aufgefasst und verknüpft werden können.

text_version.title: Grundzüge §84 — checked German

text_version.body: Word sounds pass down with their meanings from generation to generation and from tribe to tribe. But the concept is more mobile than the sound perceptible to the senses and makes transitions more readily, depending on circumstances that lie sometimes in the concept itself, sometimes in the individual, and sometimes in external conditions. Meanings therefore shift more frequently than sound does. Word sounds may therefore be regarded as forms that have survived from hoary antiquity down to our own time, preserving within themselves a more or less variable content through which a thread always winds, though it often binds the parts together only loosely. On this ground alone, the study of the structure of language requires a separation of the word as sound from the word as concept, even though this separation does not exist in nature. For the continuous sequence of presentations, just like the continuous sequence of sounds, requires division into units of thought corresponding to the word sounds, by means of which ideal objects can be apprehended and connected.

text_version.body: Word-sounds do indeed pass, together with their meanings, from generation to generation and from tribe to tribe; but since the concept is more mobile than the sensibly perceptible sound, and forms easier transitions according to relations that lie now in it, now in the individual, now also in external circumstances, deflections of meanings arise more frequently than deflections of tone. One may therefore regard word-sounds as forms that have preserved themselves down to us from hoary antiquity, and have preserved within themselves a more or less changing content, through which, however, there always winds a thread, albeit often only a loosely connecting one. Already in this respect there becomes necessary, in the investigation of linguistic structure, a separation of the word as sound and as concept, a separation that admittedly does not exist in nature. For the continuous series of presentations requires, just as does the continuous series of tones, division into units of thought corresponding to the word-sounds, through which ideal Objects can be apprehended and connected.

text_version.body: Jeder solcher Gedankeneinheiten, mithin jedem Worte entspricht ein Gegenstand, entweder ein in der Natur körperlich aufzuzeigender, oder ein durch den Geist, mehr oder minder unabhängig von sinnlicher Wahrnehmung, gebildeter. Denn obgleich das Wort selbst in diesem letzteren Fall dieser Gegenstand ist, so muss man das Wort im Allgemeinen und an sich von dem in einem bestimmten Augenblick von einem bestimmten Individuum gedachten, ebenso wie auf gleiche Weise die ganze Sprache unterscheiden. Das Wort macht, dass sich die Seele den in demselben gegebenen Gegenstand vorstellt. Diese Vorstellung muss von dem Gegenstande unterschieden werden ; sie kann individuell verschieden seyn, und muss es, da sie von allen Seiten bestimmt ist, der Gegenstand aber, als Object, immer nur allgemeiner gefasst werden kann; sie hat neben dem objectiven Theil, der sich auf den Gegenstand bezieht, einen subjectiven, in der Art der Auffassung liegenden, sowohl in der intellectuellen Ansicht, als in der diese begleitenden Empfindung. Wiederum aber bedarf es kaum der Bemerkung, dass diese Trennung nur auf der Abstraction beruht, dass das Wort keine Stätte ausser dem Denken haben kann, und ebensowenig der Gegenstand desselben, wenn dieser ein unkörperlicher ist, dass es selbst jedesmal ganz von dem Geiste hervorgebracht wird, dass es wahrhaft seine Vollständigkeit und Individualität nur in dem jedesmaligen Denken hat, und als Bestandtheil der Sprache, als Object der Sprachuntersuchung, nur eine allgemeine, auf verschiedene, jedoch durch seine Natur beschränkte Weise individualisirbare Form ist. Auch bei sinnlichen Gegenständen bleibt dies der Fall, da niemals sie geradezu, sondern immer nur diejenige Vorstellung von ihnen der Seele gegenwärtig werden, welche das Wort von ihnen giebt.

text_version.body: To each such unit of thought, and hence to every word, there corresponds an object, either one that can be pointed out in corporeal form in nature or one formed by the mind more or less independently of sense perception. For although in the latter case the word itself is this object, we must distinguish the word in general and in itself from the word thought by a particular individual at a particular moment, and make the same distinction for language as a whole. The word causes the soul to form a presentation of the object given in it. This presentation must be distinguished from the object. It can and must vary from one individual to another, since it is determinate in every respect, whereas the object, considered as object, can only ever be grasped in more general terms. Alongside the objective part, which relates to the object, the presentation has a subjective part that lies in the mode of apprehension, both in the intellectual view and in the feeling that accompanies it. Again, it hardly needs saying that this separation rests solely on abstraction. The word can have no place outside thinking, and neither can its object if that object is incorporeal. The mind produces the word in its entirety on every occasion. The word truly has its completeness and individuality only in each act of thinking, and as a constituent of language and an object of linguistic inquiry it is merely a general form that can be individualised in various ways within the limits set by its nature. The same holds for objects of sense, since what becomes present to the soul is always the presentation that the word gives of them, never the objects themselves directly.

text_version.body: Darauf dass jedes Wort einer Sprache eine gewisse Weite für die Möglichkeit verschiedenartiger Vorstellungen besitzt, beruht die Möglichkeit, dass sich in derselben Sprache die Vorstellungsweisen ganz verschiedener Individualitäten der Menschen und Zeiten vereinigen, und bei der Einerleiheit der allgemeinen Sprache dennoch jedes (50.) seine eigene haben kann. Denn das Verstehen ist kein Zusammentreffen der Vorstellungsweisen in einem untheilbaren Punkt, sondern ein Zusammentreffen von Gedankensphären, von welchen der allgemeinere Theil sich deckt, der individuellere überragt. Dadurch wird das geistige Fortschreiten des Menschengeschlechts möglich, indem jede gewonnene Erweiterung des Denkens in den Besitz Anderer übergehen kann, ohne in ihnen der Freiheit Fesseln anzulegen, welche zur Aneignung, und zu neuer Erweiterung nothwendig ist, und indem zugleich die Formen des Denkens, die Sprachen, die Veränderungen erfahren, welche ihnen, wie Allem, was an irdische Erscheinung gebunden ist, in ihrem Entwicklungsgange vorgeschrieben sind. In jeder Bedeutung eines Worts ist also die Aufmerksamkeit darauf zu richten, wie es die individuelle Vorstellungsweise frei lässt und bestimmt, und es kann eine Geschichte der Wörter und ihrer einzelnen Bedeutungen durch alle die verschiedenen Arten durchgeführt werden, wie sie genommen und gebraucht worden sind.

text_version.body: Each word in a language allows a certain latitude for different presentations. This makes it possible for the modes of presentation of very different individuals and ages to come together in the same language, and for each to have a language of its own even while the common language remains the same (50). For understanding is no coincidence of modes of presentation at an indivisible point. It is a meeting of spheres of thought whose more general parts coincide and whose more individual parts extend beyond the overlap. This makes possible the intellectual progress of humankind. Every advance in the scope of thinking can pass into the possession of others without fettering the freedom they need to make it their own and extend it further. At the same time, the forms of thinking, the languages, undergo the changes prescribed in the course of their development for them, as for everything bound to appear on earth. In every meaning of a word, then, we must attend to how it leaves the individual mode of presentation free and how it determines it. A history of words and their particular meanings can trace all the different ways in which they have been understood and used.

Through this the mental progress of the human race becomes possible, in that every enlargement of thinking that has been won can pass into the possession of others without laying fetters in them on the freedom that is necessary for appropriation and for new enlargement, and in that at the same time the forms of thinking, the languages, undergo the changes prescribed for them, as for everything bound to earthly appearance, in their course of development. In every meaning of a word, therefore, attention is to be directed to how it leaves the individual mode of presentation free and how it determines it, and a history of words and of their individual meanings can be carried through all the different ways in which they have been taken and used.

text_version.body: Der zu der Klarheit und Bestimmtheit des Worts gesteigerte Begriff ist allemal der Erfolg des Zusammenwirkens der ganzen Seelenkraft, und da es nun die Eigenthümlichkeit des Wortes ist, diesen Begriff durch den Ton, wie durch einen elektrischen Schlag, hervorzurufen, so strahlt die Wirkung desselben durch die ganze Seele nach allen Richtungen hin. Die Einheit einer Kraft lässt sich nicht in Theile zerspalten, indess leuchten in der Bildung und dem Einfluss des Worts doch drei grosse und hauptsächliche Beziehungen hervor, unter denen jedes betrachtet und geprüft werden kann: seine logische Construction, seine sinnliche Geltung und sein Eindruck auf das Gefühl. Jedes dieser drei Stücke erscheint aber wieder in dem Wort auf eine zwiefache Weise, da man die Vorstellung des Gegenstandes selbst (85.) von derjenigen unterscheiden muss, welche das Wort, seiner Bildung und Entstehung nach, von ihm giebt, und von diesen beiden Vorstellungen keine die andere aufhebt, sondern beide in ein gewisses Verhältniss zu einander treten.

text_version.body: A concept raised to the clarity and determinacy of a word is always the result of the whole power of the soul working together. Since it is characteristic of the word to evoke this concept through sound, as if by an electric shock, its effect radiates in every direction through the whole soul. The unity of a power cannot be split into parts. Yet three principal aspects stand out in the formation and influence of the word, and each word can be considered and examined under them. They are its logical construction, its sensory import and its impression on feeling. Each of these three aspects in turn appears in the word in two ways, since we must distinguish the presentation of the object itself (85) from the presentation the word gives of it by virtue of its formation and origin. Neither presentation cancels the other, and the two enter into a definite relation with each other.

text_version.body: Das Wort giebt dem Begriffe Gestaltung, und durch den Ton, unmittelbar vor dem Ohr, und mittelbar vor allen sinnlichen Kräften der Seele, sinnliche Geltung. Das Wort fasst jeden Begriff, als einen allgemeinen auf, bezeichnet, streng genommen, immer Classen der Wirklichkeit, selbst wenn es ein Eigenname ist, da es alsdann alle, der Zeit und dem Räume nach, verschiedenen Zustände des Bezeichneten (ihn als eine Classe vorstellend, in welcher er in allen diesen Zuständen eben so, wie verschiedene Individuen in einem Gattungsbegriffe, enthalten ist) zusammenfasst. Es macht aber sich selbst, und mithin auch den in ihm enthaltenen Begriff zu einem Individuum der Sprache. Es kann daher Jenen nur von einem einzelnen Standpunkte aus nehmen, darf jedoch nichts aufgeben von seinem Gehalt, und dies wird erreicht, indem das Wort der Seele nach jenen drei Hauptbeziehungen hin eine bestimmte Anregung ertheilt, durch welche die Begriffserzeugung zwar vollständig, aber von einer scharf bestimmten Seite aus geschieht. Dadurch entstehen in den gleichbedeutenden Wörtern mehrerer Sprachen verschiedene Vorstellungen desselben Gegenstandes, und diese Beschaffenheit des Worts trägt hauptsächlich dazu bei, dass jede Sprache eine eigne Weltansicht gewährt.

text_version.body: The word gives shape to the concept and, through sound, gives it sensory import directly for the ear and indirectly for all the sensory powers of the soul. The word apprehends every concept as a general one and, strictly speaking, always designates classes of reality. This holds even for a proper name, since it gathers together all the states of what it designates that differ in time and space, presenting it as a class in which it is contained in all these states just as different individuals are contained in a generic concept. Yet the word makes itself, and hence also the concept it contains, an individual within language. It can therefore take up the concept only from a single standpoint, yet it must give up none of the concept's content. The word achieves this by giving the soul a definite stimulus along those three principal lines, so that the concept is produced in full, but from a sharply defined side. This is how words with the same meaning in several languages give rise to different presentations of the same object. This property of the word is a principal reason why each language affords a view of the world of its own.

The word grasps every concept as a general one, designates, strictly taken, always classes of reality, even when it is a proper name, since it then comprehends together all the states of what is designated, different in time and space (presenting it as a class in which it is contained in all these states just as different individuals are contained in a generic concept). But it makes itself, and consequently also the concept contained in it, into an individual of language. It can therefore take that concept only from a single standpoint, yet it must give up nothing of its content, and this is achieved in that the word imparts to the soul, in the directions of those three principal relations, a determinate excitation, through which the generation of the concept does indeed take place completely, but from a sharply determinate side. Through this there arise, in the words of several languages that have the same meaning, different presentations of the same object, and this constitution of the word contributes principally to each language affording a world-view of its own.

text_version.body: So wie die Sprache und in ihr das Wort die individuelle Natur der Welt verallgemeinert, so vergeistigt sie die in äusserer und innerer Wahrnehmung stoffartige. So wie aber das Wort selbst wieder in der Sprache Individuum wird, so wird es auch in ihr körperlich durch Annahme des Tons, und dient dem Geiste zum Stoff neuer Wirksamkeit. Das eine und das andre geschieht aber zugleich und in untheilbarer Einheit, synthetisch, und Allgemeinheit und Individualitaet, Geistigkeit und Stoffartigkeit durchdringen einander im Wort, was, da jene Begriffe sich sonst aufheben würden, nur dadurch möglich ist, dass das Wort, als Sprachbestandtheil ausser der Seele gedacht, nichts als eine Anregung zum Denken, als vollendeter Begriff in der Seele gedacht, das Denken selbst ist, und der menschlich geistigen Kraft dies unaufhörliche Entwickeln und Rückkehren des Allgemeinen und Unsinnlichen aus Individuellem und Sinnlichem und in dasselbe eigenthümlich angehört. Blicken wir nun auf die oben (87.) erwähnten drei Hauptrichtungen zurück, nach welchen hin das Wort die Seele anregt, so kann dasselbe nur insofern sinnliche und Empfindungsgeltung besitzen, als es sich dieselbe auf dem Gebiete der Intellectualität zu erhalten vermag. Dies geschieht aber nur, indem dieser Sinnen- und Gefühlsgehalt zugleich, und wieder synthetisch, als Stoff vernichtet und als Form erhalten wird, was das Werk der Einbildungskraft ist, der Vermittlerin der entgegengesetzten Naturen in der Menschheit. Da nun auch der Verstandesgehalt des Wortes sich nur auf ihrem Gebiete mit dem sinnlichen vereinigen kann, so ist dieses Gebiet eigentlich die Sphäre, in welcher das Wort schwebt, indem die Einbildungskraft die Gesammtkräfte der Seele zum Hervorbringen oder Verstehen desselben zusammenfasst.

text_version.body: Just as language, and the word within it, generalises the individual nature of the world, so it spiritualises that nature which has the character of material in outward and inward perception. Yet just as the word itself in turn becomes an individual in language, it also takes on corporeal form in language by assuming sound, and serves the mind as material for further activity. Both take place at once and in indivisible unity, synthetically, and generality and individuality, spirituality and materiality interpenetrate in the word. Since these concepts would otherwise cancel one another, this is possible only because the word, conceived as a constituent of language outside the soul, is merely a stimulus to thinking, whereas conceived as a completed concept in the soul it is thinking itself. It is characteristic of the power of the human mind that the general and the non-sensory should ceaselessly develop out of the individual and the sensory and return into them. Returning now to the three principal directions mentioned above (87) in which the word stimulates the soul, we see that the word can have import for sense and feeling only insofar as it can retain that import in the intellectual domain. This happens only when the content of sense and feeling is at once, and again synthetically, destroyed as material and preserved as form. This is the work of the imagination, which mediates between the opposed natures in humankind. Since the intellectual content of the word can unite with the sensory content only in the domain of the imagination, this domain is properly the sphere in which the word hovers, as the imagination gathers all the powers of the soul to produce or understand it.

text_version.body: Beides liegt unläugbar in der Sprache und in jedem einzelnen ihrer Wörter; indem es die Individualitaet der Sprechenden war, hat es sich an die Laute geheftet, und kehrt durch sie in die lebendige Individualitaet zurück. Denn die wundervolle Art der Verkörperung einer geistigen Zeugung, welche eine gleiche im Andren hervorbringt, ist ja die wahrhaft eigenthümliche Natur der Sprache, und ruht vorzüglich auf ihrem Hauptbestandtheil, dem Wort. Die Form ist aber noch wichtiger, als die Materie. Denn sie hängt an der ganzen Sprache, und wenn daher diese auch als todte oder fremde von einer sehr verschiedenen Individualitaet aufgefasst wird, nöthtigt sie dieselbe dennoch, ihre Anschauungsweise anzunehmen, indem sie sie von allen Seiten mit derselben umstrickt. Die Materie vermag nicht nur dies nicht, sondern die besondere Vorstellungsweise des Gegenstandes bleibt auch nicht einmal immer im Worte erkennbar, oder wird wenigstens nicht mehr so, als bei dessen Entstehung gefühlt; die Individualitaet des Worts geht in der Allgemeinheit des Begriffes verloren. Ich habe hierauf schon im Vorigen (87.) in dem Unterschiede zwischen der Vorstellung von dem Gegenstande und der des Wortes von ihm hingedeutet. Dieser Unterschied wird freilich nur dadurch möglich, dass das Wort, als verkörperter Begriff, nach und nach von sehr verschiedenen Individualitäten verschiedenen Anschauungsweisen angepasst wird, in welchen der jedesmalige Gebrauch den Gegenstand gar nicht so darstellt, als der erste Erfinder; aber so verstanden lassen sich ganze Reihen von Beispielen davon aufzeigen. Die Ausdrücke für körperliche Gegenstände sind gewiss zum grössten Theile aus Eigenschaften entstanden, die an denselben vorzüglich auffielen, und sind nichts anders, als zu Adjectiven gewordene Substantiva, unsinnliche Begriffe werden metaphorisch nach körperlichen bezeichnet, grammatische, bloss die Verbindung der Rede bestimmende, nach Wörtern für Sachbegriffe. In allen diesen Fällen geht sehr häufig, ja mehrentheils, der Charakter der ursprünglichen Bezeichnung unter, und der Begriff des Gegenstandes tritt allgemein, oder anders genommen, an die Stelle. Schwerlich ist bei dem Indischen dwipa für Elephant immer an die Eigenschaft des doppelten Trinkens durch den Rüssel und den Mund gedacht worden, wenigen, die das deutsche Vernunft und zurück gebrauchen, fällt es ein, dass jenes von vernehmen, dieses von Rücken kommt. Viele Wörter, die ehemals gar keine solche Nebenbedeutung hatten, werden späterhin nur scherzhafter, ironischer oder verächtlicher Weise gebraucht. So wechselt die Materie des Worts ; selbst zwischen demselben Ton und demselben durch ihn bezeichneten Gegenstand findet der Geist einen Spielraum bequemer Weite, verschieden nuancirte Vorstellungsarten einzuschieben; eigentlich aber wird unter demselben Schall jedesmal ein andres Wort ausgesprochen. Denn nur das wirklich gedachte oder gesprochene ist das eigentliche Wort, das sich gleichsam todt in der Sprache forterbende nur die immer wieder, und immer etwas anders belebte Hülle. In dem gedachten oder gesprochenen ist allemal Materie und Form zugleich durch den Charakter des Worts und der Sprache und durch den des Sprechenden bestimmt.

text_version.body: Both are undeniably present in language and in every one of its words. As the individuality of the speakers, they have attached themselves to the sounds and through them return to living individuality. For this marvellous way of embodying a begetting of the mind that brings forth a like begetting in another person is precisely what is truly distinctive about language, and it depends chiefly on its principal constituent, the word. Form, however, is even more important than matter. For form inheres in the whole language. Thus even when a person of very different individuality apprehends it as a dead or foreign language, it still compels that person to adopt its mode of intuition by surrounding them with it on every side. Matter has no such power. The particular mode of presenting the object does not even always remain discernible in the word, or at least is no longer felt as it was when the word arose. The individuality of the word is lost in the generality of the concept. I already pointed to this above (87) in distinguishing the presentation of the object from the presentation the word gives of it. This distinction is admittedly possible only because the word, as an embodied concept, is gradually adapted by people of very different individualities to different modes of intuition, in which each new use presents the object quite differently from the way its first inventor did. Understood in this way, whole series of examples can be adduced. Expressions for corporeal objects have certainly arisen for the most part from properties that were especially striking in those objects and are simply nouns that have become adjectives. Non-sensory concepts are designated metaphorically in terms of corporeal ones, and grammatical concepts, which merely determine the way discourse is connected, are designated after words for concepts of things. In all these cases the character of the original designation is very often, indeed usually, lost, and the concept of the object takes its place, understood in general terms or in some other way. The Indian word *dwîpa* for ‘elephant’ can hardly have always prompted people to think of the animal's twofold manner of drinking through trunk and mouth. Few who use the German *Vernunft* and *zurück* think of the former as coming from *vernehmen* or the latter from *Rücken*. Many words that formerly had no such secondary meaning are later used only jocularly, ironically or contemptuously. This is how the matter of the word changes. Even between the same sound and the same object designated by it, the mind finds ample room to introduce differently nuanced modes of presentation. Strictly speaking, however, a different word is uttered each time under cover of the same audible sound. For the word proper is only the word actually thought or spoken. What is handed down in language as if dead is merely the shell, brought to life again and again, and always a little differently. In the word as thought or spoken, matter and form are always determined together by the character of the word and the language, and by that of the speaker.

As the individuality of the speakers, they have attached themselves to the sounds and through them return to living individuality. For this marvellous way of embodying a begetting of the mind that brings forth a like begetting in another person is precisely what is truly distinctive about language, and it depends chiefly on its principal constituent, the word. Form, however, is even more important than matter. For form inheres in the whole language. Thus even when a person of very different individuality apprehends it as a dead or foreign language, it still compels that person to adopt its mode of intuition by surrounding them with it on every side. Matter has no such power. The particular mode of presenting the object does not even always remain discernible in the word, or at least is no longer felt as it was when the word arose. The individuality of the word is lost in the generality of the concept. I already pointed to this above (§87) in distinguishing the presentation of the object from the presentation the word gives of it. This distinction is admittedly possible only because the word, as an embodied concept, is gradually adapted by people of very different individualities to different modes of intuition, in which each new use presents the object quite differently from the way its first inventor did. Understood in this way, whole series of examples can be adduced. Expressions for corporeal objects have certainly arisen for the most part from properties that were especially striking in those objects. They are simply nouns that have become adjectives. Non-sensory concepts are designated metaphorically in terms of corporeal ones. Grammatical concepts, which merely govern the linking of discourse, are designated after words for concepts of things. In all these cases the character of the original designation is very often, indeed usually, lost, and the concept of the object takes its place, understood in general terms or in some other way. It is unlikely that the Indian word *dwipa* ‘elephant’ has always called to mind the quality of drinking twice, through the trunk and through the mouth. Few people who use the German words *Vernunft* ‘reason’ and *zurück* ‘back’ think that the former comes from *vernehmen* ‘perceive’ and the latter from *Rücken* ‘back’. Many words that formerly had no such secondary meaning are later used only jocularly, ironically or contemptuously. This is how the matter of the word changes. Even between the same sound and the same object designated by it, the mind finds ample room to introduce differently nuanced modes of presentation. Strictly speaking, however, a different word is uttered each time under cover of the same audible sound. For the word proper is only the word actually thought or spoken. What is handed down in language as if dead is merely the shell, brought to life again and again, and always a little differently. In the word as thought or spoken, matter and form are always determined together by the character of the word and the language, and by that of the speaker.

text_version.body: Wenn sich in den Wörtern einer Sprache die ursprüngliche Anschauungsweise der Gegenstände nach und nach verwischt, so ist nicht zu läugnen, dass eine gewisse Individualitaet und sinnliche Lebendigkeit in ihr untergeht. Aber es ist darum nicht zu sagen, dass sie nicht vielleicht dadurch auf der andren Seite gewinnt. Denn die Vorzüge der Sprachen werden nicht durch den partiellen Reichthum von Bildern und Begriffen bestimmt, den sie der Seele zuführen, sondern durch ihre Einwirkung auf das Denken und Empfinden überhaupt. So gewährt z. B. die (90.) angeführte Bezeichnung der Gegenstände durch ihre Eigenschaften, solange sie in einer Sprache lebendig ist, grössere Fülle der Anschauung, aber sie hat auch, ohne anderer geringerer zu erwähnen, den Nachtheil, dass sie die Freiheit beim Vorstellen des Gegenstandes zu einseitig beschränkt, und, Substantiva zu sichtlich aus Adjectiven bildend, die Uebereinstimmung stört, in welcher die Sprache, der Natur auch in ihrer Form folgend, zum Ausdruck selbständiger Wesen in dieser auch mit Selbständigkeit begabte Wörter gebrauchen muss. Viel angemessener wirkt das Uebereinkommen des Begriffs mit dem Laut nach dunklem Verwandtschaftsgefühl (83.), da die Seele dadurch gestimmt und geleitet, aber nicht in der Weise der Vorstellung beschränkt wird. Wenn die Sprachuntersuchung sich auf diese Beziehungen richtet, sie in den Wörtern aufsucht, ohne sie hineinzulegen, und auf diese Weise den immer der Muttersprache, auch unbewusst, verwandten Sprachsinn der Nation weckt, und dadurch klarere Einsicht und ein feineres Gefühl der Sprache bewirkt; so kann die ursprüngliche Individualitaet der Wörter wieder heller ans Licht treten, und ordnet sich nun, ohne weiter zu schaden, der durch die Zeit freier und intellectueller gewordenen Auffassung der Gegenstände unter.

text_version.body: When the original mode of intuition of objects gradually becomes blurred in the words of a language, a certain individuality and sensory vividness undeniably perish in it. The language may nevertheless gain in another respect by this very process. For what determines the merits of languages is their effect on thinking and feeling in general, beyond the particular riches of images and concepts they bring to the soul. For example, the designation of objects by their properties, mentioned in §90, affords a greater fullness of intuition as long as it remains alive in a language. But among its disadvantages is that it restricts freedom in forming a presentation of the object by favouring one side too much. By forming nouns too visibly from adjectives, it also disrupts the correspondence with nature that requires language, if it is to follow nature in its very form, to use words endowed with independence in that form to express independent beings. The accord of concept and sound through an obscure feeling of kinship (83) has a much more fitting effect, since it attunes and guides the soul while leaving its mode of presentation unrestricted. If linguistic inquiry attends to these relations, looks for them in words without reading them into the words, and in this way awakens the nation's sense of language, which always has an affinity with its mother tongue even without conscious awareness, it brings about clearer insight and a finer feeling for language. The original individuality of words can then come to light again more distinctly and, without doing further harm, take its place under a mode of apprehending objects that has grown freer and more intellectual with time.

text_version.body: If in the words of a language the original mode of intuiting objects gradually becomes effaced, it is not to be denied that a certain individuality and sensible liveliness perishes in it. But it is not on that account to be said that it does not perhaps gain thereby on the other side. For the merits of languages are not determined by the partial wealth of images and concepts that they supply to the soul, but by their effect on thinking and feeling in general. Thus, for example, the designation of objects by their properties, cited at (90.), affords, so long as it is alive in a language, greater fullness of intuition, but it also has, not to mention other lesser ones, the disadvantage that it restricts too one-sidedly the freedom in presenting the object, and, forming substantives too visibly from adjectives, disturbs the agreement in which language, following nature also in its form, must, for the expression of independent beings, use in that form words also endowed with independence. Much more appropriately acts the agreement of the concept with the sound according to an obscure feeling of kinship (83.), since the soul is thereby attuned and guided, but not restricted in the manner of presentation. If linguistic investigation directs itself to these relations, seeks them out in the words without putting them into them, and in this way awakens the linguistic sense of the nation, which is always akin, even unconsciously, to the mother tongue, and thereby effects clearer insight and a finer feeling for the language, then the original individuality of the words can step forth again more brightly into the light, and now subordinates itself, without doing further harm, to the apprehension of objects that has in the course of time become freer and more intellectual.
